2.5 Domain: User entity and UserDetailsService

@Entity
@Table(name = "app_user")
public class AppUser {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(unique = true, nullable = false)
    private String username;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String passwordHash;           // BCrypt hash, never plain text

    private boolean enabled = true;

    @ElementCollection(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)
    @CollectionTable(name = "app_user_role", joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "user_id"))
    @Column(name = "role")
    private Set<String> roles = new HashSet<>();   // e.g. "OPERATOR", "ADMIN"

    // getters / setters omitted for brevity
}
public interface AppUserRepository extends JpaRepository<AppUser, Long> {
    Optional<AppUser> findByUsername(String username);
}
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class DbUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {

    private final AppUserRepository repo;

    @Override
    public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) throws UsernameNotFoundException {
        AppUser u = repo.findByUsername(username)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException("User not found"));
        return User.withUsername(u.getUsername())
                .password(u.getPasswordHash())
                .disabled(!u.isEnabled())
                .roles(u.getRoles().toArray(String[]::new))   // adds "ROLE_" prefix automatically
                .build();
    }
}

2.6 JwtService (jjwt 0.12 API)

@Service
public class JwtService {

    private final SecretKey key;
    private final Duration accessTtl;
    private final String issuer;

    public JwtService(@Value("${app.jwt.secret}") String base64Secret,
                      @Value("${app.jwt.access-token-ttl}") Duration accessTtl,
                      @Value("${app.jwt.issuer}") String issuer) {
        this.key = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(Decoders.BASE64.decode(base64Secret)); // HS256 needs >= 32 bytes
        this.accessTtl = accessTtl;
        this.issuer = issuer;
    }

    public String generateAccessToken(UserDetails user) {
        Instant now = Instant.now();
        List<String> roles = user.getAuthorities().stream()
                .map(GrantedAuthority::getAuthority)
                .toList();
        return Jwts.builder()
                .id(UUID.randomUUID().toString())        // jti, needed if you ever want to revoke a token
                .issuer(issuer)
                .subject(user.getUsername())
                .claim("roles", roles)
                .issuedAt(Date.from(now))
                .expiration(Date.from(now.plus(accessTtl)))
                .signWith(key)                           // algorithm inferred from key → HS256
                .compact();
    }

    /** Verifies signature + exp + iss. Throws JwtException (ExpiredJwtException, SignatureException...) on failure. */
    public Claims parseAndValidate(String token) {
        return Jwts.parser()
                .verifyWith(key)
                .requireIssuer(issuer)
                .clockSkewSeconds(30)
                .build()
                .parseSignedClaims(token)    // rejects unsigned (alg=none) tokens
                .getPayload();
    }

    public String extractUsername(Claims claims) {
        return claims.getSubject();
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public List<String> extractRoles(Claims claims) {
        return claims.get("roles", List.class);
    }
}

2.7 JwtAuthFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter

OncePerRequestFilter makes sure the filter runs once per request, even when the request is forwarded or dispatched again for errors or async work.

@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class JwtAuthFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    private static final String BEARER = "Bearer ";
    private final JwtService jwtService;

    @Override
    protected boolean shouldNotFilter(HttpServletRequest request) {
        return request.getServletPath().startsWith("/api/auth/");   // login/refresh don't need a token
    }

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
                                    HttpServletResponse response,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {

        String header = request.getHeader(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION);
        if (header == null || !header.startsWith(BEARER)) {
            chain.doFilter(request, response);          // no token → stays anonymous → AuthorizationFilter decides
            return;
        }

        String token = header.substring(BEARER.length());
        try {
            Claims claims = jwtService.parseAndValidate(token);

            if (SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() == null) {
                List<SimpleGrantedAuthority> authorities = jwtService.extractRoles(claims).stream()
                        .map(SimpleGrantedAuthority::new)
                        .toList();

                // Stateless: we trust the signed claims and skip the DB lookup.
                // To pick up "user disabled" immediately, load UserDetails here (costs one DB/cache hit).
                UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken auth =
                        UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.authenticated(
                                jwtService.extractUsername(claims), null, authorities);
                auth.setDetails(new WebAuthenticationDetailsSource().buildDetails(request));

                SecurityContext context = SecurityContextHolder.createEmptyContext();
                context.setAuthentication(auth);
                SecurityContextHolder.setContext(context);
            }
        } catch (ExpiredJwtException ex) {
            request.setAttribute("auth_error", "TOKEN_EXPIRED");    // read by AuthenticationEntryPoint (see D3)
        } catch (JwtException | IllegalArgumentException ex) {
            request.setAttribute("auth_error", "TOKEN_INVALID");
        }
        chain.doFilter(request, response);
    }
}

Why chain.doFilter even on failure? The context stays unauthenticated. AuthorizationFilter then throws AccessDeniedException for protected URLs, ExceptionTranslationFilter sees an anonymous user, and calls the AuthenticationEntryPoint, which returns a clean 401. Error handling stays in one place.

Pitfall: when JwtAuthFilter is a @Component, Spring Boot also registers it as a normal servlet filter, so it runs twice: once outside the security chain and once inside it. Stop that with a FilterRegistrationBean that sets setEnabled(false) (below), or don't annotate the filter and create it with new in the config.

2.8 SecurityConfig (Spring Security 6 lambda DSL)

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@EnableMethodSecurity                       // enables @PreAuthorize/@PostAuthorize (see D4)
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class SecurityConfig {

    private final JwtAuthFilter jwtAuthFilter;
    private final JsonAuthEntryPoint authEntryPoint;          // D3
    private final JsonAccessDeniedHandler accessDeniedHandler; // D3

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain apiChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .securityMatcher("/api/**")
            .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)            // stateless + bearer header → no CSRF risk
            .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())                  // uses CorsConfigurationSource bean
            .sessionManagement(sm -> sm.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/incidents/**").hasAnyRole("OPERATOR", "SUPERVISOR", "ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/incidents/**").hasAnyRole("OPERATOR", "ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/api/incidents/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers("/api/sensors/**").hasAuthority("sensor:read")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .exceptionHandling(ex -> ex
                .authenticationEntryPoint(authEntryPoint)     // 401
                .accessDeniedHandler(accessDeniedHandler))    // 403
            .headers(h -> h
                .contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> csp.policyDirectives("default-src 'self'"))
                .frameOptions(HeadersConfigurer.FrameOptionsConfig::deny))
            .addFilterBefore(jwtAuthFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class);
        return http.build();
    }

    @Bean
    PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12);    // strength 12 ≈ 250 ms/hash: slow on purpose
        // or PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder() → "{bcrypt}$2a$..." (allows algorithm migration)
    }

    /**
     * Exposes the AuthenticationManager Boot builds. With exactly one UserDetailsService
     * and one PasswordEncoder bean, Boot wires a DaoAuthenticationProvider for us.
     */
    @Bean
    AuthenticationManager authenticationManager(AuthenticationConfiguration config) throws Exception {
        return config.getAuthenticationManager();
    }

    @Bean
    CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource() {
        CorsConfiguration cfg = new CorsConfiguration();
        cfg.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://command-centre.smartcity.gov.in"));
        cfg.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"));
        cfg.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Authorization", "Content-Type", "X-Correlation-Id"));
        cfg.setMaxAge(3600L);
        UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource src = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
        src.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", cfg);
        return src;
    }

    /** Stop Boot from also registering the @Component filter in the plain servlet chain. */
    @Bean
    FilterRegistrationBean<JwtAuthFilter> jwtFilterRegistration(JwtAuthFilter filter) {
        FilterRegistrationBean<JwtAuthFilter> reg = new FilterRegistrationBean<>(filter);
        reg.setEnabled(false);
        return reg;
    }
}

2.9 AuthController: login endpoint

public record LoginRequest(@NotBlank String username, @NotBlank String password) {}
public record TokenResponse(String accessToken, String refreshToken, long expiresInSeconds) {}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/auth")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class AuthController {

    private final AuthenticationManager authenticationManager;
    private final JwtService jwtService;
    private final RefreshTokenService refreshTokenService;   // stores hashed refresh tokens in DB/Redis (see D5)

    @PostMapping("/login")
    public ResponseEntity<TokenResponse> login(@Valid @RequestBody LoginRequest req) {
        Authentication auth = authenticationManager.authenticate(
                UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated(req.username(), req.password()));
        // Throws BadCredentialsException / DisabledException → handled by @RestControllerAdvice (this is in the MVC layer)

        UserDetails user = (UserDetails) auth.getPrincipal();
        String access = jwtService.generateAccessToken(user);
        String refresh = refreshTokenService.issue(user.getUsername());
        return ResponseEntity.ok(new TokenResponse(access, refresh, 900));
    }
}
@RestControllerAdvice
public class AuthExceptionAdvice {
    @ExceptionHandler(BadCredentialsException.class)
    public ProblemDetail badCredentials() {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, "Invalid username or password");
    }
    @ExceptionHandler(DisabledException.class)
    public ProblemDetail disabled() {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, "Account disabled");
    }
}

2.10 Production alternative: OAuth2 Resource Server (no custom filter)

When an external IdP issues the tokens (Keycloak, Azure AD, Okta), you don't write a filter or a JwtService. Spring's BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter with a NimbusJwtDecoder validates RS256 signatures against the IdP's JWKS endpoint.

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://keycloak.smartcity.local/realms/smartcity   # discovers jwks_uri, validates iss + exp
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain resourceServer(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
        .sessionManagement(sm -> sm.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(j -> j.jwtAuthenticationConverter(keycloakRolesConverter())));
    return http.build();
}

@Bean
Converter<Jwt, AbstractAuthenticationToken> keycloakRolesConverter() {
    return jwt -> {
        Map<String, Object> realmAccess = jwt.getClaimAsMap("realm_access");
        @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
        Collection<String> roles = realmAccess == null ? List.of()
                : (Collection<String>) realmAccess.getOrDefault("roles", List.of());
        List<GrantedAuthority> authorities = roles.stream()
                .map(r -> (GrantedAuthority) new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + r.toUpperCase()))
                .toList();
        return new JwtAuthenticationToken(jwt, authorities, jwt.getClaimAsString("preferred_username"));
    };
}

2.11 How authorization works in web apps

Layer 1: URL rules (authorizeHttpRequests), checked by AuthorizationFilter through a RequestMatcherDelegatingAuthorizationManager. Rules are checked in order, first match wins, so put specific rules before general ones and finish with anyRequest().

Layer 2: method security (@PreAuthorize). This gives finer, business-level checks such as "an operator can only edit incidents in their own zone". See D4.

Layer 3: domain/data-level filtering. Queries scoped to the user, e.g. WHERE zone_id IN (:userZones), or Hibernate filters and row-level security.

Roles vs authorities

Role Authority
What it is Coarse-grained job function Fine-grained permission
Example ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_OPERATOR incident:write, sensor:read, SCOPE_profile
In code hasRole("ADMIN") → checks for authority "ROLE_ADMIN" hasAuthority("incident:write") → exact string match
Underneath Also just a GrantedAuthority, with the ROLE_ prefix convention GrantedAuthority

Common pattern: users get roles, roles map to permissions (a role→permission table), and both go into the authorities. Code checks permissions, which keeps role changes out of the code. RoleHierarchy lets ADMIN > SUPERVISOR > OPERATOR, so admins inherit everything automatically:

@Bean
static RoleHierarchy roleHierarchy() {
    return RoleHierarchyImpl.fromHierarchy("""
        ROLE_ADMIN > ROLE_SUPERVISOR
        ROLE_SUPERVISOR > ROLE_OPERATOR
        """);
}

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why addFilterBefore(UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)? It's a well-known anchor in the chain. The authentication has to be in the context before AuthorizationFilter runs, and before form login would try anything.
  • Why BCrypt and not SHA-256? BCrypt is salted and deliberately slow, with a tunable cost. SHA-256 is fast, so it can be brute-forced on GPUs. Argon2 and PBKDF2 are also acceptable.
  • How do you support two auth mechanisms (JWT for UI, basic for actuator)? Define two SecurityFilterChain beans with different securityMatchers and @Order.
  • What replaced WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter? Component-based config: SecurityFilterChain beans, WebSecurityCustomizer, and the AuthenticationManager from AuthenticationConfiguration.
D3 Handling exceptions in authentication and authorization. Hexaware
  • 401: implement AuthenticationEntryPoint. It runs when an unauthenticated user hits a protected resource (missing, invalid or expired token).
  • 403: implement AccessDeniedHandler. It runs when the user is authenticated but lacks the required role.
  • Why @ControllerAdvice doesn't catch these: security filters run before the DispatcherServlet, so exceptions thrown there never reach the controller layer. ExceptionTranslationFilter turns them into calls to the entry point and the handler. One exception: method-security AccessDeniedException thrown from a @PreAuthorize inside the controller or service can reach @ControllerAdvice. For JWT parsing errors in your own filter, catch them and write the response yourself, or delegate to a HandlerExceptionResolver.
http.exceptionHandling(ex -> ex
    .authenticationEntryPoint((req, res, e) -> {
        res.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED);
        res.setContentType("application/json");
        res.getWriter().write("{\"error\":\"Unauthorized\",\"message\":\"" + e.getMessage() + "\"}");
    })
    .accessDeniedHandler((req, res, e) -> {
        res.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_FORBIDDEN);
        res.setContentType("application/json");
        res.getWriter().write("{\"error\":\"Forbidden\"}");
    }));

3.1 Where security exceptions come from

Request ─► [Security filters ............................] ─► DispatcherServlet ─► Controller
            │                                         │           │
            │  JwtAuthFilter (our code)               │           └─ @PreAuthorize → AccessDeniedException
            │  BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter        │              (thrown inside MVC; @ControllerAdvice
            │     → AuthenticationException           │               CAN see this one, see 3.4)
            │  ExceptionTranslationFilter ◄───────────┤
            │     catches exceptions thrown BELOW it  │
            │  AuthorizationFilter → AccessDeniedException

ExceptionTranslationFilter logic:

try { chain.doFilter() }              // runs AuthorizationFilter and everything after
catch (AuthenticationException e)  → sendStartAuthentication() → AuthenticationEntryPoint.commence()   → 401
catch (AccessDeniedException e)
      if user is anonymous / remember-me → sendStartAuthentication() → AuthenticationEntryPoint → 401
      else                               → AccessDeniedHandler.handle()                         → 403

It only catches exceptions thrown after it in the chain. Anything thrown by a filter before it, our JwtAuthFilter included, never reaches it. That is why our filter doesn't throw. It records the reason and lets AuthorizationFilter reject the request.

3.2 Why @ControllerAdvice misses filter exceptions

@ControllerAdvice/@ExceptionHandler are run by the HandlerExceptionResolver that DispatcherServlet owns. Security filters run before the request reaches DispatcherServlet, in the servlet container's filter chain. An exception thrown in a filter climbs back up to Tomcat, which forwards to /error (Boot's BasicErrorController). You get a generic error body, and the advice never sees it.

Tomcat filter chain  ─► DelegatingFilterProxy ─► FilterChainProxy ─► ... ─► DispatcherServlet ─► @ControllerAdvice
                         ▲ exception thrown here never reaches here ──────────────────────────────┘

Options:

  1. Recommended: a custom AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler that write JSON.
  2. Inject HandlerExceptionResolver (qualifier handlerExceptionResolver) into the entry point or filter and call resolver.resolveException(req, res, null, ex). That forwards the exception into your @RestControllerAdvice, so all error formatting lives in one place.

3.3 JSON 401 entry point and 403 handler

@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class JsonAuthEntryPoint implements AuthenticationEntryPoint {

    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    @Override
    public void commence(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                         AuthenticationException authException) throws IOException {
        String code = Optional.ofNullable((String) request.getAttribute("auth_error")).orElse("UNAUTHENTICATED");
        String detail = switch (code) {
            case "TOKEN_EXPIRED" -> "Access token expired. Use the refresh token to get a new one.";
            case "TOKEN_INVALID" -> "Access token is malformed or its signature is invalid.";
            default -> "Authentication is required to access this resource.";
        };

        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, detail);
        pd.setTitle("Unauthorized");
        pd.setInstance(URI.create(request.getRequestURI()));
        pd.setProperty("code", code);
        pd.setProperty("timestamp", Instant.now().toString());
        pd.setProperty("correlationId", MDC.get("correlationId"));

        response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED);
        // RFC 6750: tells the client why the bearer token was rejected
        response.setHeader(HttpHeaders.WWW_AUTHENTICATE,
                "Bearer error=\"invalid_token\", error_description=\"" + code + "\"");
        response.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON_VALUE);
        mapper.writeValue(response.getOutputStream(), pd);
    }
}
@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@Slf4j
public class JsonAccessDeniedHandler implements AccessDeniedHandler {

    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    @Override
    public void handle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                       AccessDeniedException ex) throws IOException {
        Authentication auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
        log.warn("Access denied user={} path={} method={}",
                auth != null ? auth.getName() : "unknown", request.getRequestURI(), request.getMethod());

        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN,
                "You do not have permission to perform this action.");
        pd.setTitle("Forbidden");
        pd.setInstance(URI.create(request.getRequestURI()));
        pd.setProperty("code", "ACCESS_DENIED");

        response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_FORBIDDEN);
        response.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON_VALUE);
        mapper.writeValue(response.getOutputStream(), pd);
    }
}

They're wired in SecurityConfig with .exceptionHandling(ex -> ex.authenticationEntryPoint(...).accessDeniedHandler(...)) (see D2).

With the OAuth2 resource server, BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter calls the configured entry point itself when a token is invalid. Set it with .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.authenticationEntryPoint(entryPoint).jwt(...)).

3.4 Method-security exceptions

@PreAuthorize throws AccessDeniedException (AuthorizationDeniedException in 6.3+) inside the controller or service call, so it travels through DispatcherServlet. Watch out:

  • If your @RestControllerAdvice has a catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class), it swallows AccessDeniedException and returns 500 instead of 403.
  • Fix: add an explicit handler, or rethrow it so it reaches ExceptionTranslationFilter:
@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(AccessDeniedException.class)
    public ProblemDetail accessDenied(AccessDeniedException ex) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN, "Access denied");
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(AuthenticationException.class)
    public ProblemDetail authFailed(AuthenticationException ex) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, ex.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ProblemDetail generic(Exception ex) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "Unexpected error");
    }
}

3.5 Handling expired tokens end-to-end

Angular HttpInterceptor
  ├─ request with access token ──► API → 401 {code: TOKEN_EXPIRED}
  ├─ on 401 + TOKEN_EXPIRED: (single-flight, queue other requests)
  │     POST /api/auth/refresh {refreshToken}
  │        ├─ 200 new access + rotated refresh → retry original request(s)
  │        └─ 401 (refresh expired/revoked) → clear tokens, redirect to /login
  └─ on 403 → show "not permitted" toast (don't log the user out)

Backend rules: the expiry check comes from ExpiredJwtException (jjwt) or JwtValidationException with an exp failure (Nimbus). Allow a small clock skew (30–60 s). Never accept an expired token "just for refresh". The refresh token is a separate credential.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not throw from JwtAuthFilter directly? It runs before ExceptionTranslationFilter, so the exception would go to Tomcat's /error and you'd lose control of the response. Either set an attribute and continue, or call the entry point yourself and return.
  • What does ExceptionTranslationFilter do for an anonymous user who gets AccessDenied? It treats it as "not authenticated" and calls the AuthenticationEntryPoint (401), not the AccessDeniedHandler.
  • What should a 401 body never contain? Stack traces, or whether the username or the password was wrong (that enables user enumeration).
  • How do you test these? MockMvc with @WithMockUser(roles="OPERATOR") or .with(jwt().authorities(...)), asserting status().isForbidden() and the JSON fields.
D4 Pre-authorization (@PreAuthorize). Hexaware
  • Turn it on with @EnableMethodSecurity (Spring Security 6; it replaces @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity). prePostEnabled is true by default.
  • @PreAuthorize evaluates a SpEL expression before the method runs. If the result is false, it throws AccessDeniedException (403). @PostAuthorize checks the returnObject after the method runs.
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
public void deleteIncident(Long id) { ... }

@PreAuthorize("hasAnyAuthority('incident:write','ROLE_SUPERVISOR')")
public Incident update(Long id, IncidentDto dto) { ... }

@PreAuthorize("#userId == authentication.principal.id or hasRole('ADMIN')")
public UserProfile getProfile(Long userId) { ... }

@PreAuthorize("@zoneSecurity.canAccess(authentication, #zoneId)")   // custom bean check
public List<Sensor> sensorsInZone(String zoneId) { ... }

@PostAuthorize("returnObject.assignedTo == authentication.name")
public Incident getIncident(Long id) { ... }

4.1 Enabling it

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity(            // Spring Security 6; replaces @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity
    prePostEnabled = true,        // @PreAuthorize/@PostAuthorize/@PreFilter/@PostFilter (default true)
    securedEnabled = true,        // @Secured
    jsr250Enabled = true          // @RolesAllowed, @PermitAll, @DenyAll
)
public class MethodSecurityConfig { }

Internally, @EnableMethodSecurity registers AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor and AuthorizationManagerAfterMethodInterceptor as AOP advisors. Each annotated bean gets a proxy. On every call the interceptor evaluates the SpEL expression against a MethodSecurityExpressionRoot (authentication, principal, hasRole, ...) and the method arguments.

caller ─► [CGLIB/JDK proxy] ─► AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor
                                   │ evaluate @PreAuthorize SpEL
                                   │   false → throw AccessDeniedException (target never called)
                                   ▼
                               target method executes
                                   ▼
                               AuthorizationManagerAfterMethodInterceptor
                                   │ evaluate @PostAuthorize with returnObject
                                   │   false → AccessDeniedException (method already ran!)
                                   ▼
                               return to caller

4.2 The annotations

Annotation When it's checked Supports SpEL Example
@PreAuthorize Before the method runs Yes @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
@PostAuthorize After it runs, can use returnObject Yes @PostAuthorize("returnObject.reportedBy == authentication.name")
@PreFilter / @PostFilter Filters collection args or return values Yes @PostFilter("filterObject.zoneId == principal.zoneId")
@Secured Before No, role list only @Secured({"ROLE_ADMIN","ROLE_SUPERVISOR"})
@RolesAllowed (JSR-250) Before No @RolesAllowed("ADMIN") (prefix added automatically)

4.3 SpEL with method parameters and custom bean checks

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class IncidentService {

    private final IncidentRepository repo;

    // Role check
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    public void delete(Long id) { repo.deleteById(id); }

    // Combine role + param (#zoneId refers to the parameter; needs -parameters compiler flag, which Boot enables)
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('SUPERVISOR') and #zoneId == authentication.principal.claims['zoneId']")
    public List<IncidentDto> listByZone(String zoneId) { /* ... */ return List.of(); }

    // Custom bean: @beanName.method(...) keeps complex rules in testable Java code
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or @incidentSecurity.canEdit(#id, authentication)")
    public IncidentDto update(Long id, UpdateIncidentRequest req) { /* ... */ return null; }

    // Post-check on returned object
    @PostAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or returnObject.assignedTo == authentication.name")
    public IncidentDto get(Long id) { /* ... */ return null; }

    // Filter results to the caller's zone
    @PostFilter("hasRole('ADMIN') or filterObject.zoneId == @zoneResolver.zoneOf(authentication)")
    public List<IncidentDto> listAll() { /* ... */ return new ArrayList<>(); }  // must be a mutable collection
}
@Component("incidentSecurity")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class IncidentSecurity {

    private final IncidentRepository repo;

    public boolean canEdit(Long incidentId, Authentication auth) {
        return repo.findById(incidentId)
                .map(i -> i.getAssignedTo().equals(auth.getName()) && !"CLOSED".equals(i.getStatus()))
                .orElse(false);
    }
}

Meta-annotations keep the expressions in one place:

@Target({ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.TYPE})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('SUPERVISOR','ADMIN')")
public @interface IsSupervisorOrAdmin { }

4.4 Proxy limitations (frequently asked)

  1. Self-invocation: this.delete(id) from inside the same class skips the proxy, so no security check runs. Fixes: move the method to another bean, inject the bean's own proxy (@Lazy self-injection), or use AspectJ weaving (@EnableMethodSecurity(mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ)).
  2. Visibility: proxies only intercept public methods (CGLIB can technically handle protected/package methods, but don't rely on it). private and final methods are never intercepted.
  3. Only Spring beans: objects you create with new aren't proxied.
  4. @PostAuthorize runs after side effects: if the method changed the database, the change has already happened, unless a surrounding @Transactional rolls it back. Don't put it on mutating methods.
  5. Order with @Transactional: both are AOP advisors. Method security runs first by default (AuthorizationInterceptorsOrder), so a denied call never opens a transaction.
  6. Interface vs class: annotations on interface methods work, but annotate one place consistently.

4.5 Testing

@SpringBootTest
class IncidentServiceSecurityTest {
    @Autowired IncidentService service;

    @Test
    @WithMockUser(roles = "OPERATOR")
    void operatorCannotDelete() {
        assertThrows(AccessDeniedException.class, () -> service.delete(1L));
    }
}

Likely follow-ups:

  • URL security or method security? Both. URL rules give coarse protection at the edge. Method security puts the business rules next to the logic and also protects non-HTTP entry points such as Kafka listeners and schedulers.
  • What's the difference between hasRole('ADMIN') and hasAuthority('ADMIN')? hasRole adds the ROLE_ prefix (it checks ROLE_ADMIN). hasAuthority checks the exact string.
  • Does @PreAuthorize work on a @KafkaListener method? Only if there's an Authentication in the context. Listener threads have none, so you have to set one up yourself (e.g. a system principal).
  • Is @PreAuthorize slower than URL security? Barely: one SpEL evaluation per call, and the parsed expressions are cached. A custom bean check that hits the DB costs a query, so cache it if it's hot.
D5 How does JWT work? Co. 2
  • Structure: header.payload.signature, each part Base64URL-encoded.
    • Header holds the algorithm, e.g. {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}.
    • Payload holds claims: sub, roles, iat, exp, iss.
    • Signature is HMACSHA256(header + "." + payload, secret), or RS256 with a private key (services verify with the public key).
  • Signed, not encrypted. Anyone can read the payload, so never put secrets in it. The signature only proves the token was not tampered with.
  • Stateless. The server keeps no session. Every request carries Authorization: Bearer <token>, and each service checks the signature and exp locally. This scales well across microservices.
  • Expiry and refresh. Keep the access token short-lived (5–15 min). Use a longer-lived refresh token, stored server-side or in Redis so it can be revoked, to get a new access token from /auth/refresh. Rotate refresh tokens on each use.
  • Revocation is hard because tokens are stateless. Options: short TTL, a Redis blacklist of jti values, or a token version stored on the user.

5.1 Structure

A JWT (RFC 7519) is three Base64URL-encoded parts joined by dots: header.payload.signature.

eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6ImsxIn0 . eyJzdWIiOiJvcDEiLCJyb2xlcyI6WyJPUEVSQVRPUiJdLCJleHAiOjE3...} . Qm9ndXNTaWduYXR1cmU...
└──────────── HEADER ──────────────┘   └──────────────────── PAYLOAD (claims) ─────────────────┘   └── SIGNATURE ──┘

HEADER  {"alg":"RS256","typ":"JWT","kid":"k1"}       ← kid picks the key from the JWKS
PAYLOAD {"iss":"https://keycloak/realms/smartcity",
         "sub":"op1", "aud":"incident-api",
         "exp":1767225600, "iat":1767224700, "nbf":1767224700, "jti":"7f3c...",
         "roles":["OPERATOR"], "zoneId":"Z-07"}
SIGNATURE = sign( base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload), key )
  • Encoded, not encrypted. Anyone can Base64-decode the payload, so never put passwords, Aadhaar numbers, or PII in it. If the content must be confidential, use JWE (encrypted JWT).
  • Registered claims: iss (issuer), sub (subject), aud (audience), exp (expiry), nbf (not before), iat (issued at), jti (unique ID). Private/custom claims: roles, zoneId, tenant.

5.2 HS256 vs RS256 (and ES256)

HS256 (HMAC + SHA-256) RS256 (RSA + SHA-256) / ES256 (ECDSA)
Key type One shared secret Private key signs, public key verifies
Who can verify Anyone holding the secret, who can therefore also forge tokens Anyone with the public key; only the issuer can sign
Distribution The secret has to be copied to every service, which is risky Public keys published at a JWKS endpoint (/.well-known/jwks.json)
Key rotation Hard: every service must update together Easy: publish a new kid, keep the old one for a while
Speed Faster Slower (RSA); ES256 is faster and gives smaller signatures
Use when A single monolith signs and verifies its own tokens Microservices, external IdP (Keycloak, Auth0, Azure AD)

5.3 Validation steps (what a resource server must do)

1. Split into 3 parts; Base64URL-decode header & payload            → malformed? reject
2. Check header.alg is in an ALLOW-LIST (e.g. only RS256)           → never trust "alg" blindly; reject "none"
3. Pick the key by kid from the cached JWKS (refetch on unknown kid) → unknown? reject
4. Verify signature over header.payload                              → mismatch? reject
5. exp > now - skew ;  nbf <= now + skew                              → expired / not yet valid
6. iss == expected issuer                                            → token from another IdP? reject
7. aud contains this API                                             → token meant for another service? reject
8. (optional) jti not in revocation list; token type == "access"
9. Map claims → GrantedAuthorities → SecurityContext

Spring's NimbusJwtDecoder built from issuer-uri covers steps 1–6. Add audience validation like this:

@Bean
JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(@Value("${spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri}") String issuer) {
    NimbusJwtDecoder decoder = JwtDecoders.fromIssuerLocation(issuer);
    OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt> audience = new JwtClaimValidator<List<String>>(
            JwtClaimNames.AUD, aud -> aud != null && aud.contains("incident-api"));
    decoder.setJwtValidator(new DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator<>(
            JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(issuer), audience));
    return decoder;
}

5.4 Expiry, refresh tokens and rotation

Access tokens are short-lived (5–15 min) because a stateless token can't easily be revoked. A refresh token is long-lived (hours to days), opaque or a JWT, stored server-side (hashed), and used only at /auth/refresh.

           login
Client ───────────────► Auth: issue AT(15m) + RT1(7d)   [store hash(RT1), family=F1]
  ... AT expires ...
Client ─ /refresh RT1 ─► Auth: RT1 valid & unused?
                           yes → mark RT1 used, issue AT' + RT2 (same family F1)   ← ROTATION
Attacker ─ /refresh RT1 (stolen, replayed) ─► Auth: RT1 already used!
                           → REUSE DETECTED → revoke whole family F1 → user must log in again
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class RefreshTokenService {
    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
    private static final Duration TTL = Duration.ofDays(7);

    public String issue(String username) {
        String token = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding()
                .encodeToString(KeyGenerators.secureRandom(32).generateKey());
        redis.opsForValue().set("rt:" + sha256(token), username, TTL);
        return token;
    }

    /** Rotates: the old token is deleted atomically; a second use returns empty. */
    public Optional<String> consume(String token) {
        String username = redis.opsForValue().getAndDelete("rt:" + sha256(token));
        return Optional.ofNullable(username);
    }

    private static String sha256(String s) {
        try {
            byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            return HexFormat.of().formatHex(d);
        } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); }
    }
}

(Full reuse detection needs a token family ID so you can revoke every descendant token. The sketch above only shows single-use rotation.)

5.5 Revocation / blacklisting

JWTs are valid until exp by design. Ways to revoke one earlier:

Technique How it works Cost
Short expiry + refresh Revoke the refresh token; the access token dies within 15 min Simplest; there's a window of exposure
jti deny-list in Redis On logout or compromise, SET deny:<jti> 1 EX <remaining ttl>; the filter checks it One Redis lookup per request
Token version per user tokenVersion claim; bumping it in the DB invalidates every token the user holds DB/cache lookup
Introspection (opaque tokens) Resource server calls /introspect on the IdP A network call per request (cache it)
Key rotation Revokes all tokens signed with the old key Emergency use only

5.6 Where the client stores tokens

Storage XSS risk CSRF risk Notes
localStorage / sessionStorage High: any injected script can read it None Easy with Angular interceptors, but only safe with a strict CSP
JS memory (a service variable) Lower: gone on refresh, harder to steal None Pair it with a refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie
HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie JS can't read it Needs SameSite=Strict/Lax or a CSRF token Recommended for refresh tokens
BFF pattern Tokens never reach the browser; only a session cookie does CSRF protection on the BFF The current OAuth guidance for SPAs

5.7 Common vulnerabilities

  1. alg: none: an attacker strips the signature and sets alg=none. Defence: an algorithm allow-list. jjwt's parseSignedClaims() rejects unsigned tokens.
  2. Algorithm confusion (RS256→HS256): the attacker signs with HS256 using the server's public key as the HMAC secret. A library that picks the verification method from the header accepts it. Defence: fix the expected algorithm and key type.
  3. Weak HMAC secret: brute-forced offline with hashcat. Use ≥256-bit random secrets.
  4. Not validating aud/iss: a token issued for service A gets accepted by service B.
  5. kid/jku injection: the header points to an attacker's key URL. Never fetch keys from URLs inside the header.
  6. Sensitive data in the payload (it's only Base64).
  7. Long-lived access tokens with no revocation.
  8. Tokens leaking in URLs (query strings end up in logs), in logs generally, or in error messages. Mask the Authorization header in logs.

Likely follow-ups:

  • JWT vs session ID? JWTs are self-contained and stateless, which scales across services with no session store, but they're hard to revoke and larger. Sessions are simple to revoke but need sticky sessions or a shared store (Spring Session + Redis).
  • What's an ID token vs an access token? ID token (OIDC) = who logged in, meant for the client. Access token = permission to call an API, meant for the resource server. Never send the ID token to APIs.
  • What's PKCE? Proof Key for Code Exchange: the SPA sends code_challenge = SHA256(verifier) on authorize and the verifier on token exchange, so a stolen auth code is useless. It's required for public clients.
  • How big should a JWT be? Keep it under ~4–8 KB. Proxies and servers limit header size, so don't stuff in hundreds of permissions.
D6 Explain the authentication layer in your project (template; adapt to your project). Co. 2

"Our Smart City platform has an auth-service that owns users, roles (ADMIN, SUPERVISOR, OPERATOR, CITIZEN) and permissions in PostgreSQL. On login, the AuthenticationManager validates credentials through our UserDetailsService and a BCryptPasswordEncoder, then issues an RS256-signed access token (15 min) and a refresh token (7 days, stored in Redis). The API Gateway (Spring Cloud Gateway) validates the JWT for every request: it checks the signature with the public key and checks expiry, then forwards the user ID and roles as headers. Downstream services such as incident, traffic and notification also run as resource servers with oauth2ResourceServer().jwt(), so they apply @PreAuthorize rules like operator-zone checks. Service-to-service calls use client-credentials tokens. A custom AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler return consistent JSON 401/403 responses. Failed logins are rate-limited and audited."

Angular --login--> Gateway --> auth-service --(JWT + refresh)--> Angular (stores in memory)
Angular --Bearer--> Gateway [validate JWT] --> incident-service [@PreAuthorize] --> DB

Template answer: adapt names, IdP, and numbers to your real project. Interviewers want to hear a clear flow, why each choice was made, and one problem you actually solved.

Context: "On our Smart City Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC) platform, the users are city operators, supervisors, field officers (mobile app), and admins. Services include Incident Management, IoT/Traffic Sensor Ingestion, Notification, Asset Management, and User/Auth. We centralised authentication in Keycloak, an OAuth2/OIDC provider. Earlier releases used our own Spring Boot auth-service issuing JWTs, and I'll explain both."

┌──────────────┐ 1. redirect (Auth Code + PKCE)   ┌───────────────────────────┐
│  Angular SPA │ ───────────────────────────────► │ Keycloak (realm smartcity)│
│  (ICCC UI)   │ ◄─────── 2. auth code ────────── │  - users from LDAP/AD     │
│              │ ── 3. code + verifier ─────────► │  - realm roles, groups    │
│              │ ◄─ 4. access(5m)+refresh+ID ───  │  - MFA for admins         │
└──────┬───────┘                                  └────────────┬──────────────┘
       │ 5. Authorization: Bearer <AT>                         │ JWKS (public keys)
       ▼                                                       ▼
┌────────────────────────── Spring Cloud Gateway ───────────────────────────┐
│ - oauth2ResourceServer: verify RS256 signature via cached JWKS,           │
│   exp/iss/aud                                                             │
│ - coarse route rules (/api/admin/** → ROLE_ADMIN)                         │
│ - rate-limit per user (Redis), add X-Correlation-Id                       │
│ - TokenRelay: forward the same JWT downstream                             │
└──────┬─────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┬────────────────┘
       ▼                         ▼                         ▼
 incident-service         sensor-service            notification-service
 (resource server:        (resource server)         (resource server)
  re-validates JWT,       IoT devices use           consumes Kafka events;
  @PreAuthorize for       client-credentials /      system calls use
  zone-based rules)       mTLS, not user tokens     client-credentials tokens

Key points to say:

  1. Login: Angular uses the Authorization Code flow with PKCE (via angular-oauth2-oidc / keycloak-angular). There's no password handling in our code, and MFA (OTP) is enforced for the ADMIN role.
  2. Token contents: sub, preferred_username, realm_access.roles (OPERATOR, SUPERVISOR, ADMIN, FIELD_OFFICER), plus a custom zoneId mapper so we can scope data by city zone.
  3. Gateway: validates the token once at the edge and rejects bad tokens before they use backend resources. It relays the token downstream (TokenRelay filter).
  4. Services: each service is also a resource server and validates the JWT again (zero-trust; signature checks are cheap with the cached JWKS). An alternative some teams use is having the gateway pass X-User-Id/X-Roles headers. That's only safe if services can't be reached except through the gateway (network policy plus mTLS), so we preferred re-validation.
  5. RBAC:
Role Permissions
OPERATOR View dashboards, create/update incidents in own zone, acknowledge alerts
SUPERVISOR All operator rights + assign incidents across zones, close incidents, reports
FIELD_OFFICER Mobile app: view assigned incidents, update status, upload photos
ADMIN User/role management, device registration, configuration

URL rules sit at the gateway and in each service, and @PreAuthorize("@zoneGuard.canAccess(#zoneId, authentication)") covers the data-scoped rules. 6. Service-to-service calls: OAuth2 client credentials (each service has its own client in Keycloak, with scopes like notification.send). Feign attaches the token automatically through an OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager interceptor. 7. Devices / IoT gateways: they don't use user tokens. They use mTLS client certificates or per-device API keys at the ingestion endpoint (MQTT broker/HTTP). 8. Session handling: a 5-min access token, a refresh token rotated by Keycloak, and an idle timeout of 30 min (command-centre screens are shared). Logout calls Keycloak's end-session endpoint.

Problems solved (pick one you can defend):

  • Clock skew between K8s nodes caused random 401s → set the validator clock skew to 60 s and enabled NTP sync.
  • JWKS fetch on every pod start hit Keycloak hard during scaling → cached JWKS (Nimbus does this by default) and fixed the key-rotation runbook.
  • Big tokens: fine-grained permissions as claims pushed headers over 8 KB → kept only roles in the token and resolved permissions from a Redis cache.
  • Migrating from custom JWT to Keycloak: for one release the gateway accepted both issuers (JwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why validate in each service if the gateway already did? Defence in depth. If someone gets inside the cluster network they shouldn't be able to call services with forged headers.
  • How do Kafka consumers know who triggered an event? We put initiatedBy and correlationId in the event payload or headers. Consumers don't re-authenticate users; they trust the broker, which uses SASL/mTLS plus ACLs.
  • How would you force-logout a compromised user? Disable the user in Keycloak and revoke their sessions/refresh tokens. The access token expires in ≤5 min, and a jti deny-list covers the gap if that window is too long.
D7 Security layers for REST APIs; best practices; securing internal APIs.
  • Transport: HTTPS/TLS everywhere. Use mTLS between internal services, or a service mesh such as Istio.
  • Edge: the API Gateway is the single entry point. It handles JWT validation, rate limiting (Redis RequestRateLimiter), IP allow-lists and a WAF.
  • Identity: OAuth2/OIDC (Keycloak). Users use the auth-code + PKCE flow. Service-to-service calls use the client credentials flow. API keys go to third-party or IoT device clients, scoped and rotated.
  • Application:
    • Restrictive CORS (allowedOrigins set to your UI domain only, never * together with credentials).
    • Input validation with @Valid and Bean Validation.
    • Parameterized queries via JPA to prevent SQL injection.
    • Output encoding.
    • CSRF protection is only needed for cookie-based sessions.
  • Data: never log tokens, passwords or PII (mask them). Encrypt sensitive columns. Return DTOs, not entities.
  • Secrets: Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Kubernetes secrets with an encrypted Config Server. Never put secrets in Git.
  • Ops: follow the OWASP Top 10, scan dependencies (OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk), add security headers, expose only health and info actuator endpoints, and keep audit logs.
  • Internal APIs: don't expose them publicly. Put them in a private network or VPC, reachable only through the gateway, and still verify tokens (zero trust).

Think in defence in depth: each layer assumes the one in front of it can fail.

Internet
  │  ① WAF / DDoS protection (Cloudflare, AWS WAF, F5) — OWASP rule sets, geo/IP blocks
  ▼
  ② TLS 1.2+/1.3 termination at LB (HSTS, strong ciphers, cert auto-renewal)
  ▼
  ③ API Gateway — authN (JWT/OAuth2), coarse authZ, rate limiting, CORS, request size limits,
  │              IP allow-list for partner APIs, API keys for 3rd parties
  ▼
  ④ Service mesh / network — mTLS between pods (Istio/Linkerd), K8s NetworkPolicies
  │                          (only gateway → services), private subnets
  ▼
  ⑤ Service — re-validate token, method security, input validation, output encoding
  ▼
  ⑥ Data — least-privilege DB users, parameterized queries, encryption at rest, column
            encryption for PII, audit tables
  +  Cross-cutting: secrets in Vault, dependency scanning, logging with masking, monitoring/alerting
Layer / practice What & why Spring Boot implementation
TLS everywhere Encrypts traffic in transit, stops MITM and token sniffing server.ssl.*, or terminate at the LB/ingress; HSTS header; redirect HTTP→HTTPS
API Gateway Single entry point, consistent auth and throttling Spring Cloud Gateway + oauth2ResourceServer
OAuth2 / JWT for users Standard, delegated, short-lived tokens spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server
OAuth2 client credentials (service → service) Each service has its own identity and scopes, no shared passwords spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client + OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager
mTLS Both sides present certificates. Strong machine identity for internal or partner calls Mesh sidecar, or server.ssl.client-auth=need + truststore
API keys Simple identification for third parties (e.g. a weather data provider) A gateway filter checking a hashed key; rotate keys; never the only control for sensitive data
Rate limiting / throttling Stops brute force, abuse, DoS Gateway RequestRateLimiter (Redis), Resilience4j RateLimiter, Bucket4j
CORS The browser only lets allowed origins call the API CorsConfigurationSource with an explicit origin list, never * together with credentials
CSRF Only matters when the browser sends credentials automatically (cookies). Stateless bearer-header APIs can disable it csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable) for bearer APIs; CookieCsrfTokenRepository if you use cookie auth
Input validation Reject bad data early (size, format, ranges) @Valid, @NotBlank, @Size, @Pattern, custom validators; spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size
SQL injection prevention Never concatenate user input into SQL JPA/@Query with :params, JdbcTemplate with ?, Criteria API; validate sort fields against a whitelist
Output encoding / XSS Never reflect raw input Angular escapes by default; JSON content type; CSP header
Security headers Browser-side hardening Spring Security defaults: X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Cache-Control, HSTS; add CSP and Referrer-Policy
Secrets management No passwords in Git or images HashiCorp Vault (spring-cloud-vault), K8s Secrets + Sealed Secrets, AWS Secrets Manager; rotate regularly
Dependency scanning Known CVEs (Log4Shell, Spring4Shell) OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk, Trivy for images, Dependabot; SonarQube SAST in CI
Least privilege Limits the blast radius DB user per service with only the grants it needs; K8s RBAC; non-root containers
Logging & masking Audit trail without leaking secrets Log auth events and access denials; mask Authorization, passwords, phone, Aadhaar via a Logback mask converter
Error handling Don't leak internals ProblemDetail, server.error.include-stacktrace=never
Actuator hardening /actuator/env and /heapdump leak secrets Expose only health,info,prometheus; separate management port; secure with a role
Mass assignment The client sets fields it shouldn't (e.g. role) Use request DTOs, never bind entities directly
Idempotency & replay protection Retries or replays don't duplicate actions Idempotency-Key header; request timestamp + nonce for webhooks

OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023): know these names.

  1. Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA/IDOR): GET /incidents/123 returns another zone's incident → check ownership with @PreAuthorize and data scoping.
  2. Broken Authentication.
  3. Broken Object Property Level Authorization (excessive data exposure / mass assignment).
  4. Unrestricted Resource Consumption → rate limits, pagination caps, payload limits.
  5. Broken Function Level Authorization → admin endpoints reachable by operators.
  6. Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows.
  7. Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) → validate URLs your server fetches.
  8. Security Misconfiguration.
  9. Improper Inventory Management (old, forgotten API versions).
  10. Unsafe Consumption of third-party APIs.

Service-to-service with client credentials (Feign):

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          incident-svc:
            provider: keycloak
            client-id: incident-service
            client-secret: ${INCIDENT_CLIENT_SECRET}
            authorization-grant-type: client_credentials
            scope: notification.send
        provider:
          keycloak:
            issuer-uri: https://keycloak.smartcity.local/realms/smartcity
@Configuration
public class FeignOAuth2Config {

    @Bean
    OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager authorizedClientManager(ClientRegistrationRepository regs,
                                                          OAuth2AuthorizedClientService service) {
        var manager = new AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager(regs, service);
        manager.setAuthorizedClientProvider(OAuth2AuthorizedClientProviderBuilder.builder()
                .clientCredentials().build());
        return manager;
    }

    @Bean
    RequestInterceptor oauth2FeignInterceptor(OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager manager) {
        return template -> {
            OAuth2AuthorizeRequest req = OAuth2AuthorizeRequest
                    .withClientRegistrationId("incident-svc").principal("incident-service").build();
            OAuth2AuthorizedClient client = manager.authorize(req);   // cached until near expiry
            if (client == null) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Could not obtain client-credentials token");
            }
            template.header(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION, "Bearer " + client.getAccessToken().getTokenValue());
        };
    }
}

Securing internal APIs that are also exposed to clients:

  • Publish them only through the gateway, on a separate route prefix (/partner/v1/**), with their own auth (OAuth2 client credentials, or API key + IP allow-list), quotas, and an OpenAPI contract.
  • Keep internal-only endpoints (/internal/**) off the gateway routes entirely, and block them at ingress and NetworkPolicy level.
  • Return DTOs designed for external use, not internal models (no internal IDs, stack traces, or extra fields).
  • Version the API, monitor usage per client, and give each client a revocable credential.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why is disabling CSRF OK for JWT APIs? CSRF works because browsers attach cookies automatically. A bearer token in the Authorization header is never attached automatically. Once you put the token in a cookie, you need CSRF protection again.
  • How do you keep the DB password out of application.yml? Vault with spring.config.import=vault://, or K8s Secrets mounted as env vars; rotate with Vault's dynamic DB credentials.
  • How do you prevent IDOR? Never trust IDs from the client alone. Check ownership or zone in the service layer, and scope queries with the caller's identity.
  • What is mTLS? Both client and server present X.509 certificates and verify each other, which gives mutual authentication at the transport layer. A service mesh automates certificate issuance and rotation.
D8 What are microservices; key things to take care of. Hexaware

Microservices split an application into small, independently deployable services. Each one owns a single business capability and its own data, and they communicate over APIs or events.

Key things to take care of:

  • Boundaries: use domain-driven design (DDD), keep each service cohesive, and give each one its own database.
  • Communication: choose sync or async deliberately, version your APIs, and design for idempotency.
  • Resilience: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks.
  • Data consistency: use the Saga or Outbox pattern instead of distributed transactions.
  • Observability: centralized logs (ELK), metrics (Prometheus/Grafana), tracing with correlation IDs.
  • Security: gateway authentication, propagated JWTs, service-to-service authentication.
  • Config & discovery: Config Server, Eureka or Kubernetes DNS.
  • DevOps: a CI/CD pipeline per service, Docker/Kubernetes, health checks, contract tests.

Definition: microservices are an architectural style where an application is a set of small, independently deployable services. Each one is built around a business capability, owns its data, runs in its own process, and talks to the others over lightweight protocols (HTTP/gRPC/messaging). A small team can build, deploy, and scale each service independently.

Monolith                                  Microservices
┌─────────────────────────┐               ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────────┐
│ UI │ Incident │ Sensor  │               │Incident│ │ Sensor │ │Notification│
│    │ Notify   │ User    │      ──►      │  svc   │ │  svc   │ │    svc     │
│      ONE DEPLOYABLE     │               └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘ └─────┬──────┘
│      ONE DATABASE       │                   ▼          ▼            ▼
└─────────────────────────┘               PostgreSQL  TimescaleDB   MongoDB
                                          (each service owns its DB, deploys alone)

Benefits: independent deployment and scaling (sensor ingestion scales to 20 pods while the user service runs 2), fault isolation, technology freedom, smaller codebases, team autonomy. Costs: distributed-systems complexity (network failures, latency), data consistency, operational overhead, harder testing and debugging. Don't start with microservices for a small team or an unclear domain. A modular monolith is often better at first.

Key things to take care of:

# Concern What to do
1 Bounded contexts (DDD) Split by business capability, not technical layer. "Incident", "Device/Sensor", "Notification", "Identity". A service that has to call 5 others for every request is split wrong
2 Database per service No shared tables. Others get the data through APIs or events. That keeps services loosely coupled and lets each choose its store (polyglot persistence)
3 Communication style Sync REST/gRPC for queries that need an immediate answer; async events (Kafka) for state changes and to cut coupling
4 Resilience Timeouts on every remote call, circuit breakers, retries with backoff, bulkheads, fallbacks (D11–D13)
5 Observability Centralised logs (ELK/Loki) with correlation IDs, metrics (Micrometer → Prometheus/Grafana), distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry → Jaeger/Zipkin), health checks
6 API versioning & contracts /v1/ URIs or headers, backward-compatible changes, OpenAPI specs, consumer-driven contract tests (Spring Cloud Contract/Pact)
7 Idempotency Retries and at-least-once messaging cause duplicates. Use idempotency keys, unique constraints, and a processed-event table
8 Distributed transactions No 2PC. Use the Saga pattern (choreography or orchestration) with compensating actions, plus the Transactional Outbox for reliable event publishing
9 Security Gateway auth, token propagation, service identity (client credentials/mTLS), secrets management (D7)
10 Service discovery & config Eureka/Consul or K8s DNS; Spring Cloud Config or K8s ConfigMaps; externalised, per-environment config
11 CI/CD A pipeline per service: build → unit/contract tests → image scan → deploy (blue-green/canary) → smoke tests; GitOps (ArgoCD)
12 Containers & orchestration Docker images (small, non-root), Kubernetes for scaling, self-healing, rolling updates; resource requests and limits
13 Data consistency for reads Eventual consistency, CQRS/read models, API composition at the gateway or BFF
14 Testing strategy Unit → slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) → Testcontainers integration → contract → a few E2E
15 Team ownership "You build it, you run it." Each team owns its services end to end (Conway's law)

Likely follow-ups:

  • How big should a microservice be? Big enough to own one business capability, small enough for one team to understand and redeploy safely. Size by cohesion, not lines of code.
  • What's a distributed monolith? Services that must be deployed together or share a DB, with chatty synchronous chains between them. It has all the costs of microservices and none of the benefits.
  • When would you not use microservices? Small team, early product, unclear domain boundaries, no DevOps maturity.
D9 Explain the microservices architecture used in your project (template; adapt to your project). Co. 2HexawareG2 
                 Angular UI / Mobile / IoT devices
                              |
                     [ Load Balancer / ALB ]
                              |
                 [ API Gateway (Spring Cloud Gateway) ]  <- JWT validation, rate limit, routing
                   |        |          |          |
             auth-svc  incident-svc  traffic-svc  notification-svc
                |          |    \        |     \         ^
            Postgres   Postgres  \   TimescaleDB \       |
                                  \      ^        \      |
                                   +--> [ Kafka topics ] +   (incident.created, sensor.readings)
                                              ^
                                      IoT ingestion-svc (MQTT -> Kafka)

   Shared infra: Eureka (discovery) | Config Server (Git-backed) | Redis (cache, rate-limit)

"Clients go through the gateway, which validates the JWT and routes to services registered in Eureka. Services pull their configuration from the Config Server. Synchronous calls use Feign with Resilience4j. Events such as incident.created go through Kafka, so the notification service sends SMS, email or push messages asynchronously. Redis caches master data such as zones and sensor metadata."

Template answer: replace the service names, counts, and tools with your real ones. Draw this on the whiteboard as you talk, moving left to right.

One-line pitch: "Our Smart City ICCC platform collects real-time data from traffic signals, ANPR cameras, environmental sensors, and citizen complaints, raises and manages incidents, and notifies field teams. It's built as about 10 Spring Boot microservices on Kubernetes, talking over REST and Kafka."

        PostgreSQL   PostgreSQL│        │ TimescaleDB   │   MongoDB         Elasticsearch
                       Redis   │        │ (time series) │ (templates, log)  / PostgreSQL RO
                               ▼        ▼               ▲      ▲                ▲
                   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                   │                    Apache Kafka (3 brokers, KRaft)               │
                   │ sensor.readings.raw | sensor.alerts | incident.events |          │
                   │ notification.requests | *.dlt                                    │
                   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Platform services:
   ┌───────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   │ Config Server │ │ Eureka (or K8s│ │ Vault (secrets)        │ │ Observability:               │
   │ (Git-backed)  │ │ Service DNS)  │ │                        │ │ ELK/EFK logs, Prometheus +   │
   └───────────────┘ └───────────────┘ └────────────────────────┘ │ Grafana, Zipkin/Jaeger traces│
                                                                  └──────────────────────────────┘

Talk through each piece (2–3 sentences each):

  1. Frontend: an Angular 16+ SPA with lazy-loaded modules (dashboard, incidents, devices, admin), an OpenLayers/Leaflet map, and WebSocket (STOMP) for live alerts. An HTTP interceptor adds the token and handles 401s.
  2. Ingress + API Gateway: NGINX Ingress terminates TLS. Spring Cloud Gateway handles routing (/api/incidents/** → lb://incident-service), JWT validation, Redis-backed rate limiting, a X-Correlation-Id filter, and a circuit breaker with fallbacks for non-critical widgets.
  3. Service discovery & config: Eureka with Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, which we later moved to Kubernetes Services/DNS. Spring Cloud Config Server is backed by Git, one file per profile (dev/uat/prod), with secrets pulled from Vault.
  4. Core services:
    • sensor-ingestion-service: receives about 5k msgs/sec from MQTT and HTTP device gateways, validates and normalises them, writes raw readings to Kafka sensor.readings.raw (keyed by deviceId), applies threshold rules, and publishes sensor.alerts.
    • incident-service: consumes alerts, auto-creates incidents with deduplication, and handles the lifecycle (NEW → ASSIGNED → IN_PROGRESS → RESOLVED → CLOSED) and SLA timers. It publishes incident.events through a transactional outbox.
    • notification-service: consumes incident.events and notification.requests, renders templates (MongoDB), and sends SMS (gateway API), email, FCM push, and WebSocket updates. Retry topics plus a DLT.
    • user-service: user profiles, zones, and shift rosters, synced with Keycloak.
    • reporting-service: builds read models (incidents per zone, MTTR) from events, CQRS-style, for the dashboards.
  5. Data: a database per service: PostgreSQL (incidents, users), TimescaleDB/InfluxDB (sensor time series), MongoDB (notification templates and logs), Redis (cache, rate limits, distributed locks), Elasticsearch (search and reporting).
  6. Messaging: Kafka with 3 brokers, replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2, idempotent producers, consumer groups per service. Partitions are sized for throughput (12 for sensor topics).
  7. Deployment: Docker images (Eclipse Temurin 17/21 JRE, non-root, layered jars), Helm charts, Kubernetes with HPA on CPU and Kafka lag, readiness/liveness probes from Actuator, rolling updates.
  8. Observability: JSON logs via Logback → Filebeat/Fluent Bit → Elasticsearch → Kibana; Micrometer → Prometheus → Grafana dashboards and Alertmanager (Slack/email); Micrometer Tracing → Zipkin.

Numbers worth having ready (make them real): ~10 services, ~3 environments, ~5k sensor events/sec at peak, ~2k concurrent operators, p95 API latency < 300 ms, 99.9% availability target.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why Kafka rather than calling incident-service from sensor-service directly? It decouples them and absorbs bursts. Sensor data keeps flowing while incident-service is down or redeploying, and several consumers (reporting, notification) can read the same stream.
  • Why Eureka if you're on K8s? Legacy from the VM deployment. On K8s, the built-in Service DNS plus Spring Cloud Kubernetes (or plain http://incident-service) makes Eureka unnecessary.
  • How do you deploy without downtime? Rolling updates with readiness probes, graceful shutdown (server.shutdown=graceful), backward-compatible DB migrations (Flyway, expand/contract), and a PodDisruptionBudget.
D10 How do microservices communicate? Hexaware
  • Synchronous: REST over HTTP using OpenFeign (declarative), WebClient (non-blocking) or RestClient, or gRPC (binary protobuf, fast, good for internal calls). Use it when the caller needs an immediate answer. The downside is tight runtime coupling.
  • Asynchronous: Kafka (high-throughput event streams, replay) or RabbitMQ (task queues, routing). Use it for events and for decoupling services and absorbing load spikes.
  • Example answer: "We use Feign plus Spring Cloud LoadBalancer for queries such as incident-svc fetching user details, and Kafka for events such as sensor readings and incident notifications."
@FeignClient(name = "user-service")
public interface UserClient {
    @GetMapping("/api/users/{id}")
    UserDto getUser(@PathVariable Long id);
}

10.1 Two styles

SYNCHRONOUS (request/response)                ASYNCHRONOUS (event/message)
A ──HTTP/gRPC──► B                            A ──publish──► [Kafka topic] ──► B
A waits (blocks/awaits) for B's answer        A continues immediately; B processes later
Criterion Sync (REST/gRPC) Async (Kafka/RabbitMQ)
Coupling Temporal coupling: B must be up Decoupled in time; the broker buffers
Latency to caller Immediate response Eventual; caller doesn't get B's result inline
Failure handling Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers Retries, DLT, replay; broker durability
Consistency Easier read-your-writes Eventual consistency
Scalability under bursts B must scale with A Queue smooths load; consumers scale independently
Fan-out A calls each consumer One event, many consumers (pub/sub)
Debugging Simpler call chain Harder; needs tracing across the broker
Best for Queries, validations that need an answer now ("is this user active?") State-change notifications, long jobs, integration, high-volume streams

10.2 REST clients in Spring

Client Style Status
RestTemplate Sync, blocking Maintenance mode; still common in existing code
WebClient Reactive, non-blocking For WebFlux or high-concurrency fan-out
RestClient (Spring 6.1+) Sync, fluent API Recommended new sync client
OpenFeign Declarative interface Popular in Spring Cloud stacks
HTTP Interface (@HttpExchange) Declarative, built into Spring 6 A Feign alternative with no extra dependency

RestClient with timeouts:

@Configuration
public class HttpClientsConfig {

    @Bean
    @LoadBalanced                                 // only if using Spring Cloud LoadBalancer / Eureka
    RestClient.Builder loadBalancedBuilder() {
        return RestClient.builder();
    }

    @Bean
    RestClient userServiceClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {
        var factory = new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory();
        factory.setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));
        factory.setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3));
        return builder
                .baseUrl("http://user-service")
                .requestFactory(factory)
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.ACCEPT, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class UserClient {
    private final RestClient userServiceClient;

    public UserDto getUser(String id) {
        return userServiceClient.get()
                .uri("/api/users/{id}", id)
                .retrieve()
                .onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is4xxClientError, (req, res) -> {
                    throw new UserNotFoundException(id);
                })
                .body(UserDto.class);
    }
}

OpenFeign:

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableFeignClients
public class IncidentServiceApplication { public static void main(String[] a) { SpringApplication.run(IncidentServiceApplication.class, a); } }

@FeignClient(name = "user-service", path = "/api/users", fallbackFactory = UserClientFallbackFactory.class)
public interface UserFeignClient {
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    UserDto getUser(@PathVariable("id") String id);

    @GetMapping
    List<UserDto> findByZone(@RequestParam("zoneId") String zoneId);
}

@Component
@Slf4j
class UserClientFallbackFactory implements FallbackFactory<UserFeignClient> {
    @Override
    public UserFeignClient create(Throwable cause) {
        return new UserFeignClient() {
            public UserDto getUser(String id) {
                log.warn("user-service unavailable for {}: {}", id, cause.toString());
                return UserDto.unknown(id);
            }
            public List<UserDto> findByZone(String zoneId) { return List.of(); }
        };
    }
}
spring:
  cloud:
    openfeign:
      circuitbreaker:
        enabled: true            # wraps Feign calls with Resilience4j so the fallbacks are used
      client:
        config:
          default:
            connect-timeout: 2000
            read-timeout: 3000
            logger-level: basic

        .retrieve().bodyToMono(UserDto.class).timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));

10.3 Kafka (Spring Kafka)

spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka-0:9092,kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        linger.ms: 5
    consumer:
      group-id: notification-service
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      enable-auto-commit: false
      key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
        spring.json.trusted.packages: "com.smartcity.events"
    listener:
      ack-mode: record
public record IncidentEvent(String eventId, String type, Long incidentId, String zoneId,
                            String severity, Instant occurredAt) {}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@Slf4j
public class IncidentEventPublisher {
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, IncidentEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    public void publish(IncidentEvent event) {
        // key = incidentId → every event for one incident goes to the same partition → ordered
        kafkaTemplate.send("incident.events", String.valueOf(event.incidentId()), event)
                .whenComplete((result, ex) -> {
                    if (ex != null) {
                        log.error("Publish failed for {}", event.eventId(), ex);
                    } else {
                        log.debug("Published {} to partition {} offset {}", event.eventId(),
                                result.getRecordMetadata().partition(), result.getRecordMetadata().offset());
                    }
                });
    }
}

@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@Slf4j
public class IncidentEventListener {
    private final NotificationService notificationService;
    private final ProcessedEventRepository processed;   // idempotency table

    @KafkaListener(topics = "incident.events", groupId = "notification-service", concurrency = "3")
    public void onEvent(IncidentEvent event,
                        @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_PARTITION) int partition,
                        @Header(KafkaHeaders.OFFSET) long offset) {
        if (processed.existsById(event.eventId())) {
            log.info("Duplicate event {} skipped", event.eventId());
            return;
        }
        notificationService.notifyForIncident(event);
        processed.save(new ProcessedEvent(event.eventId(), Instant.now()));
    }
}

10.4 gRPC

gRPC carries Protocol Buffers (binary, schema-first) over HTTP/2. It gives multiplexing, streaming (unary, server, client, bidirectional), generated clients, and fast serialisation. It suits internal high-throughput, low-latency calls (e.g. sensor-service → rules engine). Downsides: browsers can't call it directly (you need gRPC-Web), payloads aren't human-readable, and it needs HTTP/2-aware load balancing. Spring has the spring-grpc project (or grpc-spring-boot-starter).

syntax = "proto3";
service RuleEngine {
  rpc Evaluate (SensorReading) returns (RuleResult);
  rpc StreamReadings (stream SensorReading) returns (stream RuleResult);
}
message SensorReading { string device_id = 1; double value = 2; int64 ts = 3; }
message RuleResult   { bool breached = 1; string rule_id = 2; }

Other options: RabbitMQ (smart broker, routing, per-message ack, good for task queues), WebSockets/SSE (server → browser push), GraphQL (client-shaped queries at the BFF).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Feign vs RestClient? Feign is declarative and integrates with Spring Cloud LoadBalancer and circuit breakers. RestClient is built in, with explicit control and no extra dependency. Both are fine; be consistent.
  • How do you propagate the JWT or correlation ID in Feign? A RequestInterceptor that copies headers from the current request (or TokenRelay at the gateway). Micrometer Tracing propagates trace headers automatically.
  • How do you guarantee an event is published when the DB commit succeeds? The Transactional Outbox (D24). Writing to the DB and then calling kafkaTemplate.send is a dual write, and either half can fail.
  • How does a consumer handle a poison message? ErrorHandlingDeserializer plus a DefaultErrorHandler with a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, so the bad record goes to the DLT instead of blocking the partition.
D11 Circuit breaker. Hexaware

A circuit breaker stops calling a failing service so that failures don't cascade, and returns a fallback instead.

It has three states:

  • CLOSED: calls go through normally. The breaker tracks the failure rate.
  • OPEN: the failure rate went over the threshold. Calls fail fast to the fallback for the wait duration.
  • HALF_OPEN: after the wait, a few trial calls are allowed. If they succeed the breaker goes back to CLOSED; if they fail it returns to OPEN.
CLOSED --(failure rate > 50%)--> OPEN --(wait 10s)--> HALF_OPEN --(trial ok)--> CLOSED
                                   ^-------------(trial fails)---------|
@CircuitBreaker(name = "userService", fallbackMethod = "userFallback")
public UserDto getUser(Long id) { return userClient.getUser(id); }

private UserDto userFallback(Long id, Throwable ex) {
    return new UserDto(id, "Unknown", "N/A");   // or a cached value
}
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.userService:
  sliding-window-size: 10
  failure-rate-threshold: 50
  wait-duration-in-open-state: 10s
  permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 3

11.1 Why

Without a breaker, when service B is slow, every call from A waits until timeout, so A's threads pile up and A goes down too: a cascading failure. A circuit breaker fails fast once B is clearly unhealthy, gives B time to recover, and probes it periodically.

11.2 State machine

                failure rate ≥ threshold OR slow-call rate ≥ threshold
                (evaluated over sliding window, after minimumNumberOfCalls)
     ┌────────┐ ─────────────────────────────────────────────► ┌────────┐
     │ CLOSED │                                                │  OPEN  │  all calls rejected
