     │ calls  │ ◄──────────┐                                   │        │  immediately with
     │ pass   │            │                                   └───┬────┘  CallNotPermittedException
     └────────┘            │ trial calls OK                        │       → fallback
          ▲                │ (failure rate < threshold)            │ waitDurationInOpenState elapses
          │           ┌────┴──────┐                                │
          └───────────│ HALF_OPEN │◄───────────────────────────────┘
                      │ permit N  │
                      │ trial     │──── trial calls fail ────► back to OPEN
                      │ calls     │
                      └───────────┘
  Extra states: DISABLED (always allow), FORCED_OPEN (always reject), METRICS_ONLY

11.3 Sliding windows

  • COUNT_BASED: the last N calls (a ring buffer). Example: size 10 with 5 failures = 50% failure rate.
  • TIME_BASED: calls in the last N seconds, stored as N one-second buckets. Better when traffic is uneven.
  • minimumNumberOfCalls: no decision is made until this many calls are recorded, so 1 failure out of 1 call doesn't open the circuit.
  • Slow calls: calls longer than slowCallDurationThreshold count toward slowCallRateThreshold. The breaker can open on latency alone, before any errors appear.

11.4 Resilience4j configuration

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.github.resilience4j</groupId>
  <artifactId>resilience4j-spring-boot3</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-aop</artifactId>   <!-- needed for the annotations -->
</dependency>
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    configs:
      default:
        register-health-indicator: true
        sliding-window-type: COUNT_BASED
        sliding-window-size: 20
        minimum-number-of-calls: 10
        failure-rate-threshold: 50              # %
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 2s
        slow-call-rate-threshold: 60            # %
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s
        permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 5
        automatic-transition-from-open-to-half-open-enabled: true
        record-exceptions:
          - java.io.IOException
          - java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException
          - org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException
        ignore-exceptions:
          - com.smartcity.common.exception.BusinessValidationException   # 4xx are not B's fault
    instances:
      userService:
        base-config: default
      smsGateway:
        base-config: default
        sliding-window-type: TIME_BASED
        sliding-window-size: 60                 # seconds
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 60s
  timelimiter:
    instances:
      userService:
        timeout-duration: 3s
        cancel-running-future: true

management:
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,circuitbreakers,circuitbreakerevents,prometheus
  health.circuitbreakers.enabled: true
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@Slf4j
public class AssigneeLookupService {

    private final UserClient userClient;
    private final CacheManager cacheManager;

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "userService", fallbackMethod = "getAssigneeFallback")
    public UserDto getAssignee(String userId) {
        UserDto user = userClient.getUser(userId);
        Objects.requireNonNull(cacheManager.getCache("users")).put(userId, user);  // keep last-known-good copy
        return user;
    }

    /** Same signature + Throwable as the last param. A more specific exception type wins. */
    private UserDto getAssigneeFallback(String userId, CallNotPermittedException ex) {
        log.warn("Circuit OPEN for userService, serving cached user {}", userId);
        return cachedOrPlaceholder(userId);
    }

    private UserDto getAssigneeFallback(String userId, Throwable ex) {
        log.warn("userService call failed for {}: {}", userId, ex.toString());
        return cachedOrPlaceholder(userId);
    }

    private UserDto cachedOrPlaceholder(String userId) {
        Cache cache = cacheManager.getCache("users");
        UserDto cached = cache != null ? cache.get(userId, UserDto.class) : null;
        return cached != null ? cached : UserDto.unknown(userId);
    }
}

Monitor the breaker state and transitions in Grafana (resilience4j_circuitbreaker_state) and alert when a breaker opens.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Which exceptions should count as failures? Infrastructure failures (timeouts, connection refused, 5xx). Not client errors (400, 404, validation): those don't mean B is unhealthy.
  • What should a fallback return? Cached or stale data, a default, an empty list, or a "degraded" flag. Or queue the work for later. Never quietly return fake success for writes.
  • Gateway-level or service-level breaker? Both have a place. The gateway's CircuitBreaker filter protects edge routes; service-level breakers protect specific dependencies with business-aware fallbacks.
  • What replaced Hystrix? Resilience4j. Hystrix has been in maintenance mode since 2018.
D12 Retry mechanism. Hexaware
  • Retry is for transient failures such as network blips and 503s. Don't retry 4xx errors or business errors.
  • Use exponential backoff with jitter so retries don't create a thundering herd.
  • Only retry idempotent operations, or make writes idempotent with an idempotency key.
  • Put Retry inside the CircuitBreaker so that retries count toward the failure rate.
@Retry(name = "trafficApi", fallbackMethod = "fallback")
@CircuitBreaker(name = "trafficApi", fallbackMethod = "fallback")
public SignalStatus fetchStatus(String junctionId) { return client.status(junctionId); }
resilience4j.retry.instances.trafficApi:
  max-attempts: 3
  wait-duration: 500ms
  enable-exponential-backoff: true
  exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2
  retry-exceptions: [java.io.IOException, java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException]
  • Spring Retry is an alternative: @EnableRetry, then @Retryable(retryFor = IOException.class, maxAttempts = 3, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 500, multiplier = 2)) with a @Recover method.
  • Kafka: use @RetryableTopic(attempts = "4", backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2)). Failed messages go to retry topics and finally to a DLT (@DltHandler) for alerting or manual replay. Alternatively use DefaultErrorHandler with DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer.

12.1 When to retry

Retry only transient failures: connection reset, timeouts, 503, 429 (honour Retry-After), Kafka NotLeaderForPartition. Don't retry permanent failures (400, 401, 403, 404, validation errors), because the result will never change.

Only retry idempotent operations, or make them idempotent first. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics. A POST that creates an incident isn't. A retry after a timeout (where the first request actually succeeded) creates a duplicate. Fix it with an Idempotency-Key header that the server stores together with the result, or with a unique business key.

12.2 Backoff and jitter

Fixed:        |--500ms--|--500ms--|--500ms--|       → synchronized clients hammer B together
Exponential:  |-500-|---1000---|-------2000-------| → gives B time to recover
+ Jitter:     each wait = random(0.5x .. 1.5x)       → spreads retries; avoids the "thundering herd"

Retry storms multiply: with 3 layers that each retry 3 times, one user request becomes 27 calls to the bottom service. Retry at one layer (usually the one closest to the failing dependency), and cap the total time with timeouts.

12.3 Resilience4j @Retry

resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      userService:
        max-attempts: 3                        # including the first call
        wait-duration: 500ms
        enable-exponential-backoff: true
        exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2      # 500ms, 1000ms
        enable-randomized-wait: true           # combined with exponential → exponential random backoff
        randomized-wait-factor: 0.5
        retry-exceptions:
          - java.io.IOException
          - org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException$ServiceUnavailable
        ignore-exceptions:
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpClientErrorException
@Retry(name = "userService")
@CircuitBreaker(name = "userService", fallbackMethod = "fallback")
public UserDto getUser(String id) {
    return userClient.getUser(id);
}

private UserDto fallback(String id, Throwable t) {
    return UserDto.unknown(id);
}

12.4 Order: retry vs circuit breaker

Resilience4j's default aspect order (outermost first):

Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter ( Bulkhead ( yourMethod ) ) ) ) )
  • Retry outside the circuit breaker (the default, recommended): every attempt is recorded by the breaker. Once the breaker opens, the next retry gets CallNotPermittedException straight away. Make that exception non-retryable (don't list it in retry-exceptions, or put it in ignore-exceptions) so you don't retry against an open circuit.
  • The fallback is attached to the outermost decorator you put fallbackMethod on. Usually that's only the circuit breaker, or the retry if you want the fallback after every attempt has failed.
  • Order can be changed with resilience4j.retry.retry-aspect-order and resilience4j.circuitbreaker.circuit-breaker-aspect-order (a higher value means higher priority, i.e. it runs outermost).

12.5 Spring Retry (alternative)

@Configuration
@EnableRetry
class RetryConfig { }

@Service
class SmsGatewayClient {
    @Retryable(retryFor = {ResourceAccessException.class},
               maxAttempts = 4,
               backoff = @Backoff(delay = 500, multiplier = 2, maxDelay = 5000, random = true))
    public void send(SmsRequest req) { /* call SMS provider */ }

    @Recover
    public void recover(ResourceAccessException ex, SmsRequest req) {
        // after all attempts: queue for later / mark FAILED
    }
}

12.6 Kafka consumer retries: non-blocking retry topics + DLT

A blocking retry (DefaultErrorHandler with FixedBackOff) stops the whole partition while it retries one bad record. @RetryableTopic moves the failed record to delay topics, so the main topic keeps flowing:

incident.events ──fail──► incident.events-retry-0 (1s) ──fail──► -retry-1 (2s) ──fail──► -retry-2 (4s) ──fail──► incident.events-dlt
                                                                                                                  │
                                                                                     @DltHandler: alert, persist, manual replay
@Component
@Slf4j
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class NotificationListener {

    private final NotificationService service;

    @RetryableTopic(
            attempts = "4",                                     // 1 original + 3 retries
            backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2.0, maxDelay = 10000),
            dltTopicSuffix = "-dlt",
            exclude = {DeserializationException.class, IllegalArgumentException.class}, // straight to DLT
            autoCreateTopics = "true")
    @KafkaListener(topics = "incident.events", groupId = "notification-service")
    public void onIncident(IncidentEvent event) {
        service.notifyForIncident(event);   // throws → goes to the next retry topic
    }

    @DltHandler
    public void onDlt(IncidentEvent event,
                      @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_TOPIC) String topic,
                      @Header(KafkaHeaders.EXCEPTION_MESSAGE) String error) {
        log.error("DLT {} event={} error={}", topic, event.eventId(), error);
        // save to failed_events table + raise alert; ops can replay after fixing
    }
}

(@Backoff here is org.springframework.retry.annotation.Backoff in Spring Kafka 3.x.) Note that retry topics break strict ordering for the retried key. If ordering matters, use a blocking retry with a short backoff instead.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How many retries? Usually 2–3 for sync calls, with the total bounded by the caller's timeout or SLA. More retries just add latency.
  • What is a retry budget? Cap retries to a percentage of traffic (e.g. ≤10%) so retries can't overload a struggling service.
  • How do you make a POST idempotent? The client sends an Idempotency-Key (UUID). The server stores key → response under a unique constraint and returns the stored response on a repeat.
  • What's in the DLT and how do you reprocess it? The original record plus exception headers. A small admin tool or consumer republishes it to the main topic once the bug is fixed.
D13 If Microservice B is down, what should A do? Hexaware
  1. Timeouts: never wait forever. Set connect and read timeouts, and use a Resilience4j @TimeLimiter.
  2. Retry a few times with backoff, but only for transient errors.
  3. Circuit breaker + fallback: fail fast and return a default, a cached last-known response (Redis), or a partial response.
  4. Go async: if B's work can wait, publish to Kafka or a queue. B consumes the message when it recovers. The user gets "202 Accepted, processing".
  5. Graceful degradation: for example, the incident dashboard still loads but shows "weather data unavailable".
  6. Bulkhead: isolate the thread pools for calls to B so A's other features keep working.
  7. Alerting/monitoring: health checks, Prometheus alerts on circuit state, Kubernetes restarts the pods, and multiple B replicas behind a load balancer.

Principle: A must degrade gracefully, never hang, and never cascade the failure. Layer the techniques:

A ── call ─► [Timeout] ─► [Retry (transient only)] ─► [Circuit Breaker] ─► [Bulkhead] ─► B
                                                          │ open / failed
                                                          ▼
                                    Fallback: cache / default / queue for later / partial response
# Technique What A does Example in Smart City
1 Timeouts Connect 1–2 s, read 2–5 s. Never wait forever (RestTemplate's default is infinite) Incident detail page calls user-service with a 2 s timeout
2 Retry with backoff 1–2 retries for transient errors, idempotent calls only GET user profile
3 Circuit breaker Stop calling B once it's unhealthy, fail fast, probe in half-open userService breaker opens at 50% failures
4 Fallback Return a sensible degraded response Show "Assignee: unavailable" while the incident still renders
5 Cached / stale data Serve the last-known-good copy from Redis or a local cache (Caffeine) Zone and user names change rarely, so serve them from cache
6 Async via queue For commands, don't call B synchronously. Publish an event/message; B processes it when it's back Incident created → notification.requests on Kafka; notification-service catches up after restarting
7 Transactional outbox Save the business change and the outbox row in one DB transaction; a relay publishes when the broker or B is reachable Incident status change always produces an event eventually
8 Bulkhead Separate thread pools or semaphores per dependency, so slow B can't use up all of A's threads SMS gateway gets max 20 concurrent calls; the dashboard APIs are unaffected
9 Graceful degradation / feature flags Turn off non-critical features Hide the "live camera feed" widget while video-service is down
10 Health checks & self-healing K8s liveness restarts a hung B; readiness takes it out of the Service endpoints; multiple replicas, PodDisruptionBudget, anti-affinity B pod OOM → restarted automatically; other replicas serve meanwhile
11 Alerting Breaker opens, error rate rises, up == 0 → Alertmanager → on-call Grafana alert "user-service 5xx > 5% for 5m"
12 Clear error to the client When there's no fallback, return 503 with Retry-After, not a raw 500 or a hang ProblemDetail "Service temporarily unavailable"

Bulkhead config:

resilience4j:
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      smsGateway:
        max-concurrent-calls: 20
        max-wait-duration: 100ms         # wait this long for a permit, then BulkheadFullException → fallback
  thread-pool-bulkhead:
    instances:
      reportService:
        core-thread-pool-size: 4
        max-thread-pool-size: 8
        queue-capacity: 50
@Bulkhead(name = "smsGateway", fallbackMethod = "queueSms")
@CircuitBreaker(name = "smsGateway")
public void sendSms(SmsRequest req) { smsClient.send(req); }

private void queueSms(SmsRequest req, Throwable t) {
    kafkaTemplate.send("notification.sms.retry", req.phone(), req);   // retry later; never lose the message
}

What to say in an interview: "It depends on whether A needs B's answer right now. For reads, I use a timeout, a circuit breaker, and cached or default data, and show a partial response. For writes/commands, I move to async: publish to Kafka through an outbox so the work happens when B is back, and tell the user 'accepted' (HTTP 202). In both cases, monitoring and K8s self-healing bring B back quickly, and alerts tell the team."

Likely follow-ups:

  • What if B is critical, like payment or authentication? Fail fast with a clear 503 and don't fake success. Use redundancy (multi-AZ replicas) and make sure it's caught by alerting. A queue is only acceptable if the business accepts a deferred result.
  • What's the difference between liveness and readiness? Liveness failing → K8s restarts the container. Readiness failing → the pod is removed from load balancing but not restarted (e.g. while it warms up or loses its DB connection).
  • How do you stop A's Kafka consumer from hammering B while B is down? Pause the listener container (KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry...pause()) when the breaker opens, and resume it when it closes, or rely on retry topics with backoff.
D14 API Gateway (Spring Cloud Gateway). Hexaware
  • It is the single entry point for all clients.
  • Responsibilities:
    • routing by path or host
    • authentication (JWT validation)
    • rate limiting (Redis)
    • load balancing (lb://service-name via discovery)
    • CORS
    • request/response header rewriting
    • circuit breaker and fallback at the edge
    • logging and correlation ID injection
    • SSL termination
    • API aggregation and versioning
  • Spring Cloud Gateway is reactive (Netty/WebFlux), built on routes, predicates and filters.
spring.cloud.gateway.routes:
  - id: incident-service
    uri: lb://INCIDENT-SERVICE
    predicates: [ Path=/api/incidents/** ]
    filters:
      - name: RequestRateLimiter
        args: { redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 50, redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 100 }
      - name: CircuitBreaker
        args: { name: incidentCB, fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/incidents }

14.1 What it is

An API Gateway is the single entry point for all clients. It sits in front of the microservices and handles cross-cutting concerns, so the services don't each have to.

 Angular / Mobile / Partners
            │
            ▼
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                       API GATEWAY                          │
 │ Routing • AuthN (JWT) • coarse AuthZ • Rate limiting       │
 │ CORS • TLS • Request/response rewriting • Circuit breaker  │
 │ Retry • Load balancing (lb://) • Correlation-ID • Logging  │
 │ Response aggregation (BFF) • API versioning • Caching      │
 └───────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬─────────────┬────────┘
         ▼              ▼              ▼             ▼
   incident-svc    sensor-svc     user-svc     notification-svc

Responsibilities:

  1. Routing: path, host, or header → service (with service discovery via lb://).
  2. Security: token validation, rejecting unauthenticated traffic at the edge, CORS, IP allow-lists.
  3. Rate limiting / throttling: per user, IP, or API key.
  4. Resilience: timeouts, circuit breakers, retries, fallbacks per route.
  5. Transformation: add, remove, or rewrite headers and paths, strip prefixes.
  6. Observability: access logs, metrics per route, trace propagation, correlation IDs.
  7. Aggregation / BFF: combine several backend calls into one client response.
  8. Hiding the internal topology: clients never see service hosts or ports.

14.2 Spring Cloud Gateway: how it works

It's built on Spring WebFlux and Netty (reactive, non-blocking), so a few threads handle many concurrent connections. Spring Cloud 2025 also ships a WebMVC (servlet) variant. Core concepts:

  • Route = ID + destination URI + predicates + filters
  • Predicate: matches requests (Path, Method, Header, Host, Query, After/Before, Weight)
  • Filter: changes the request or response, pre and post (GatewayFilter per route, GlobalFilter for all routes)
Request → Gateway Handler Mapping (match predicates → route)
        → Filter chain (pre: auth, rate limit, add header, ...)
        → Proxy to lb://incident-service
        ← Filter chain (post: add response headers, log latency)
← Response

14.3 Route configuration (YAML)

spring:
  application:
    name: api-gateway
  cloud:
    gateway:
      # NOTE: since Spring Cloud 2025.0 the preferred prefix is spring.cloud.gateway.server.webflux.*
      default-filters:
        - DedupeResponseHeader=Access-Control-Allow-Origin Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, RETAIN_UNIQUE
        - name: RequestRateLimiter
          args:
            redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 20       # tokens/sec per key
            redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 40
            redis-rate-limiter.requestedTokens: 1
            key-resolver: "#{@userKeyResolver}"
      globalcors:
        cors-configurations:
          '[/**]':
            allowedOrigins: "https://command-centre.smartcity.gov.in"
            allowedMethods: [GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS]
            allowedHeaders: [Authorization, Content-Type, X-Correlation-Id]
            maxAge: 3600
      routes:
        - id: incident-service
          uri: lb://incident-service
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/incidents/**
          filters:
            - TokenRelay=
            - name: CircuitBreaker
              args:
                name: incidentCB
                fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/incidents
            - name: Retry
              args:
                retries: 2
                methods: GET
                statuses: BAD_GATEWAY,SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
                backoff:
                  firstBackoff: 100ms
                  maxBackoff: 1s
                  factor: 2

        - id: sensor-service
          uri: lb://sensor-ingestion-service
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/sensors/**
          filters:
            - RewritePath=/api/sensors/(?<segment>.*), /v1/sensors/${segment}

        - id: notification-service-v2-canary
          uri: lb://notification-service-v2
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/notifications/**
            - Weight=notifications, 10          # 10% canary
        - id: notification-service-v1
          uri: lb://notification-service
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/notifications/**
            - Weight=notifications, 90

      httpclient:
        connect-timeout: 2000
        response-timeout: 5s

  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://keycloak.smartcity.local/realms/smartcity

The TokenRelay filter needs the gateway to be an OAuth2 client (spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client, session-based login at the gateway, i.e. the BFF style). When the SPA already sends a bearer token, the Authorization header is forwarded unchanged by default, so you only need oauth2ResourceServer on the gateway.

14.4 Gateway security, key resolver and a custom global filter

@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
public class GatewaySecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain springSecurityFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
        return http
                .csrf(ServerHttpSecurity.CsrfSpec::disable)
                .authorizeExchange(ex -> ex
                        .pathMatchers("/actuator/health/**", "/fallback/**").permitAll()
                        .pathMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                        .anyExchange().authenticated())
                .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    KeyResolver userKeyResolver() {
        return exchange -> exchange.getPrincipal()
                .map(Principal::getName)
                .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.ofNullable(exchange.getRequest().getRemoteAddress())
                        .map(a -> a.getAddress().getHostAddress()).orElse("anonymous"));
    }
}
@Component
public class CorrelationIdGlobalFilter implements GlobalFilter, Ordered {

    public static final String HEADER = "X-Correlation-Id";

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, GatewayFilterChain chain) {
        String id = Optional.ofNullable(exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst(HEADER))
                .orElse(UUID.randomUUID().toString());
        ServerHttpRequest mutated = exchange.getRequest().mutate().header(HEADER, id).build();
        exchange.getResponse().getHeaders().add(HEADER, id);
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        return chain.filter(exchange.mutate().request(mutated).build())
                .doFinally(sig -> {
                    long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
                    // log: method, path, status, ms, correlation id
                });
    }

    @Override
    public int getOrder() { return Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE; }
}
@RestController
class FallbackController {
    @RequestMapping("/fallback/incidents")
    Mono<ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail>> incidents() {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE,
                "Incident service is temporarily unavailable. Please retry shortly.");
        return Mono.just(ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE).body(pd));
    }
}

14.5 API Gateway vs Load Balancer

Load Balancer (L4/L7) API Gateway
Main job Spread traffic over identical instances of one service Route to many different services and apply API policies
Awareness Connections and HTTP basics API semantics: auth, users, quotas, versions
Features Health checks, algorithms, TLS termination Auth, rate limiting, transformation, aggregation, circuit breaking
Examples AWS ALB/NLB, NGINX, HAProxy, F5 Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway
Typical layout Internet → LB → Gateway (N replicas) → services The gateway itself sits behind an LB and load-balances to services

Pitfalls: the gateway can become a single point of failure (run several replicas behind an LB) or a bottleneck, and putting business logic in it turns it into a "god gateway". Keep it thin.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why is Spring Cloud Gateway reactive? A gateway spends almost all its time waiting on network I/O. Non-blocking Netty handles thousands of connections with few threads. Never call blocking code in its filters.
  • How does lb:// work? ReactiveLoadBalancerClientFilter resolves the service name through DiscoveryClient (Eureka/K8s) and picks an instance (round-robin by default).
  • Gateway vs BFF? A BFF is a gateway built for one client type (web vs mobile), with aggregation and response shapes tailored to that client.
  • How does rate limiting work? A token bucket per key, held in Redis by a Lua script so it's atomic across gateway replicas. When the bucket is empty the client gets 429 with X-RateLimit-* headers.
D15 Load Balancer; Application Load Balancer. Hexaware
  • A load balancer distributes traffic across instances to give scalability and high availability. It health-checks instances and removes unhealthy ones.
  • L4 (transport, TCP/UDP): routes by IP and port. It is fast but cannot see content. AWS NLB is an example.
  • L7 (application, HTTP): routes by path, host, headers or cookies. It can do SSL termination and sticky sessions. AWS ALB is an example: /api/traffic/* goes to the traffic target group, and admin.city.gov goes to the admin UI.
  • Server-side vs client-side load balancing: an ALB or Nginx sits in front of the system (server-side). Spring Cloud LoadBalancer is client-side: the caller gets the instance list from Eureka and picks one itself (round-robin by default). Feign and @LoadBalanced WebClient/RestTemplate use it automatically.
@Bean @LoadBalanced
WebClient.Builder webClientBuilder() { return WebClient.builder(); }
// webClientBuilder.build().get().uri("http://traffic-service/api/signals")...

15.1 L4 vs L7

OSI:  L7 Application (HTTP, gRPC)   ← ALB / NGINX / Envoy: sees URL, headers, cookies
      L4 Transport (TCP/UDP)        ← NLB / HAProxy TCP mode: sees IP:port only
Layer 4 (Network LB) Layer 7 (Application LB)
Decides by IP, port, protocol URL path, host, headers, cookies, HTTP method, query
TLS Passes through (or terminates at TLS level) Terminates TLS, inspects HTTP
Speed Very fast, millions of req/s, static IPs, ultra-low latency Slightly more overhead
Features Simple forwarding, preserves client IP Path/host routing, redirects, header rewrites, WAF integration, auth (OIDC), sticky cookies, HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSockets
AWS NLB ALB
Use Non-HTTP (MQTT on 8883, databases), extreme throughput, static IP needs Web/API traffic, microservice routing

Smart City usage: an NLB in front of the MQTT brokers (TCP 8883 from IoT devices) and an ALB (or NGINX Ingress) in front of the API gateway and Angular static content.

15.2 Algorithms

Algorithm How Good for
Round robin Next server in turn Similar servers, similar requests
Weighted round robin More traffic to bigger servers or the stable version Mixed instance sizes, canary
Least connections Fewest active connections Long-lived or uneven requests (WebSockets)
Least response time / "least outstanding requests" (ALB) Fastest/least busy Variable latency
IP hash / consistent hashing Same client → same server Cache affinity, sharded state
Random / power of two choices Pick 2 at random, choose the less loaded Large clusters, low overhead

15.3 Health checks

  • Active: the LB polls GET /actuator/health/readiness every N seconds; after x failures the target is marked unhealthy and taken out of rotation, and after y successes it goes back in.
  • Passive: watch real traffic (errors/timeouts) and eject bad hosts (Envoy outlier detection).
  • Use the readiness endpoint (does it depend on DB/Kafka?) for LB health. Keep liveness cheap and free of dependencies.
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true            # /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState, db, redis

15.4 Sticky sessions

The LB keeps sending a client to the same instance, based on a cookie (AWSALB) or the source IP. You need it for stateful apps that keep HTTP sessions in memory. Downsides: uneven load, sessions lost when an instance dies, harder scaling. Prefer stateless services (JWT) or an external session store (Spring Session + Redis). Sticky sessions are still sometimes used for WebSocket/STOMP connections.

15.5 AWS ALB / NLB specifics

  • ALB: listeners (HTTP/HTTPS) → rules (path /api/*, host admin.city.gov, header) → target groups (EC2, IPs, Lambda, ECS/EKS pods via the AWS Load Balancer Controller). Supports ACM certificates, WAF, OIDC/Cognito auth, slow start, deregistration delay (connection draining), and HTTP/2 and gRPC.
  • NLB: TCP/UDP/TLS, static Elastic IPs, preserves the source IP, handles huge scale. Good for MQTT, or as the entry point for a PrivateLink service.
  • GWLB: for inline security appliances (firewalls).
  • Cross-zone load balancing and multi-AZ targets give high availability.

15.6 Server-side vs client-side load balancing

Server-side:  A ──► [LB] ──► B1 | B2 | B3          (ALB, NGINX, K8s Service/kube-proxy)
Client-side:  A (knows B1,B2,B3 from registry) ──► picks B2 directly
              (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer + Eureka, gRPC client LB, service-mesh sidecar)
@Bean
@LoadBalanced                      // RestClient resolves "http://user-service" through DiscoveryClient
RestClient.Builder restClientBuilder() { return RestClient.builder(); }

Client-side LB removes a network hop and the LB as a bottleneck, but every client needs the logic and a registry. In K8s, a ClusterIP Service gives L4 load balancing through kube-proxy. Since gRPC uses long-lived HTTP/2 connections, it needs L7 or client-side LB (a headless Service or a mesh).

Likely follow-ups:

  • What is connection draining? When a target is deregistered (during deploys), the LB stops sending new requests but lets in-flight ones finish (ALB deregistration delay, default 300 s). Pair it with Spring's server.shutdown=graceful.
  • How does the backend get the real client IP behind an ALB? From the X-Forwarded-For header. Set server.forward-headers-strategy=framework (or native) in Spring Boot.
  • Is the LB a single point of failure? Managed LBs (ALB/NLB) are redundant across AZs. With self-hosted NGINX/HAProxy, run an active-passive pair with keepalived/a VIP.
D16 Distributed caching and distributed tracing. Hexaware
  • Distributed caching means a cache shared by all instances. Redis is the usual choice; Hazelcast is an embedded or clustered alternative. Each instance's local cache would go stale independently, so a shared cache keeps them consistent.
    • Use it for master data, sessions, refresh tokens and rate limits.
    • Spring setup: @EnableCaching plus @Cacheable("zones"), @CachePut, @CacheEvict.
    • Always set a TTL. Handle cache invalidation and stampede (locking, or jittered TTLs).
  • Distributed tracing follows one request across services.
    • A traceId is shared by the whole request. A spanId identifies one operation or hop.
    • In Spring Boot 3, use Micrometer Tracing (Brave or OpenTelemetry bridge) and export to Zipkin or Jaeger.
    • The IDs propagate through HTTP headers (W3C traceparent) and Kafka headers, and they appear in logs through MDC, so you can grep ELK by traceId.
management.tracing.sampling.probability: 1.0      # lower in prod, e.g. 0.1
management.zipkin.tracing.endpoint: http://zipkin:9411/api/v2/spans
logging.pattern.level: "%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId},%X{spanId}]"

Part A: Distributed caching

Why distributed rather than local? With 6 pods of incident-service, a local cache (Caffeine) gives 6 different copies: inconsistent, invalidated separately, and each pod warms up cold. A distributed cache (Redis/Hazelcast) is shared by all instances and survives pod restarts.

Two-level cache: L1 Caffeine in-process (microseconds, small, short TTL) + L2 Redis (sub-ms network hop, shared). This works well for very hot reference data such as zones and device types.

Redis topologies:

Standalone            Sentinel (HA)                    Cluster (HA + sharding)
┌──────┐              ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐       16384 hash slots split across masters
│Redis │              │Sent 1│ │Sent 2│ │Sent 3│       ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐
└──────┘              └──┬───┘ └──┬───┘ └──┬───┘       │Master A│ │Master B│ │Master C│
                         ▼ monitor & failover          │0-5460  │ │5461-   │ │10923-  │
                      ┌──────┐   ┌───────┐             └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘
                      │Master│──►│Replica│              Replica A'  Replica B'  Replica C'
                      └──────┘   └───────┘             slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384
  • Sentinel: one master with replicas; Sentinels detect failure and promote a replica. Good for HA when the data fits on one node.
  • Cluster: shards data across masters by hash slot, each with replicas, so it scales writes and memory. Multi-key operations only work when the keys share a slot (use hash tags: {incident:42}:details, {incident:42}:history).

Caching patterns:

Pattern Flow Pros / Cons
Cache-aside (lazy loading) App reads the cache → on a miss, reads the DB → writes the cache. On update: write the DB, evict the cache Most common; only caches what's used. The first read is slow; there's a stale window
Read-through The cache library loads from the DB on a miss Simpler app code; needs cache-provider support
Write-through Write the cache and the DB synchronously Cache always fresh; slower writes
Write-behind (write-back) Write the cache; flush to the DB asynchronously Fast writes; risk of data loss
Refresh-ahead Refresh hot keys before their TTL runs out No miss spikes; extra load

Common problems:

  • Cache stampede / dogpile: a hot key expires and 1,000 requests hit the DB. Fixes: @Cacheable(sync = true) (per-JVM lock), a distributed lock, refresh-ahead, randomised TTLs.
  • Cache penetration: requests for IDs that don't exist always miss. Fixes: cache null results briefly, a Bloom filter.
  • Cache avalanche: many keys expire at once. Fix: TTL jitter.
  • Consistency: evicting on update is better than updating the cache. For cross-service invalidation, publish events.
  • Hot keys and big values: shard the key, compress, avoid values over 100 KB.

Spring Boot + Redis:

spring:
  data:
    redis:
      cluster:
        nodes: redis-0:6379,redis-1:6379,redis-2:6379
      password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD}
      timeout: 500ms
  cache:
    type: redis
@Configuration
@EnableCaching
public class CacheConfig {

    @Bean
    RedisCacheManager cacheManager(RedisConnectionFactory cf) {
        RedisCacheConfiguration defaults = RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig()
                .entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
                .disableCachingNullValues()
                .serializeValuesWith(RedisSerializationContext.SerializationPair
                        .fromSerializer(new GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer()));
        return RedisCacheManager.builder(cf)
                .cacheDefaults(defaults)
                .withCacheConfiguration("zones", defaults.entryTtl(Duration.ofHours(12)))
                .withCacheConfiguration("incidentSummary", defaults.entryTtl(Duration.ofSeconds(30)))
                .build();
    }
}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class ZoneService {
    private final ZoneRepository repo;

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "zones", key = "#zoneId", sync = true)
    public ZoneDto get(String zoneId) { return repo.findById(zoneId).map(ZoneDto::from).orElseThrow(); }

    @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "zones", key = "#zone.id")
    @Transactional
    public ZoneDto update(ZoneDto zone) { /* save */ return zone; }
}

Remember that @Cacheable is proxy-based too: self-invocation bypasses the cache.

Part B: Distributed tracing

Problem: one user click → gateway → incident-service → user-service → Kafka → notification-service. When it's slow or fails, where? Logs from five services don't line up unless they share an ID.

Concepts:

  • Trace: the whole journey of one request, identified by a traceId (128-bit).
  • Span: one unit of work inside it (an HTTP server request, a DB query, a Kafka send) with a spanId, parentSpanId, start/end time, and tags.
  • Context propagation: trace IDs travel in headers. The W3C Trace Context standard is traceparent: 00-<traceId>-<spanId>-01 (plus tracestate). Older Zipkin B3 headers are X-B3-TraceId, X-B3-SpanId, X-B3-Sampled, or the single b3 header.
  • Sampling: record 100% in dev and 5–10% in prod (or tail-based sampling in the OTel Collector so all errors are kept).
traceId=4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736
├─ span A  gateway  GET /api/incidents/42                    [0 ─────────────── 480ms]
│  └─ span B  incident-service  GET /api/incidents/{id}       [5 ────────────── 470ms]
│     ├─ span C  SELECT incident ... (JDBC)                   [10 ── 40ms]
│     ├─ span D  user-service GET /api/users/op7              [45 ───────── 430ms]  ← the slow one
│     │   └─ span E  SELECT user ... (JDBC)                   [50 ──────── 420ms]  ← missing index!
│     └─ span F  kafka send incident.events                   [440 ─ 450ms]
│        └─ span G  notification-service consume (async, linked)

Spring Boot 3 setup (Micrometer Tracing replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth):

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel</artifactId>   <!-- or micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave -->
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.opentelemetry</groupId>
  <artifactId>opentelemetry-exporter-zipkin</artifactId>   <!-- or opentelemetry-exporter-otlp for Jaeger/Tempo/OTel Collector -->
</dependency>
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 0.1          # 10% in prod; 1.0 in dev
    propagation:
      type: w3c                 # or b3
  zipkin:
    tracing:
      endpoint: http://zipkin:9411/api/v2/spans
  # OTLP alternative:
  # otlp:
  #   tracing:
  #     endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces

logging:
  pattern:
    level: "%5p [${spring.application.name:},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}]"

spring:
  kafka:
    template:
      observation-enabled: true   # propagate trace context into Kafka headers
    listener:
      observation-enabled: true
  • Auto-instrumented: incoming HTTP (Spring MVC/WebFlux), outgoing RestTemplate/RestClient/WebClient when built from the Spring-injected builder, Feign (with feign-micrometer), Kafka (with observation enabled), JDBC (with datasource-micrometer), @Observed methods.
  • MDC: Micrometer puts traceId and spanId into the SLF4J MDC, so every log line carries them. In Kibana, search traceId:4bf92f... and you get the logs from every service for that request.
  • Custom span:
@Observed(name = "incident.assign", contextualName = "assign-incident")
public void assign(Long incidentId, String officerId) { /* ... */ }

(Needs an ObservedAspect bean.)

Tools: Zipkin (simple), Jaeger (CNCF), Grafana Tempo, Elastic APM, AWS X-Ray. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics, and logs, with the OTel Collector in between to route and sample.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Correlation ID vs trace ID? A correlation ID is a business or request ID you control, often shown to users or support. A trace ID comes from the tracing system. Many teams use the trace ID as the correlation ID, or log both.
  • How does trace context cross Kafka? The producer puts traceparent in the record headers and the consumer continues the trace (a child span or a span link).
  • Why is my traceId missing in @Async threads? The context is ThreadLocal. Use a context-propagating TaskDecorator (ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator) on the executor.
  • What do you cache, and what don't you? Cache read-heavy data that changes rarely and tolerates brief staleness (zones, device metadata, user profiles). Don't cache rapidly changing or strongly consistent data (incident status during assignment, balances).
D17 What is Kafka and its working flow. Hexaware

Kafka is a distributed, durable, high-throughput event streaming platform built on an append-only log.

Producer --(key)--> Topic "sensor.readings" [P0][P1][P2]  (on Brokers, replicated)
                                 |    |    |
                   Consumer Group "analytics": C1<-P0,P1   C2<-P2
                   Consumer Group "alerts":    C3<-P0,P1,P2   (each group gets all messages)
  • Producer sends records to a topic. The key decides the partition (hash(key) % partitions), so records with the same key, such as the same sensor ID, land in the same partition and keep their order.
  • Topic is split into partitions, which are the unit of parallelism. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition.
  • Broker is a Kafka server. A cluster holds the partitions. Each partition has a leader plus followers (replication factor of 3 is typical). acks=all together with min.insync.replicas=2 gives durability.
  • Consumer group: each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in a group. Adding consumers (up to the partition count) scales consumption. Different groups each read every message independently.
  • Offsets are a consumer's position in a partition, committed to __consumer_offsets. Messages are retained by time or size, not deleted on read, so they can be replayed.
  • Reliability: idempotent producers and transactions give exactly-once semantics. Manual offset commits combined with idempotent consumers give safe processing.

17.1 Core concepts

                         Kafka Cluster (KRaft mode: controllers inside Kafka, no ZooKeeper)
 Producers               ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 sensor-ingestion ──►    │ Topic: sensor.readings.raw  (6 partitions, RF=3)         │
   key=deviceId          │                                                          │
                         │  Broker 1          Broker 2          Broker 3            │
                         │  P0 (Leader)       P0 (Follower)     P0 (Follower)       │
                         │  P1 (Follower)     P1 (Leader)       P1 (Follower)       │
                         │  P2 (Follower)     P2 (Follower)     P2 (Leader)  ...    │
                         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                │                         │
          Consumer Group "incident-service"      Consumer Group "reporting-service"
          C1 ← P0,P1   C2 ← P2,P3   C3 ← P4,P5    R1 ← P0..P5  (independent offsets)
  • Broker: a Kafka server that stores partitions and serves reads and writes.
  • Topic: a named stream of records, e.g. incident.events.
  • Partition: an ordered, append-only, immutable log. Partitions are the unit of parallelism and ordering. Each record has an offset, its position in the partition.
  • Segment: each partition is stored as segment files on disk (.log, .index, .timeindex). Old segments get deleted or compacted.
  • Replication: each partition has one leader (it handles all reads and writes by default) and followers that copy it. ISR (In-Sync Replicas) = replicas caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms. If the leader dies, a new leader is elected from the ISR.
  • KRaft: since Kafka 3.3 it's production-ready, and in Kafka 4.0 it's the only mode. Metadata lives in an internal Raft-replicated __cluster_metadata topic managed by controller nodes. ZooKeeper is gone, so it's simpler to operate, fails over faster, and supports millions of partitions.

17.2 Producer flow

send(record) → serializer → partitioner → RecordAccumulator (batch per partition)
            → Sender thread → leader broker → write to log → followers fetch → ack
  • Partitioning: with a key, murmur2(key) % numPartitions, so the same key always goes to the same partition, which keeps ordering per key (e.g. all events for incident 42 stay in order). With no key, the sticky partitioner fills a batch for one partition before moving to the next.
  • Ordering: guaranteed only within a partition. Adding partitions later changes the key→partition mapping, so plan partition counts up front.
  • acks:
    • acks=0: fire and forget. Fastest, can lose data.
    • acks=1: the leader wrote it. Lost if the leader dies before followers copy it.
    • acks=all (-1): all ISR replicas have it. Combine with min.insync.replicas=2 and RF=3: the write survives one broker failure, and if the ISR shrinks below 2 the producer gets NotEnoughReplicasException instead of silently losing durability.
  • Idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true, the default since Kafka 3.0): the broker dedupes retries using producer ID + sequence number, so there are no duplicates from producer retries and ordering is kept with max.in.flight.requests.per.connection ≤ 5.
  • Throughput tuning: batch.size, linger.ms, compression.type=lz4/zstd.

17.3 Consumer groups and rebalancing

  • Consumers in the same group split the partitions: each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group. Parallelism is capped at the partition count (with 6 partitions, a 7th consumer sits idle).
  • Different groups each get every message (pub/sub). incident-service and reporting-service both read sensor.alerts on their own.
  • A group coordinator (a broker) tracks membership through heartbeats (session.timeout.ms, heartbeat.interval.ms) and poll calls (max.poll.interval.ms). If processing takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, the consumer is kicked out and a rebalance happens.
  • Rebalancing reassigns partitions when consumers join or leave or partitions change.
    • Eager (old): everyone stops and gives up every partition, a "stop the world" pause.
    • Cooperative incremental (CooperativeStickyAssignor): only the moved partitions are revoked.
    • Static membership (group.instance.id): a pod restart within the session timeout doesn't trigger a rebalance.
    • KIP-848 (Kafka 4.0): a new consumer rebalance protocol with server-side assignment.

17.4 Offsets and commit strategies

Committed offsets live in the internal __consumer_offsets topic, per (group, topic, partition). The committed value is the next offset to read.

Strategy How Risk
Auto-commit (enable.auto.commit=true, every 5 s) Commits in the background during poll() A crash after commit but before processing → loss; a crash before commit → duplicates
Manual after processing (Spring AckMode.RECORD/BATCH, the Spring default is BATCH) Commit once the records are processed At-least-once: duplicates on a crash before commit, so make the consumer idempotent
AckMode.MANUAL(_IMMEDIATE) Call ack.acknowledge() in code Full control
Commit offsets in the DB transaction Store offset with the result in the same DB Effectively exactly-once into that DB 
@KafkaListener(topics = "sensor.alerts", groupId = "incident-service",
               properties = {"max.poll.records=100"})
public void onAlert(ConsumerRecord<String, SensorAlert> rec, Acknowledgment ack) {
    incidentService.createFromAlert(rec.value());   // idempotent: unique(alert_id)
    ack.acknowledge();                              // needs listener.ack-mode: manual
}

17.5 Delivery semantics

  • At-most-once: commit before processing. Can lose messages.
  • At-least-once: process, then commit. Can duplicate. This is the usual choice, paired with idempotent consumers.
  • Exactly-once (EOS): idempotent producer + transactions (transactional.id), consumer isolation.level=read_committed. Gives atomic consume-transform-produce within Kafka (Kafka Streams processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2). Side effects outside Kafka (DB, SMS) still need idempotency or an outbox.

17.6 Retention and compaction

  • Delete policy: keep records for retention.ms (default 7 days) or retention.bytes, then delete whole segments. Consumers can replay anything inside the retention window by resetting offsets.
  • Compact policy (cleanup.policy=compact): keep the latest value per key (a tombstone, i.e. a null value, deletes the key). Good for "current state" topics such as device.status or changelogs.
  • Kafka is fast because of sequential disk writes, the OS page cache, zero-copy (sendfile), batching, and compression.

17.7 End-to-end Smart City flow

Traffic sensor ─MQTT─► sensor-ingestion ─► [sensor.readings.raw, key=deviceId]
                                              │ consumer group: rules-engine
                                              ▼
                                    threshold breached? ─► [sensor.alerts, key=junctionId]
                                              │ consumer group: incident-service
                                              ▼
                       create/dedupe incident in PostgreSQL + outbox row (one transaction)
                                              │ outbox relay / Debezium CDC
                                              ▼
                                   [incident.events, key=incidentId]
                    ┌─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┐
           notification-service       reporting-service           audit-service
           (SMS/push to officer)      (MTTR dashboards)           (immutable log)

Likely follow-ups:

  • How many partitions should a topic have? Enough for peak throughput divided by per-consumer throughput, plus room to grow (12 for sensor.readings.raw). Too many means more open files, longer elections, and slower rebalances.
  • What happens when a consumer is slow? Consumer lag grows (watch it with Burrow, Kafka Exporter, or KEDA). Scale consumers up to the partition count, speed up processing, or batch. If max.poll.interval.ms is exceeded it gets kicked out and the partitions are rebalanced.
  • Kafka vs RabbitMQ? Kafka is a distributed log: replay, very high throughput, ordering per partition, consumers pull. RabbitMQ is a smart broker: complex routing, per-message ack and TTL, push-based, messages removed once consumed. Kafka suits event streams; RabbitMQ suits task queues and RPC.
  • How do you handle schema changes? Schema Registry with Avro or Protobuf and backward-compatible evolution rules (only add optional fields).
D18 Explain one microservice you worked on (template: Incident Management Service; adapt to your project). Hexaware

Responsibility: create, assign, track and close city incidents (accidents, waterlogging, sensor alarms) raised by operators, citizens or IoT alerts. APIs: POST /api/incidents, GET /api/incidents?zone=&status=&page=, PUT /api/incidents/{id}/assign, PATCH /api/incidents/{id}/status, GET /api/incidents/{id}/timeline. Stack: Spring Boot 3, Spring Data JPA, PostgreSQL (with PostGIS for location queries), Redis cache for zones and SLA configuration, Flyway migrations. Events: it consumes sensor.alerts and auto-creates incidents when a threshold is breached. It publishes incident.created, incident.assigned and incident.closed, which the notification-svc (SMS/email/push) and the dashboard (WebSocket) consume. Security: JWT, with @PreAuthorize checks so operators only see their own zone. Challenges and fixes:

  • Duplicate alerts from flapping sensors: fixed with idempotency keys plus a Redis de-dup window.
  • Slow list API: fixed with pagination, composite indexes on (zone, status, created_at), and DTO projections to avoid N+1 queries.
  • Lost events when the DB commit succeeded but the Kafka publish failed: fixed with the Outbox pattern.
  • SLA escalation: a scheduled job runs with ShedLock so only one instance executes it.

Template answer: Incident Management Service. Speak in the first person and give real numbers. Structure: purpose → design → integration → hard problem → impact. Adapt everything to your own service.

1. Purpose and domain. "The Incident Management Service owns the lifecycle of city incidents, such as signal failures, waterlogging, accidents, garbage overflow, and air-quality breaches. Incidents come from three sources: auto-generated from sensor alerts, raised manually by ICCC operators, and citizen complaints from the mobile app. It handles creation with deduplication, assignment to a field officer or department, SLA tracking and escalation, status updates with an audit history, and closure."

Lifecycle (state machine):

NEW ──assign──► ASSIGNED ──accept──► IN_PROGRESS ──resolve──► RESOLVED ──verify──► CLOSED
 │                 │  ▲                   │                      │
 │                 └──┘ reassign          └──── on-hold ────┐    └── reopen ──► IN_PROGRESS
 └── duplicate/invalid ──► REJECTED              ON_HOLD ◄──┘
 SLA timer: per category/severity (e.g. P1 = 30 min response); breach → ESCALATED flag + supervisor notified

2. Tech stack: Java 17, Spring Boot 3.2, Spring Data JPA (Hibernate 6), PostgreSQL 15 with PostGIS (incident locations), Flyway, Redis, Spring Kafka, Resilience4j, OpenFeign, MapStruct, Spring Security as an OAuth2 resource server, Testcontainers, Docker/Helm on Kubernetes, 3–6 pods with HPA.

3. Main endpoints:

Method Path Role Notes
POST /api/v1/incidents OPERATOR, CITIZEN_APP Idempotency-Key header; validates category and location
GET /api/v1/incidents?status=&zone=&severity=&from=&to=&page=&size= OPERATOR+ Paginated, zone-scoped for operators; sort whitelist
GET /api/v1/incidents/{id} OPERATOR+ Includes timeline and assignee (Feign → user-service, cached)
PATCH /api/v1/incidents/{id}/status FIELD_OFFICER, OPERATOR Checks the state-machine transition; optimistic locking
POST /api/v1/incidents/{id}/assign SUPERVISOR Publishes IncidentAssigned
POST /api/v1/incidents/{id}/attachments FIELD_OFFICER Pre-signed MinIO/S3 URL; the service never streams large files
GET /api/v1/incidents/nearby?lat=&lng=&radiusM= OPERATOR PostGIS ST_DWithin
GET /api/v1/incidents/stats SUPERVISOR Cached 30 s

4. Database schema outline:

CREATE TABLE incident (
  id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  reference_no    VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE NOT NULL,          -- INC-2025-000123
  category_code   VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,                 -- SIGNAL_FAILURE, WATERLOGGING ...
  severity        VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,                 -- P1..P4
  status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  zone_id         VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  location        GEOGRAPHY(POINT, 4326),
  source          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,                 -- SENSOR / OPERATOR / CITIZEN
  source_ref      VARCHAR(64),                          -- alertId / complaintId (dedupe)
  assigned_to     VARCHAR(64),
  sla_due_at      TIMESTAMPTZ,
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  version         INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,               -- @Version optimistic locking
  CONSTRAINT uq_source UNIQUE (source, source_ref)
);
CREATE INDEX ix_incident_zone_status_created ON incident (zone_id, status, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX ix_incident_location ON incident USING GIST (location);
CREATE INDEX ix_incident_open_sla ON incident (sla_due_at) WHERE status NOT IN ('RESOLVED','CLOSED');

CREATE TABLE incident_history (id BIGSERIAL PK, incident_id BIGINT REFERENCES incident, from_status, to_status,
                               changed_by, remarks, changed_at);
CREATE TABLE incident_attachment (id, incident_id, object_key, content_type, uploaded_by, uploaded_at);
CREATE TABLE outbox_event (id UUID PK, aggregate_type, aggregate_id, event_type, payload JSONB,
                           created_at, published_at NULL);
CREATE TABLE idempotency_key (key VARCHAR(64) PK, response_hash, response_body JSONB, created_at);

5. Kafka events:

Direction Topic Event Purpose
Consumes sensor.alerts SensorThresholdBreached Auto-create incident (dedupe on source_ref and a 15-min window per junction)
Consumes citizen.complaints ComplaintSubmitted Create a CITIZEN incident
Consumes user.events UserDeactivated Unassign their open incidents
Produces incident.events (key = incidentId) IncidentCreated, IncidentAssigned, IncidentStatusChanged, IncidentSlaBreached, IncidentClosed Notification, reporting, audit, citizen app updates

6. Caching: categories and SLA rules in Caffeine (reloaded on a config event), user/assignee lookups in Redis (10-min TTL), stats in Redis (30 s). Evicted on update.

7. Security: JWT resource server; URL rules plus @PreAuthorize("@zoneGuard.canAccess(#zoneId, authentication)"); field officers only see incidents assigned to them; audit history keeps who did what and when.

8. Challenges and how I solved them (pick 2–3 real ones):

Challenge Root cause Solution Result
Duplicate incidents during sensor storms (one junction sent 200 alerts in 5 min) At-least-once delivery + many alerts per fault Unique (source, source_ref) + a time-window dedupe check using a Redis SET NX key dedupe:{junction}:{category} with a 15-min TTL; extra alerts are attached to the existing incident ~95% fewer duplicate incidents; operators stopped complaining about noise
Lost events: incident saved but notification never sent Dual write: DB commit OK, then kafkaTemplate.send failed Transactional Outbox: insert into outbox_event in the same transaction; a scheduled relay (@Scheduled + SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) publishes and marks the rows No lost events since; the relay is idempotent
Concurrent updates: two operators assigned the same incident Last write wins @Version optimistic locking → 409 Conflict with the latest state; the UI refreshes Clean conflict handling
Slow incident list API (2.5 s p95) N+1 on history and attachments, OFFSET pagination on large tables, no composite index DTO projection query, @EntityGraph, composite index (zone_id, status, created_at), keyset pagination for infinite scroll p95 dropped to ~180 ms
SLA escalation job ran on every pod @Scheduled on 4 replicas ShedLock (@SchedulerLock) with a JDBC lock provider Exactly one escalation run per minute

9. Metrics and observability: custom Micrometer metrics incidents_created_total{source,category}, incident_sla_breaches_total, and a incident_open_gauge; Grafana dashboard for MTTA/MTTR; alerts on Kafka consumer lag and SLA-breach spikes.

10. Testing: unit tests for the state machine (parameterised for every transition), @WebMvcTest for controllers and security, Testcontainers (PostgreSQL + Kafka) integration tests, contract tests with notification-service; about 80% coverage gated in SonarQube.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How did you implement the state machine? An enum with the allowed transitions (Map<Status, Set<Status>>) checked in the domain method incident.transitionTo(newStatus, actor). That was simpler than Spring Statemachine for our needs.
  • How does the outbox relay avoid publishing the same event twice from several pods? FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED row locks plus idempotent consumers (they dedupe on eventId). An alternative is Debezium CDC reading the outbox table.
  • What would you improve? Moving the outbox relay to Debezium, adding Schema Registry for event contracts, and moving reporting queries to a separate read model.
D19 When integrating 2–3 microservices, do they connect directly or through shared services? Hexaware

Both. Services call each other directly over the network (Feign/WebClient, using a service name), but they rely on shared infrastructure to do it:

  • Service registry (Eureka/Kubernetes DNS): finds instances by name. No hard-coded IPs.
  • Config Server: central configuration (URLs, timeouts, feature flags).
  • API Gateway: handles external client traffic. Internal calls usually skip it.
  • Message broker (Kafka): for async and decoupled integration, so services don't need to know about each other at all.
  • Rules: services must never share a database. Share contracts (OpenAPI, event schemas), not code-level coupling.

Short answer: both. Business calls go service to service, synchronously over HTTP/gRPC or asynchronously through a broker. They rely on shared infrastructure services to find each other, get configuration, and stay decoupled. What services should never share is a database.

                       ┌──────────────── Shared platform services ────────────────┐
                       │ API Gateway │ Service Registry │ Config Server │ Broker  │
                       │  (edge)     │ (Eureka/K8s DNS) │ (Git/Vault)   │ (Kafka) │
                       └──────┬──────┴────────┬─────────┴───────┬───────┴────┬────┘
 client ──► gateway ──► incident-svc ──(1) lookup "user-service"─┘            │
                            │   (2) direct HTTP call to the chosen instance ─► user-svc
                            └──(3) publish event ─────────────────────────────┴──► notification-svc
Shared component Role Pros Cons / risks
API Gateway Edge entry for external clients; usually not used for internal east-west calls Central security, routing, throttling SPOF/bottleneck if not replicated; avoid a "god gateway"
Service registry / discovery (Eureka, Consul, K8s DNS) Services register themselves; callers look up healthy instances by name No hard-coded hosts; elastic scaling Another component to run (K8s DNS removes it); stale entries
Config Server (Spring Cloud Config, K8s ConfigMaps, Consul KV) Externalised, versioned, per-environment config; @RefreshScope / Spring Cloud Bus for live refresh One source of truth, audited in Git Startup dependency (use optional:configserver: + fail-fast with retry)
Message broker (Kafka/RabbitMQ) Async, decoupled integration and event streaming Temporal decoupling, buffering, fan-out, replay Eventual consistency, broker operations, harder debugging
Shared libraries (common DTOs, security auto-config, logging, error format) Reuse cross-cutting code as a versioned internal starter (smartcity-common-starter) Consistency, less boilerplate Coupling: one shared domain library forces lock-step releases. Share infrastructure code, not domain models; prefer contracts (OpenAPI/Avro) and generate clients
Service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) A sidecar handles mTLS, retries, traffic splitting, telemetry Resilience and security out of process, language-agnostic Operational complexity, extra latency and resources
Shared database Anti-pattern Easy joins, quick to start Tight coupling, schema changes break other services, no independent scaling: a distributed monolith

Direct vs mediated communication:

Direct (A → B over HTTP via discovery) Via broker (A → Kafka → B)
Coupling A knows B's API and needs B up A only knows the topic/event schema
Use Queries that need an immediate answer Events, commands that can be deferred, fan-out
Failure Needs timeouts, circuit breakers Broker absorbs B's downtime

Likely follow-ups:

  • Should internal calls go through the API gateway? Generally no. It adds a hop and makes the gateway a bottleneck. Use discovery or K8s DNS directly, or a mesh. Some organisations put an internal gateway between domains.
  • Eureka vs Kubernetes service discovery? On K8s, use the built-in Services/DNS: no extra server, and kube-proxy load-balances. Eureka is useful outside K8s or in hybrid VM setups.
  • How do you share DTOs without coupling? Publish an OpenAPI or Avro contract, generate client code per consumer, and version the contract. Use a tolerant reader (ignore unknown fields).
D20 Complete API request flow through microservices. Hexaware 
Angular  -> HTTPS GET /api/incidents/42  (Authorization: Bearer <JWT>)
 -> ALB -> API Gateway: GlobalFilter adds X-Correlation-Id, validates JWT, rate limit, route lb://INCIDENT-SERVICE
 -> Spring Cloud LoadBalancer picks instance from Eureka
 -> incident-service: Servlet filters -> SecurityFilterChain (JwtAuthFilter/resource server -> SecurityContextHolder)
 -> DispatcherServlet -> @RestController @RequestMapping("/api/incidents") -> @GetMapping("/{id}") (@PathVariable, @Valid)
 -> @Service (@PreAuthorize, @Transactional(readOnly = true)) -> may call user-service via @FeignClient (+ @CircuitBreaker)
 -> @Repository (JpaRepository) -> Hibernate -> HikariCP -> PostgreSQL
 -> map Entity -> DTO -> (for writes) KafkaTemplate.send("incident.updated", event) after commit
 -> ResponseEntity<IncidentDto> -> Jackson JSON -> back through gateway -> client
Errors anywhere in the MVC layer -> @RestControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler -> standard error JSON
Security errors in filters -> AuthenticationEntryPoint (401) / AccessDeniedHandler (403)
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/incidents")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class IncidentController {
    private final IncidentService service;

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<IncidentDto> get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(service.findById(id));
    }
}

Scenario: an operator creates an incident from Angular: POST /api/v1/incidents. Incident-service validates the reporter through user-service (Feign), saves to PostgreSQL, and publishes an event to Kafka, which notification-service consumes.

Browser ─► DNS ─► LB/Ingress (TLS) ─► API Gateway ─► incident-service ─► PostgreSQL
                                                           │ └─Feign─► user-service
                                                           └─Kafka─► notification-service

Step by step:

# Where What happens Key class / annotation
1 Angular A component calls incidentService.create(dto) → HttpClient.post('/api/v1/incidents', body). The AuthInterceptor adds Authorization: Bearer <JWT>, X-Correlation-Id, and an Idempotency-Key HttpInterceptor
2 Browser Cross-origin → CORS preflight OPTIONS first (if the origin differs); DNS lookup; TCP + TLS handshake (HTTP/2) —
3 LB / Ingress Terminates TLS (or passes it through), adds X-Forwarded-For/Proto, picks a healthy gateway pod ALB / NGINX Ingress
4 API Gateway CorrelationIdGlobalFilter → Spring Security WebFlux validates the JWT (signature via JWKS, exp, iss, aud) → RequestRateLimiter (Redis token bucket) → route predicate Path=/api/incidents/** matches → CircuitBreaker filter → ReactiveLoadBalancerClientFilter resolves lb://incident-service to a pod IP → proxied over Netty SecurityWebFilterChain, GlobalFilter, route YAML
5 Tomcat (incident-service) Connector accepts the request; a worker thread from the pool (server.tomcat.threads.max) is assigned (or a virtual thread with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) —
6 Servlet filters ServerHttpObservationFilter (starts a tracing span, MDC traceId) → CharacterEncodingFilter → DelegatingFilterProxy → FilterChainProxy → SecurityFilterChain: BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter decodes the JWT → JwtAuthenticationToken in SecurityContextHolder → AuthorizationFilter checks hasAnyRole('OPERATOR','ADMIN') for POST /api/v1/incidents/** SecurityFilterChain, OncePerRequestFilter
7 DispatcherServlet HandlerMapping (RequestMappingHandlerMapping) finds the controller method → HandlerAdapter → HandlerInterceptor.preHandle (e.g. tenant/zone resolution) DispatcherServlet, HandlerInterceptor
8 Argument resolution HttpMessageConverter (Jackson MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter) deserialises JSON → CreateIncidentRequest record; @Valid triggers Bean Validation (@NotBlank, @Size, @NotNull) → on failure MethodArgumentNotValidException → 400 @RequestBody, @Valid, @RequestHeader
9 Controller @RestController method: maps the request and calls the service; returns ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(dto) @RestController, @RequestMapping, @PostMapping
10 Service (AOP proxy) The proxy applies, in order: method security @PreAuthorize("@zoneGuard.canAccess(#req.zoneId(), authentication)") → @Transactional (TransactionInterceptor gets a connection from the HikariCP pool, setAutoCommit(false)) → optional @Retry/@CircuitBreaker on the Feign call @Service, @PreAuthorize, @Transactional
11 Idempotency check idempotencyRepo.findById(key). If present, return the stored response —
12 Feign call to user-service UserFeignClient.getUser(reporterId) → RequestInterceptor adds the client-credentials token and correlation ID → Spring Cloud LoadBalancer picks an instance → HTTP call wrapped by Resilience4j CB/timeout. user-service runs its own steps 5–14 and returns UserDto @FeignClient, @CircuitBreaker
13 Domain logic Map DTO → entity (MapStruct), compute slaDueAt from SLA rules (Caffeine cache, @Cacheable), generate referenceNo, set status NEW @Cacheable, @Mapper
14 Repository incidentRepository.save(incident) → Spring Data proxy → EntityManager.persist → Hibernate assigns an ID (sequence). Then outboxRepository.save(new OutboxEvent("IncidentCreated", payload)) in the same transaction @Repository / JpaRepository, @Entity, @Version
15 Commit The method returns → TransactionInterceptor commits → Hibernate flushes (INSERT incident, INSERT outbox_event, INSERT history), JDBC commit, connection back to the pool. On a RuntimeException → rollback @Transactional
16 Event publish The outbox relay (@Scheduled + ShedLock) reads unpublished rows → kafkaTemplate.send("incident.events", incidentId, event) (acks=all, idempotent) → marks them published. (A simpler variant: @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) sends to Kafka, but a crash before the send loses the event.) KafkaTemplate, @Scheduled, @SchedulerLock
17 Response path Controller returns ResponseEntity 201 with a Location header → HandlerInterceptor.postHandle/afterCompletion → Jackson serialises the IncidentDto → filters unwind (the security filter clears the context, the tracing span ends, the access log is written) → Tomcat writes the response ResponseEntity, HttpMessageConverter
18 Errors (any step 8–15) Exception → DispatcherServlet → ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver → @RestControllerAdvice @ExceptionHandler → ProblemDetail JSON (400 validation, 404 not found, 409 optimistic lock / duplicate, 503 downstream unavailable). Security errors in filters → AuthenticationEntryPoint / AccessDeniedHandler (D3) @RestControllerAdvice, @ExceptionHandler, ProblemDetail
19 Gateway → browser Gateway post-filters add response headers and log latency → LB → browser. Angular gets 201, shows a toast, navigates to the incident page —
20 Async consumer notification-service's @KafkaListener(topics="incident.events") receives the event (trace context continued from Kafka headers) → idempotency check on eventId → sends SMS/push, retried via @RetryableTopic, DLT on final failure → pushes a WebSocket update to dashboards (SimpMessagingTemplate.convertAndSend("/topic/incidents", ...)) @KafkaListener, @RetryableTopic, @DltHandler

Code skeleton for steps 8–15:

public record CreateIncidentRequest(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 30) String categoryCode,
        @NotNull @Pattern(regexp = "P[1-4]") String severity,
        @NotBlank String zoneId,
        @NotNull @DecimalMin("-90") @DecimalMax("90") Double lat,
        @NotNull @DecimalMin("-180") @DecimalMax("180") Double lng,
        @Size(max = 2000) String description,
        @NotBlank String reporterId) {}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/incidents")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class IncidentController {

    private final IncidentService incidentService;

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<IncidentDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateIncidentRequest req,
                                              @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String idemKey) {
        IncidentDto dto = incidentService.create(req, idemKey);
        URI location = URI.create("/api/v1/incidents/" + dto.id());
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(dto);
    }
}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class IncidentService {

    private final IncidentRepository incidentRepository;
    private final OutboxRepository outboxRepository;
    private final UserFeignClient userClient;
    private final IncidentMapper mapper;
    private final SlaPolicy slaPolicy;
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;

    @PreAuthorize("@zoneGuard.canAccess(#req.zoneId(), authentication)")
    @Transactional
    public IncidentDto create(CreateIncidentRequest req, String idemKey) {
        UserDto reporter = userClient.getUser(req.reporterId());       // Feign + circuit breaker
        if (!reporter.active()) {
            throw new BusinessValidationException("Reporter is inactive");
        }
        Incident incident = mapper.toEntity(req);
        incident.setStatus(IncidentStatus.NEW);
        incident.setSlaDueAt(slaPolicy.dueAt(req.categoryCode(), req.severity()));
        Incident saved = incidentRepository.save(incident);

        outboxRepository.save(OutboxEvent.of("Incident", saved.getId(), "IncidentCreated",
                toJson(mapper.toEvent(saved))));                       // same TX as the insert
        return mapper.toDto(saved);
    }

    private String toJson(Object o) {
        try { return objectMapper.writeValueAsString(o); }
        catch (JsonProcessingException e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); }
    }
}

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ProblemDetail validation(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Validation failed");
        pd.setProperty("errors", ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
                .map(f -> Map.of("field", f.getField(), "message", String.valueOf(f.getDefaultMessage())))
                .toList());
        return pd;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
    public ProblemDetail conflict() {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Incident was modified by someone else");
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(CallNotPermittedException.class)
    public ProblemDetail downstream() {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, "Dependent service unavailable");
    }
}

Design note: a remote Feign call inside @Transactional holds a DB connection while it waits on the network. Under load this can drain the HikariCP pool. A better approach is to do the remote validation before opening the transaction (a separate non-transactional method or an orchestrating bean), then open a short transaction just for the DB writes.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Where does @Transactional start and end? At the proxy boundary of the service method. It commits when the method returns normally, and rolls back on a RuntimeException/Error (checked exceptions don't trigger a rollback unless you set rollbackFor).
  • What does spring.jpa.open-in-view do and should it be on? It keeps the Hibernate session open through view rendering, so lazy loading works in controllers but connections are held longer. Set it to false in REST APIs.
  • What's the difference between a filter and an interceptor? Filters are servlet-level (before DispatcherServlet, they see raw requests; security lives here). Interceptors are Spring MVC-level (they know the handler method and run around the controller).
D21 API works internally but not for the client: primary investigation. Hexaware
  1. Reproduce and get the facts. Get the exact URL, the status code (none, 401, 403, 404, 502, CORS error?) and a timestamp or correlation ID.
  2. Network: check DNS resolution, firewall and security groups, VPN/whitelisting, proxies, and whether the port is actually exposed externally.
  3. Gateway/LB: check whether a route is defined for that path, path rewrites and prefix stripping, and ALB target health.
  4. CORS: a browser-only failure with a preflight OPTIONS failing usually means the client origin is not in allowedOrigins.
  5. Auth: check whether the client's token is valid, unexpired, issued by the right issuer/audience, and carries the right roles. 401 means authentication failed; 403 means it lacks the role.
  6. SSL/TLS: look for expired or self-signed certificates, hostname mismatches, or TLS version mismatches.
  7. Contract: check API version, request payload/headers, Content-Type, and environment-specific base URLs or config (profile differences).
  8. Logs: trace the correlation ID through gateway and service logs and Zipkin to see where the request stops.

Mindset: "Works for us, fails for them" means something in the client's path or context is different. Narrow it down layer by layer, from the outside in, and confirm each step with evidence before moving on.

Client ─► Client's network/proxy ─► Internet/DNS ─► WAF/Firewall ─► LB (TLS) ─► Gateway ─► Service ─► DB/downstream
   ①            ②                       ②              ②             ③④          ③⑥⑦       ⑧⑨⑩
Step Check How / commands Typical finding
1. Reproduce with the client's exact request Get the full request (URL, method, headers, body, time, client IP) and the exact error (status code, body, client log). Replay it with curl -v / Postman from outside your network curl -v -X POST https://api.city.gov/api/v1/incidents -H "Authorization: Bearer ..." -d @body.json Different URL (http vs https, missing /v1), different payload
2. Network / DNS / firewall / whitelisting Does the client's DNS resolve the right IP? Can it reach the port? Is the client IP allow-listed at the WAF, security group, or partner firewall? Corporate proxy? nslookup api.city.gov, dig, traceroute, telnet host 443 / nc -vz host 443; WAF/SG logs Client IP not in allow-list; WAF rule blocking a payload pattern; split-horizon DNS pointing to an internal IP
