3. Gateway route & load balancer Is the route exposed on the external gateway/ingress, or only the internal one? Path rewrite correct? Do LB target-group health checks pass? Does it fail on only one AZ or pod? Gateway access logs, /actuator/gateway/routes, ALB target health, ingress config Route only on the internal ingress; 502/504 from an unhealthy target; LB idle timeout < API duration
4. TLS certificate Expired cert, incomplete chain (missing intermediate), hostname mismatch, client trusts an old CA, TLS version or cipher mismatch, mTLS client cert missing or expired openssl s_client -connect api.city.gov:443 -servername api.city.gov -showcerts; SSL Labs Missing intermediate cert (browsers cope, Java/curl clients fail); client on TLS 1.0
5. CORS (browser clients only) Browser console: "blocked by CORS policy". Preflight OPTIONS returns 401/403, or the origin isn't allowed DevTools → Network → preflight; check Access-Control-Allow-Origin Client's origin (https://partner.app) missing from the allowed list; security blocks OPTIONS; duplicate CORS headers from gateway + service
6. Authentication / authorization / scopes 401: token from a different issuer or environment, expired, wrong audience, clock skew. 403: missing role or scope; client registered without the scope Decode the JWT (jwt.io, locally); compare iss, aud, scope, exp with config; security debug logs Client uses a UAT token on prod; aud mismatch; scope incident.write not granted
7. Rate limits / quotas 429s? A per-client quota smaller than for internal callers? WAF bot protection? Gateway rate-limit metrics, X-RateLimit-Remaining headers Partner's batch job hits 20 req/s and gets throttled
8. Payload / contract / version Different API version, content-type (text/plain vs application/json), encoding, date formats, field names, enum values, required headers (Idempotency-Key), request size limit Compare against OpenAPI; server logs of the 400/415 detail; spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size, nginx client_max_body_size (413) The client sends the old v1 schema; a 413 from nginx on large uploads; the timezone format differs
9. Environment-specific config Does the client hit a different environment, region, or tenant? Feature flags, config-server profile, secrets differ? Is a downstream service only reachable internally? Compare the config between envs; /actuator/env (secured); check which pod/version served it Prod config missing the new route or flag; external DNS still points to the old cluster
10. Logs via correlation ID / trace Ask the client for the X-Correlation-Id from the response (or the timestamp + client ID). Search Kibana and Zipkin: did the request reach the gateway? The service? Where did it stop? Kibana correlationId:"..."; Zipkin trace; gateway access logs The request never reached the gateway (so a network problem), or the service threw a specific exception

Key principle: if there's no log at all at the gateway, the problem is before it (DNS, firewall, TLS, LB). If the gateway logged a 401/403/429, it's a policy problem. If the service logged an error, it's app/data/config.

Communicate: acknowledge to the client, share findings with evidence, fix (config change, allow-list, cert chain), confirm with the client, and add monitoring or a synthetic check (an external probe such as a Blackbox exporter) so it's caught earlier next time.

Likely follow-ups:

  • A Java client fails with PKIX path building failed but browsers work. Why? The server isn't sending the intermediate certificate (browsers fetch or cache it, Java doesn't), or the client's truststore lacks the CA. Fix the chain on the server.
  • The client gets 504 only for large reports. The LB, gateway, or client timeout is shorter than processing time. Make it async (202 + polling or a webhook), or paginate and stream.
  • Postman works but the browser doesn't. Almost always CORS, or a cookie/SameSite issue. Postman doesn't enforce CORS.
D22 API response is slow: primary investigation. Hexaware
  • Measure first, don't guess. Use APM or tracing (Zipkin) to see which span is slow: gateway, service code, DB, or a downstream call. Check whether it is slow always or only under load (p95/p99 in Grafana).
  • DB (most common cause):
    • check query time in logs (spring.jpa.show-sql or the Hibernate statistics)
    • N+1 queries (fix with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph)
    • missing indexes
    • fetching too much data (use pagination and projections)
  • External calls: slow downstream services or missing timeouts. Fix with parallel calls (CompletableFuture/WebClient) or caching.
  • Resources:
    • Thread pool exhaustion (Tomcat threads) or HikariCP connection pool exhaustion: look for "connection is not available" errors.
    • CPU, memory, GC pauses (GC logs, heap dump).
    • Thread dumps for locks or blocking.
  • Payload: large JSON responses. Fix with compression, pagination, or returning fewer fields.
  • Fixes: caching (Redis), indexes, async processing, scaling out.

Method: measure → locate → diagnose → fix → verify. Never guess. Profile or trace first.

1. MEASURE   What's slow? Which endpoint, which percentile (p50 vs p99), since when, for whom, at what load?
             Is it every request or spikes? Correlated with deploys, traffic, batch jobs, time of day?
2. LOCATE    Distributed trace / APM → which span takes the time: gateway, service code, DB, downstream, Kafka?
3. DIAGNOSE  Drill into that layer (DB, downstream, JVM/app, network/payload)
4. FIX       The smallest change for the biggest gain (index, cache, async, pool size)
5. VERIFY    Load test (JMeter/Gatling/k6) before vs after; watch p95/p99 in Grafana after release

Step 1: measure (tools)

  • Grafana / Prometheus using Actuator's http_server_requests_seconds (enable histograms with management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true). Look at the p95/p99 trend per uri, error rate, and throughput.
  • Confirm whether it's the server or the client/network: compare the gateway's latency with the service's latency.

Step 2: locate with tracing. Zipkin/Jaeger/APM (Elastic APM, Dynatrace, New Relic, Glowroot) show the span waterfall. That tells you whether 80% of the time is in a SQL span, a Feign call, or the service itself (a gap with no child spans = CPU, locks, GC, or waiting on a pool).

Step 3: diagnose by layer

Layer Symptoms What to check Tools
Database Long JDBC spans, many SQL spans per request Slow queries, N+1 (100 SELECTs per request), missing indexes, locks/blocking, large result sets, no pagination spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true, logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug, p6spy/datasource-proxy, pg_stat_statements, slow query log, EXPLAIN ANALYZE (D23)
Connection pool Time spent before SQL runs HikariCP hikaricp_connections_pending > 0, hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds high; pool too small, or connections held during remote calls or long transactions Actuator Hikari metrics, leak-detection-threshold
Downstream services Long HTTP client spans The downstream is slow itself, no timeouts, sequential calls that could run in parallel, retries piling up Traces, CB metrics, client metrics http_client_requests_seconds
App: threads Gaps in the trace, high latency under load only Tomcat thread pool exhausted (tomcat_threads_busy = max), blocking calls in WebFlux event loops, synchronized hot spots, deadlocks Thread dumps (jstack <pid>, jcmd <pid> Thread.print, /actuator/threaddump); take 3 dumps 5 s apart and look for many threads BLOCKED on the same lock or WAITING on the pool
App: GC / memory Periodic latency spikes, high CPU Long GC pauses, heap near max, high allocation rate, memory leak GC logs (-Xlog:gc*), jvm_gc_pause_seconds, JFR (jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=rec.jfr → JDK Mission Control), heap dump + Eclipse MAT
App: CPU / code High CPU, gap spans Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) loops), regex, heavy JSON serialisation of huge objects, excessive logging (DEBUG in prod), reflection-heavy mapping JFR method profiling, async-profiler flame graphs
Network / payload Large response sizes, slow on mobile Responses in MBs (no pagination, entire entity graphs), no compression, chatty APIs (10 calls per screen) Response size metric, server.compression.enabled=true, DevTools waterfall
Infrastructure All services slow CPU throttling from K8s limits (container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total), noisy neighbours, node pressure, DB server CPU/IO Kubernetes metrics, node exporter
Cache Slow after a deploy or at expiry times Cold cache, stampede, low hit ratio cache_gets_total{result="miss"}

Common fixes:

  • N+1 → JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph / @BatchSize / DTO projections
  • Missing index → add a composite or covering index
  • Big results → pagination (keyset for deep pages), projections, compression
  • Sequential downstream calls → parallel (CompletableFuture / WebClient zip), cache, or precompute with events
  • Pool exhaustion → keep transactions short, don't make remote calls inside transactions, tune the pool (maximum-pool-size ≈ what the DB can handle, not "bigger is better")
  • Heavy work in the request path → move it async (Kafka, @Async) and return 202
  • GC → right-size the heap, cut allocations, use G1/ZGC
  • High-concurrency I/O → virtual threads (Java 21, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true)

Example story: "The incident dashboard API's p95 went from 300 ms to 3 s after a release. Zipkin showed 120 SELECT spans per request. Hibernate statistics confirmed an N+1 on incident.history, caused by a new field in the DTO mapping. I replaced it with a DTO projection query and @EntityGraph, and added a composite index on (zone_id, status, created_at). p95 came back to 180 ms, which I verified with a Gatling run at 200 rps. I then added a Grafana alert on p95 > 800 ms."

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why look at p99 rather than the average? Averages hide tail latency. A few very slow requests hurt users and pile up across fan-out calls.
  • How do you read a thread dump for a slowness issue? Group threads by state and stack. Many http-nio-* threads WAITING in HikariPool.getConnection = pool starvation. Many BLOCKED on the same monitor = lock contention.
  • What is JFR's overhead? Very low (~1–2%) with the default profile, so it's safe to run briefly in production.
D23 Delay caused by a stored procedure / SQL query: identify and fix.

Identify:

  • the DB slow query log (MySQL), pg_stat_statements (Postgres), or AWR/SQL Profiler (Oracle/SQL Server)
  • APM traces, and Hibernate SQL logs with timings

Analyze: run EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE (the execution plan) and look for:

  • full table scans
  • wrong join order
  • high row estimates versus actual rows
  • sorts or temp tables spilling to disk
  • functions on indexed columns (WHERE DATE(created_at) = ... kills the index)

Fix:

  • Indexes: composite indexes in the right column order, covering indexes.
  • Queries: avoid SELECT *. Rewrite correlated subqueries as joins or EXISTS. Filter early.
  • Paging: use pagination (keyset paging for big tables).
  • Statistics: update stats or ANALYZE, rebuild fragmented indexes.
  • Stored procedure internals: remove row-by-row cursors and use set-based logic. Watch for parameter sniffing.
  • Writes: batch them (hibernate.jdbc.batch_size).
  • Reads: cache frequently read results. Use materialized views or summary tables for reports. Archive or partition old data (for example, sensor readings by month).
  • Verify: re-run the execution plan and compare timings before and after.

23.1 Identify the slow statement

  1. Confirm the DB is where the time goes. A trace span or JDBC timing (datasource-proxy/p6spy) shows the slow SQL or the {call proc(?)}.
  2. DB-side tooling:
    • PostgreSQL: pg_stat_statements (top queries by total_exec_time, mean_exec_time), log_min_duration_statement = 500ms, auto_explain (logs plans of slow queries, including the ones inside functions with auto_explain.log_nested_statements=on), pg_stat_activity (running and blocked queries), pg_locks.
    • MySQL: slow query log (long_query_time), performance_schema, SHOW PROCESSLIST.
    • SQL Server: Query Store, sys.dm_exec_query_stats, Extended Events, actual execution plans.
    • Oracle: AWR/ASH reports, V$SQL, DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR.
  3. Inside a stored procedure: find which statement is slow. Add timing logs (RAISE NOTICE clock_timestamp() in PL/pgSQL, SET STATISTICS TIME ON in T-SQL), use nested-statement plan logging, or run each statement on its own with representative parameters.

23.2 Read the execution plan

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT i.id, i.reference_no, i.status, i.created_at
FROM incident i
WHERE i.zone_id = 'Z-07' AND i.status = 'NEW'
ORDER BY i.created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;
BEFORE:
Limit  (actual time=1830..1830 rows=50)
  -> Sort  (Sort Key: created_at DESC)  Sort Method: top-N heapsort
       -> Seq Scan on incident i  (actual rows=4120 loops=1)
            Filter: (zone_id = 'Z-07' AND status = 'NEW')
            Rows Removed by Filter: 2895880          ← scanned 2.9M rows to find 4k
            Buffers: shared read=48210                ← heavy disk IO
Execution Time: 1832 ms

AFTER  CREATE INDEX ix_incident_zone_status_created ON incident (zone_id, status, created_at DESC);
Limit  (actual time=0.05..0.21 rows=50)
  -> Index Scan using ix_incident_zone_status_created on incident i
       Index Cond: (zone_id = 'Z-07' AND status = 'NEW')   ← no sort needed: index order matches
Execution Time: 0.3 ms

What to look for in a plan:

  • Seq Scan / Table Scan / Full Table Scan on large tables with selective filters → missing or unusable index.
  • Estimated vs actual rows far apart (estimate 10, actual 2M) → stale statistics, which lead to the wrong join type.
  • Nested Loop with a large outer side, Hash Join spilling to disk, Sort spilling (external merge Disk) → work_mem, indexes, query shape.
  • Key Lookup / bookmark lookup (SQL Server), many heap fetches → make it a covering index.
  • High Buffers: shared read → IO-bound. loops=N multiplies the cost.

23.3 Fixes

Problem Fix Example
Missing index B-tree on filter/join/order columns CREATE INDEX ON incident (assigned_to)
Composite index column order Equality columns first, then range/sort columns. The leftmost-prefix rule applies (zone_id, status, created_at) serves WHERE zone_id=? AND status=? ORDER BY created_at
Covering index Put every selected column in the index → index-only scan, no table lookup PG: CREATE INDEX ... (zone_id, status) INCLUDE (reference_no, severity); SQL Server INCLUDE
Partial / filtered index Index only the "hot" rows CREATE INDEX ... ON incident (sla_due_at) WHERE status NOT IN ('RESOLVED','CLOSED')
Non-sargable predicates (the index can't be used) Don't wrap indexed columns in functions or casts; avoid leading wildcards; avoid implicit type conversion; OR across columns → UNION ALL ❌ WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2025-06-01' → ✅ WHERE created_at >= '2025-06-01' AND created_at < '2025-06-02'; ❌ WHERE LOWER(email)=? → functional index ON (LOWER(email)); ❌ LIKE '%abc' → trigram (pg_trgm) / full-text index; ❌ varchar_col = 123 (implicit cast)
Parameter sniffing (SQL Server, also Oracle bind peeking, PG generic plans) The plan is compiled for the first parameter value (e.g. a tiny zone) and reused for a huge zone → a bad plan OPTION (RECOMPILE), OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, split procedures per data shape, local variables; PG: plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan
Stale statistics Wrong row estimates → wrong join or scan choice PG ANALYZE incident; / tune autovacuum; SQL Server UPDATE STATISTICS; Oracle DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS
Cursors / row-by-row loops in the procedure ("RBAR") Rewrite as set-based SQL: one UPDATE/INSERT...SELECT instead of a loop of 100k single-row statements See below
Deep OFFSET pagination OFFSET 100000 reads and throws away 100k rows Keyset/seek pagination: WHERE (created_at, id) < (:lastCreated, :lastId) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50
Huge tables (sensor readings, billions of rows) Partitioning by time (range) → partition pruning, cheap retention (drop the old partition) PARTITION BY RANGE (reading_ts), monthly partitions, or TimescaleDB hypertables
Locking / blocking Long transactions, lock escalation, missing FK index causing table locks Short transactions, index the FK columns, SKIP LOCKED for queue tables, right isolation level
Repeated expensive aggregates Caching / materialized views / summary tables refreshed by events CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW zone_daily_stats ...; REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY
N+1 from the ORM Batch fetching @BatchSize(size = 50), hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50, JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph
Bulk writes from Java JDBC batching hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50, order_inserts=true, sequence-based IDs (IDENTITY disables insert batching), or JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate / COPY
SELECT * and wide rows Select only what you need; DTO projections SELECT new com..IncidentRow(i.id, i.status) FROM Incident i ...

Cursor → set-based example (escalate overdue incidents):

-- BEFORE (PL/pgSQL loop: 1 UPDATE + 1 INSERT per row, 40k rows → ~90 s)
FOR r IN SELECT id FROM incident WHERE status IN ('NEW','ASSIGNED') AND sla_due_at < now() LOOP
    UPDATE incident SET escalated = true WHERE id = r.id;
    INSERT INTO incident_history(incident_id, to_status, remarks, changed_at)
    VALUES (r.id, 'ESCALATED', 'SLA breach', now());
END LOOP;

-- AFTER (set-based with a data-modifying CTE → ~1 s)
WITH esc AS (
    UPDATE incident
       SET escalated = true
     WHERE status IN ('NEW','ASSIGNED') AND sla_due_at < now() AND escalated = false
 RETURNING id
)
INSERT INTO incident_history (incident_id, to_status, remarks, changed_at)
SELECT id, 'ESCALATED', 'SLA breach', now() FROM esc;

Calling a procedure from Spring with a timeout:

@Repository
public interface ReportRepository extends JpaRepository<Incident, Long> {
    @Procedure(procedureName = "generate_zone_report")
    void generateZoneReport(@Param("p_zone") String zone, @Param("p_from") LocalDate from);
}

// or JdbcTemplate/SimpleJdbcCall with a statement timeout so a slow proc can't hold threads forever
jdbcTemplate.setQueryTimeout(10);   // seconds

Process: reproduce with production-like data volume (a small dev dataset hides the problem) → capture the actual plan → make one change at a time → compare plans and timings → check the write overhead of new indexes (each one slows INSERT/UPDATE) → deploy through Flyway (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in PG, so the table isn't locked) → monitor.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not just add indexes on every column? Each index slows writes, uses storage and memory, and the planner may still ignore it. Index for real query patterns.
  • Why does a query run fast in SSMS/psql but slow from the app? Different parameter values or types (parameter sniffing, implicit nvarchar conversion from JDBC sendStringParametersAsUnicode), different session settings, or the app fetches all rows.
  • When would you move logic out of stored procedures? When business logic needs versioning, testing, and scaling with the app. Keep set-based, data-heavy operations in SQL.
D24 Design patterns used in microservices, and in code. G2

Microservice / architecture patterns:

Pattern One-liner (Smart City example)
API Gateway Single entry point for auth, routing and rate limiting (Spring Cloud Gateway)
Service Registry/Discovery Services register and find each other by name (Eureka)
Circuit Breaker Fail fast plus fallback when a dependency is down (Resilience4j)
Database per Service Each service owns its own schema; no shared DB
Saga Distributed transaction as local transactions plus compensations (choreography via Kafka or an orchestrator)
CQRS Separate write model from read model (e.g. dashboard read store)
Event Sourcing Store state changes as events (incident timeline) and rebuild state by replaying them
Outbox Write the event to an outbox table in the same DB transaction; a relay/Debezium publishes it to Kafka
Strangler Fig Gradually route features from the legacy monolith to new services
Sidecar Helper container next to the service (Envoy/Istio proxy, log shipper)
Externalized Config Config Server / ConfigMaps

Code-level patterns:

  • Singleton: Spring beans are singleton-scoped by default.
  • Factory: NotificationSenderFactory returns an SMS, Email or Push sender. Spring's BeanFactory is another example.
  • Builder: Lombok @Builder for DTOs and events. WebClient.builder() is another example.
  • Strategy: a NotificationChannel interface with multiple implementations, injected as a Map<String, NotificationChannel> and picked at runtime.
  • Observer: Spring ApplicationEventPublisher with @EventListener; Kafka pub/sub follows the same idea.
  • Others worth naming:
    • Template Method (JdbcTemplate, KafkaTemplate)
    • Proxy (Spring AOP, @Transactional)
    • Adapter (wrappers for third-party IoT vendor APIs)
public interface NotificationChannel { void send(Alert alert); }

@Component("SMS")   class SmsChannel   implements NotificationChannel { public void send(Alert a) { /* ... */ } }
@Component("EMAIL") class EmailChannel implements NotificationChannel { public void send(Alert a) { /* ... */ } }

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
class NotificationService {
    private final Map<String, NotificationChannel> channels;   // Strategy selected at runtime
    void notify(Alert alert) { channels.get(alert.channel()).send(alert); }
}

Part A: Microservice architecture patterns

Pattern Problem it solves How Where we use it (Smart City)
API Gateway Clients shouldn't know about N services; cross-cutting concerns One entry point: routing, auth, rate limits Spring Cloud Gateway in front of all services (D14)
Service Discovery Instances change dynamically Registry (client-side) or platform DNS (server-side) Eureka → K8s Services
Circuit Breaker Cascading failures Fail fast when a dependency is unhealthy Resilience4j on user-service and SMS gateway calls (D11)
Bulkhead One slow dependency uses up every thread Isolated pools or semaphores per dependency SMS gateway limited to 20 concurrent calls (D13)
Retry / Timeout Transient faults Bounded retries with backoff + jitter Feign GETs, Kafka retry topics (D12)
Database per Service Coupling through a shared schema Each service owns its data, others use APIs/events PostgreSQL per service, TimescaleDB for sensors
Saga A business transaction across services with no 2PC A sequence of local transactions + compensating actions Incident → work order → crew dispatch
CQRS Read and write models need different shapes and scaling Separate command model from read model(s), synced by events reporting-service builds dashboard read models from incident.events
Event Sourcing Need a full audit and the ability to rebuild state Store events as the source of truth; derive state by replaying them Device state history / incident audit trail (often only partially used)
Transactional Outbox Dual write: DB + broker not atomic Write an outbox row in the same transaction; a relay or CDC (Debezium) publishes it incident-service events (D18)
Strangler Fig Migrating a monolith safely Route features one at a time to new services behind a facade/gateway until the monolith is gone The legacy ICCC monolith's complaint module was moved first
Sidecar Cross-cutting infrastructure kept out of app code A helper container in the same pod (Envoy proxy, log shipper, Vault agent) Istio Envoy for mTLS; Fluent Bit sidecar
BFF (Backend for Frontend) Web and mobile need different payloads A dedicated gateway/aggregator per client type Mobile field-officer BFF returning compact payloads
Externalized Configuration Config per environment without rebuilding Config Server / ConfigMaps / Vault Spring Cloud Config
Health Check / Observability (log aggregation, distributed tracing, metrics) Operating many services Actuator, ELK, Prometheus, Zipkin D16
Anti-Corruption Layer Legacy or third-party models leaking into your domain A translation layer/adapter Adapter for different vendors' sensor payload formats

Saga: choreography vs orchestration

CHOREOGRAPHY (events, no central coordinator)
incident-svc ──IncidentApproved──► workorder-svc ──WorkOrderCreated──► crew-svc ──CrewAssigned──► incident-svc
                                                                         │ failure
                                       workorder-svc ◄──CrewUnavailable──┘  → compensate: cancel work order
                                       incident-svc  ◄──WorkOrderCancelled── → set incident ON_HOLD
 + loose coupling, simple for 2–4 steps     − flow is implicit and hard to follow, cyclic deps risk

ORCHESTRATION (central saga orchestrator sends commands)
                    ┌──────────── Dispatch Saga Orchestrator ────────────┐
                    │ 1. CreateWorkOrder → workorder-svc   (reply OK)    │
                    │ 2. AssignCrew      → crew-svc        (reply FAIL)  │
                    │ 3. compensate: CancelWorkOrder → workorder-svc     │
                    │ 4. MarkIncidentOnHold → incident-svc               │
                    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
 + explicit flow, easy to monitor and change, good for many steps    − orchestrator is extra; risk of a "god service"
 Tools: Camunda/Zeebe, Temporal, Axon, Eventuate Tram, or a hand-rolled state table + Kafka

Saga rules: every step must be idempotent, compensations must be semantic undo operations (cancel, refund), not DB rollbacks, and a saga gives no isolation, so watch out for dirty reads (use a "PENDING" state and semantic locks).

Outbox relay sketch:

@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class OutboxRelay {
    private final OutboxRepository outbox;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 1000)
    @SchedulerLock(name = "outboxRelay", lockAtMostFor = "PT30S")   // ShedLock: one pod at a time
    @Transactional
    public void publish() {
        // repository query: SELECT ... WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
        for (OutboxEvent e : outbox.lockNextBatch(100)) {
            kafka.send("incident.events", e.getAggregateId(), e.getPayload()).join();  // wait for ack
            e.markPublished(Instant.now());
        }
    }
}

Part B: Code-level (GoF) patterns and where Spring uses them

Pattern Intent Where in Spring / our code
Singleton One shared instance Spring beans are singleton-scoped by default (one per container, not the classic static GoF singleton). Our stateless @Services, so don't keep mutable request state in fields
Factory / Factory Method Create objects without naming concrete classes BeanFactory/ApplicationContext, FactoryBean, @Bean methods; our NotificationSenderFactory returns SMS/Email/Push senders by channel
Abstract Factory Families of related objects ConnectionFactory, EntityManagerFactory
Builder Build complex objects step by step, immutably Lombok @Builder, RestClient.builder(), UriComponentsBuilder, Jwts.builder(), HttpSecurity DSL, ResponseEntity.ok()
Strategy Swap algorithms at runtime PasswordEncoder, AuthenticationProvider, Resilience4j IntervalFunction; our SLA calculation per incident category and notification channel strategies
Observer Notify subscribers about events ApplicationEventPublisher + @EventListener / @TransactionalEventListener; Kafka pub/sub at the system level
Template Method Fixed algorithm skeleton, steps varied by subclasses or callbacks JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate, KafkaTemplate, TransactionTemplate, OncePerRequestFilter.doFilterInternal, AbstractAuthenticationProcessingFilter
Proxy Control access by wrapping the target Spring AOP: JDK dynamic or CGLIB proxies for @Transactional, @Cacheable, @PreAuthorize, @Async, @Retry; Spring Data repository interfaces; Feign clients; @Lazy
Decorator Add behaviour without changing the class Resilience4j Decorators.ofSupplier(...).withCircuitBreaker(...).withRetry(...), BufferedReader, HttpServletRequestWrapper (e.g. caching the request body)
Adapter Convert one interface to another HandlerAdapter in Spring MVC; our vendor-specific sensor payload adapters → a common SensorReading
Chain of Responsibility Pass a request along handlers Servlet FilterChain, Spring Security SecurityFilterChain, HandlerInterceptors, gateway filters; our incident validation-rule chain
Front Controller One handler for every request DispatcherServlet
Dependency Injection / IoC Invert object creation The core of Spring
State Behaviour depends on state Incident lifecycle (IncidentStatus enum with allowed transitions)

Strategy + Factory example (notification channels):

public interface NotificationSender {
    Channel channel();
    void send(Notification n);
}

@Component class SmsSender implements NotificationSender {
    public Channel channel() { return Channel.SMS; }
    public void send(Notification n) { /* call SMS gateway */ }
}
@Component class EmailSender implements NotificationSender {
    public Channel channel() { return Channel.EMAIL; }
    public void send(Notification n) { /* JavaMailSender */ }
}
@Component class PushSender implements NotificationSender {
    public Channel channel() { return Channel.PUSH; }
    public void send(Notification n) { /* FCM */ }
}

@Component
public class NotificationSenderFactory {
    private final Map<Channel, NotificationSender> senders;

    public NotificationSenderFactory(List<NotificationSender> all) {          // Spring injects every implementation
        this.senders = all.stream().collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableMap(NotificationSender::channel, s -> s));
    }

    public NotificationSender get(Channel channel) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(senders.get(channel))
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("No sender for " + channel));
    }
}
// Adding WhatsApp = one new @Component; nothing else changes (Open/Closed Principle)

Observer within a service (Spring events):

public record IncidentClosedEvent(Long incidentId, String closedBy) {}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
class IncidentCloser {
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;

    @Transactional
    public void close(Long id, String user) {
        // ... update status
        events.publishEvent(new IncidentClosedEvent(id, user));
    }
}

@Component
class IncidentClosedHandlers {
    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)   // only fires if the TX committed
    public void updateStats(IncidentClosedEvent e) { /* refresh cached stats */ }
}

Likely follow-ups:

  • CQRS vs Event Sourcing? They're independent. CQRS separates read and write models. Event sourcing stores state as events. They're often combined, but CQRS works fine with a normal DB plus events to build the read model.
  • How does Spring decide between a JDK proxy and CGLIB? Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB (proxyTargetClass=true), which subclasses the class. A JDK proxy only implements interfaces. Either way, final methods and self-invocation aren't intercepted.
  • When would you choose orchestration over choreography? When the flow has more than ~4 steps, needs clear visibility or timeouts, or changes often. Choreography suits simple, stable reactions between a few services.
  • Is a Spring singleton thread-safe? Only if it's stateless or its shared state is thread-safe. Spring doesn't synchronise anything for you.
E

SQL, Angular/JavaScript, Project & HR

E1 Find the second-highest salary (3 ways) + employees who earn it Co. 2 
-- 1) Subquery: the highest salary below the overall MAX (works on every DB)
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employee
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee);

-- 2) DISTINCT + LIMIT/OFFSET (MySQL / PostgreSQL)
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employee
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
--    Oracle 12c+ / SQL Server 2012+
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employee
ORDER BY salary DESC
OFFSET 1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY;

-- 3) DENSE_RANK: handles ties and generalises to the Nth highest
SELECT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employee
) t WHERE rnk = 2
GROUP BY salary;   -- or use DISTINCT

-- Name + salary of every employee on the second-highest salary
SELECT name, salary FROM (
  SELECT name, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employee
) t
WHERE rnk = 2;

Use DISTINCT (or DENSE_RANK) so that duplicate top salaries don't push the real second-highest value out. Way 1 returns NULL when no second value exists. For the Nth highest, change 2 to N, or use OFFSET N-1.

Expected answer: 95000, earned by Priya and Karan.

Approach 1: subquery with MAX (works in every dialect)

SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employee
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee);
second_highest
95000
  • The inner query returns 120000. The outer query returns the highest salary below that.
  • Ties are handled correctly: the three 120000 rows are all excluded together.
  • NULLs are safe: MAX ignores NULLs, and NULL < 120000 is UNKNOWN, so that row is filtered out.
  • No second-highest (one distinct salary, or an empty table): returns one row containing NULL. That is often what the interviewer wants (it is the LeetCode #176 requirement).
  • It only works for N = 2. For N = 3 you would have to nest it again, so it does not generalise.

Approach 2: DISTINCT + LIMIT/OFFSET (or OFFSET…FETCH)

-- MySQL / PostgreSQL
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM employee
WHERE salary IS NOT NULL          -- required in PostgreSQL, where NULL sorts first in DESC
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;                 -- MySQL also accepts: LIMIT 1, 1

-- SQL Server 2012+ / Oracle 12c+ / PostgreSQL
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM employee
WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY salary DESC
OFFSET 1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY;

-- SQL Server, older style with TOP
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee
WHERE salary NOT IN (SELECT TOP 1 salary FROM employee ORDER BY salary DESC);

-- Oracle 11g and older, with ROWNUM
SELECT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary, ROWNUM rn FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employee
    WHERE salary IS NOT NULL ORDER BY salary DESC)
) WHERE rn = 2;

Common mistake: leaving out DISTINCT.

SELECT salary FROM employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
-- returns 120000 (the second of three 120000 rows), which is WRONG

Getting NULL instead of an empty result: when no second salary exists, LIMIT/OFFSET returns zero rows. To return NULL, wrap it as a scalar subquery:

SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employee
        WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
        ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1) AS second_highest;

Approach 3: DENSE_RANK (best for "Nth highest" and for getting the names)

SELECT name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT name, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employee
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
) ranked
WHERE rnk = 2;
name salary
Priya 95000
Karan 95000

Why DENSE_RANK and not RANK or ROW_NUMBER?

salary ROW_NUMBER RANK DENSE_RANK
120000 1 1 1
120000 2 1 1
120000 3 1 1
95000 4 4 2
95000 5 4 2
90000 6 6 3
  • ROW_NUMBER() = 2 gives a 120000 row, which is wrong.
  • RANK() = 2 gives no rows, because RANK jumps from 1 to 4.
  • DENSE_RANK() = 2 gives the two 95000 rows, which is correct.

A CTE version reads more cleanly:

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) rnk
  FROM employee e WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT name, salary FROM ranked WHERE rnk = 2;

Approach 4: correlated subquery for the Nth highest (no window functions)

Logic: a salary is the Nth highest when exactly N−1 distinct salaries are greater than it.

-- N = 2
SELECT DISTINCT e1.salary
FROM employee e1
WHERE e1.salary IS NOT NULL       -- important, see the note below
  AND 1 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary)
           FROM employee e2
           WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary);
  • For 95000, the distinct salaries above it are {120000}, so the count is 1 = N−1. It matches.
  • NULL trap: without e1.salary IS NOT NULL, the NULL row gives a count of 0 (x > NULL is never true), so for N = 1 it would wrongly match alongside 120000.
  • Cost is O(n²). That is fine on small tables but slow on large ones. Prefer DENSE_RANK.

To get the names of the Nth-highest earners with this method:

SELECT name, salary FROM employee
WHERE salary = (SELECT DISTINCT e1.salary FROM employee e1
                WHERE e1.salary IS NOT NULL
                  AND 1 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary) FROM employee e2
                           WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary));

Getting the names with Approach 1

SELECT name, salary
FROM employee
WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee
                WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee));

Nth highest as a reusable MySQL function (classic follow-up)

DELIMITER $$
CREATE FUNCTION getNthHighestSalary(N INT) RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2)
DETERMINISTIC READS SQL DATA
BEGIN
  DECLARE off INT DEFAULT N - 1;      -- LIMIT does not accept an expression such as N-1
  RETURN (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employee
          WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
          ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET off);
END$$
DELIMITER ;

Approach summary

Approach Handles ties Generalises to N Result when none exists Portable
MAX with subquery Yes No NULL Yes
DISTINCT with LIMIT/OFFSET Only with DISTINCT Yes Empty set Syntax varies
DENSE_RANK Yes Yes Empty set All modern databases (MySQL 8+)
Correlated COUNT Yes Yes Empty set Yes, but O(n²)

Likely follow-ups:

  • What if the table is empty? MAX returns NULL, while LIMIT and DENSE_RANK return no rows. Wrap the query in a scalar subquery (or use COALESCE) if you need exactly one row.
  • Which is fastest on a large table? With an index on salary, the MAX subquery and ORDER BY…LIMIT both use an index scan. DENSE_RANK needs a sort or window pass, so it is a little heavier, but it is the most flexible.
  • Second highest per department? Add PARTITION BY dept_id to the DENSE_RANK.
  • Does MySQL 5.7 support window functions? No, they arrived in MySQL 8.0. Use Approach 1 or 4 on 5.7.
E2 Highest-paid employee(s) in each department (ties included) 
-- Window function (MySQL 8+, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server)
SELECT name, salary, dept_id FROM (
  SELECT e.*, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employee e
) t
WHERE rnk = 1;

-- Without window functions (correlated / tuple subquery)
SELECT e.name, e.salary, d.name AS dept
FROM employee e JOIN department d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE (e.dept_id, e.salary) IN (
  SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) FROM employee GROUP BY dept_id
);

RANK/DENSE_RANK keep ties. ROW_NUMBER returns exactly one row per department and drops the ties. SQL Server has no tuple IN, so use WHERE e.salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee x WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id).

Expected result (Arjun has no department, so he is excluded once we join to department):

department name salary
Analytics Karan 95000
Engineering Ravi 120000
Engineering Vikas 120000
Operations Meena 120000

Engineering has a tie, so a correct answer must return both Ravi and Vikas.

Approach 1: window function (preferred)

SELECT department, name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT d.name AS department, e.name, e.salary,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employee e
  JOIN department d ON d.id = e.dept_id
  WHERE e.salary IS NOT NULL      -- otherwise Neha (NULL) ranks 1st in Analytics on PostgreSQL/Oracle
) t
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY department, name;
  • RANK or DENSE_RANK = 1 keeps ties. ROW_NUMBER = 1 picks one arbitrary row per department. Use it only when the requirement is exactly one row per group, and add a tie-breaker such as ORDER BY salary DESC, id.
  • PostgreSQL alternative: ORDER BY e.salary DESC NULLS LAST instead of the WHERE filter.

Approach 2: join with the grouped MAX (works everywhere, including MySQL 5.7)

SELECT d.name AS department, e.name, e.salary
FROM employee e
JOIN (SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) AS max_sal
      FROM employee
      GROUP BY dept_id) m
  ON m.dept_id = e.dept_id
 AND m.max_sal = e.salary
JOIN department d ON d.id = e.dept_id
ORDER BY department, e.name;
  • The derived table is {1:120000, 2:120000, 3:95000, NULL:60000}. Joining back on both columns keeps every tied row.
  • The NULL group (Arjun) is dropped because NULL = NULL is not true in a join.

Approach 3: correlated subquery

SELECT d.name AS department, e.name, e.salary
FROM employee e
JOIN department d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary = (SELECT MAX(e2.salary)
                  FROM employee e2
                  WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id);

This is easy to read. It runs the subquery once per row, though the optimizer often rewrites it, so an index on (dept_id, salary) makes it fast.

Approach 4: NOT EXISTS (no one in the same department earns more)

SELECT d.name, e.name, e.salary
FROM employee e
JOIN department d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary IS NOT NULL        -- without this, Neha is returned (see trap)
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employee e2
                  WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id
                    AND e2.salary > e.salary);

Trap: for Neha, e2.salary > NULL is never true, so NOT EXISTS is TRUE and she would show up as a top earner. That is why the explicit NULL filter is needed.

Wrong answer interviewers like to catch

SELECT dept_id, name, MAX(salary) FROM employee GROUP BY dept_id;

name is neither grouped nor aggregated. PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle and MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY (the default since 5.7) reject it. Older MySQL returned an arbitrary name that was not necessarily the top earner.

Variations

  • Include departments with no employees (Finance shows up with NULLs): FROM department d LEFT JOIN (...ranked...) t ON t.dept_id = d.id AND t.rnk = 1.
  • Top 3 per department: WHERE rnk <= 3. Use DENSE_RANK if you mean the top three salary levels.
  • Only the max value per department (no names): SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) FROM employee GROUP BY dept_id.

Likely follow-ups:

  • RANK vs ROW_NUMBER here? RANK keeps ties. ROW_NUMBER forces exactly one row per department, which you might want for "pick one", and then you should add a tie-breaker.
  • What index would help? A composite index on (dept_id, salary DESC) serves the grouping, the correlated subquery and the window partition sort.
  • How do you show the department average next to each person? Use AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id). See E4.
E3 Name and salary of employees in each department 
SELECT d.name AS department, e.name AS employee, e.salary
FROM employee e
JOIN department d ON d.id = e.dept_id
ORDER BY d.name, e.salary DESC;

Use LEFT JOIN department ... starting from department if departments with no employees should still appear (FROM department d LEFT JOIN employee e ON ...).

Basic INNER JOIN (only employees that have a department)

SELECT d.name AS department, e.name AS employee, e.salary
FROM employee e
INNER JOIN department d ON d.id = e.dept_id
ORDER BY d.name, e.salary DESC, e.name;
department employee salary
Analytics Karan 95000
Analytics Neha NULL
Engineering Ravi 120000
Engineering Vikas 120000
Engineering Priya 95000
Engineering Asha 90000
Operations Meena 120000
Operations John 75000
  • Arjun is missing because his dept_id is NULL. Finance is missing because it has no employees.
  • e.name is the tie-breaker, so Ravi and Vikas always come out in the same order. Without a full ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed.

Include empty departments: LEFT JOIN from department

SELECT d.name AS department, e.name AS employee, e.salary
FROM department d
LEFT JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id
ORDER BY d.name, e.salary DESC;

This returns the same rows plus Finance | NULL | NULL.

Include employees without a department: LEFT JOIN from employee

SELECT COALESCE(d.name, 'Unassigned') AS department, e.name, e.salary
FROM employee e
LEFT JOIN department d ON d.id = e.dept_id;

This adds Unassigned | Arjun | 60000.

Both directions: FULL OUTER JOIN (MySQL has none, so emulate it with UNION)

-- PostgreSQL / SQL Server / Oracle
SELECT d.name, e.name, e.salary
FROM department d FULL OUTER JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id;

-- MySQL
SELECT d.name, e.name, e.salary FROM department d LEFT JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id
UNION
SELECT d.name, e.name, e.salary FROM department d RIGHT JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id;

One row per department with names aggregated

-- MySQL
SELECT d.name, GROUP_CONCAT(e.name ORDER BY e.name SEPARATOR ', ') AS employees
FROM department d LEFT JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id GROUP BY d.name;

-- PostgreSQL / SQL Server 2017+
SELECT d.name, STRING_AGG(e.name, ', ') AS employees ...   -- PostgreSQL also allows ORDER BY inside STRING_AGG

-- Oracle
SELECT d.name, LISTAGG(e.name, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY e.name) ...

Count per department: the COUNT(*) gotcha

SELECT d.name, COUNT(*) AS wrong_cnt, COUNT(e.id) AS right_cnt, AVG(e.salary) AS avg_sal
FROM department d LEFT JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.name;
name wrong_cnt right_cnt avg_sal
Analytics 2 2 95000
Engineering 4 4 106250
Finance 1 0 NULL
Operations 2 2 97500

COUNT(*) counts the NULL-padded row that the LEFT JOIN creates for Finance. COUNT(e.id) counts only actual matches.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why use a table alias? To avoid ambiguous column names (name exists in both tables) and to keep the query short.
  • Is a WHERE condition on the right table of a LEFT JOIN safe? No. WHERE e.salary > 50000 removes the NULL-padded rows, which turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. Put the condition in the ON clause instead.
  • How would you do this in JPA? @ManyToOne Department dept on Employee, then JPQL SELECT d.name, e.name, e.salary FROM Employee e JOIN e.dept d, or a LEFT JOIN for optional departments.
E4 Window functions

A window function calculates a value across a set of related rows (the "window"). Unlike GROUP BY, it does not collapse those rows. Syntax: fn() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... [ROWS ...]).

SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn,
  RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk,
  LAG(salary)  OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS prev_salary,
  LEAD(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS next_salary,
  SUM(salary)  OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)                      AS dept_total,
  SUM(salary)  OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS running_total
FROM employee;
salary ROW_NUMBER RANK DENSE_RANK
900 1 1 1
800 2 2 2
800 3 2 2
700 4 4 (gap) 3 (no gap)
  • ROW_NUMBER: a unique sequence. Typical uses are de-duplication and top-N per group.
  • RANK: tied rows get the same rank, and the next rank skips numbers.
  • DENSE_RANK: tied rows get the same rank, with no gaps.
  • LAG/LEAD: read the previous or next row's value, e.g. to compare with the last reading or compute deltas.
  • SUM/AVG OVER: per-group totals or running totals, without needing GROUP BY.

What they are

A window function computes a value across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them. GROUP BY returns one row per group; a window function keeps every row and adds a computed column.

function_name(args) OVER (
    [PARTITION BY col, ...]          -- split rows into groups (like GROUP BY, but rows are kept)
    [ORDER BY col [ASC|DESC], ...]   -- order inside each partition
    [frame_clause]                   -- which rows relative to the current row (ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN ...)
)

Categories

Category Functions
Ranking ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), NTILE(n), PERCENT_RANK(), CUME_DIST()
Offset/value LAG(col, n, default), LEAD(col, n, default), FIRST_VALUE(), LAST_VALUE(), NTH_VALUE()
Aggregate as window SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX with OVER(...)

Logical execution order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window functions → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. This is why you cannot use a window function in WHERE. Wrap it in a subquery or CTE and filter outside. (Some databases, such as Snowflake, BigQuery and Teradata, support QUALIFY for this; MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server do not.)

Ranking comparison table

SELECT name, salary,
  ROW_NUMBER()   OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS row_num,
  RANK()         OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)     AS rnk,
  DENSE_RANK()   OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)     AS dense_rnk,
  NTILE(4)       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS quartile,
  ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC), 2) AS pct_rank,
  ROUND(CUME_DIST()    OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC), 3) AS cume_dist
FROM employee
WHERE salary IS NOT NULL;
name salary row_num rnk dense_rnk quartile pct_rank cume_dist
Ravi 120000 1 1 1 1 0.00 0.375
Meena 120000 2 1 1 1 0.00 0.375
Vikas 120000 3 1 1 2 0.00 0.375
Priya 95000 4 4 2 2 0.43 0.625
Karan 95000 5 4 2 3 0.43 0.625
Asha 90000 6 6 3 3 0.71 0.750
John 75000 7 7 4 4 0.86 0.875
Arjun 60000 8 8 5 4 1.00 1.000
Function Ties Gaps after ties Typical use
ROW_NUMBER Different numbers (arbitrary unless a tie-breaker is given) n/a Deduplication, pagination, "pick one per group"
RANK Same number Yes (1,1,1,4) Competition ranking
DENSE_RANK Same number No (1,1,1,2) Nth highest value
NTILE(n) May split ties across buckets n/a Quartiles, percentiles, load-splitting
PERCENT_RANK Same value (rank−1)/(n−1) Relative position from 0 to 1
CUME_DIST Same value rows ≤ current / n "Top x% of earners"

NTILE: 8 rows into 4 buckets gives 2 per bucket. With 9 rows, the first bucket would get the extra row (3, 2, 2, 2).

PARTITION BY: aggregate without collapsing

SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)            AS dept_avg,
       salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)   AS diff_from_avg,
       COUNT(*)    OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)            AS dept_headcount
FROM employee
WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL;

Ravi gets dept_avg 106250 and diff 13750; Asha gets 106250 and −16250; Neha gets 95000 and NULL. That is impossible with plain GROUP BY unless you join back to an aggregated subquery.

LAG / LEAD, running total and moving average

SELECT id, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id)                                   AS running_total,
  LAG(amount)  OVER (ORDER BY id)                                  AS prev_amount,
  LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id)                                  AS next_amount,
  amount - LAG(amount, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY id)                    AS change_vs_prev,
  ROUND(AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id
        ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2)              AS moving_avg_3
FROM transactions;
id amount running_total prev_amount next_amount change_vs_prev moving_avg_3
1 500 500 NULL 700 500 500.00
2 700 1200 500 1500 200 600.00
3 1500 2700 700 200 800 900.00
4 200 2900 1500 1200 −1300 800.00
5 1200 4100 200 500 1000 966.67
6 500 4600 1200 NULL −700 633.33

Running total per receiver: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY receiver_id ORDER BY id).

Frames: ROWS vs RANGE (the most commonly misunderstood part)

ROWS  BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW   -- physical rows
RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW   -- all rows with the same ORDER BY value (peers) included
ROWS  BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING
ROWS  BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  • Default frame: with ORDER BY and no frame, it is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Without ORDER BY, the frame is the whole partition.
  • Consequence 1 (ties): SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary) gives all three 120000 rows the same running total, because they are peers. Use ROWS (or add a unique tie-breaker) for a true row-by-row running total.
  • Consequence 2 (the LAST_VALUE trap): LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary) returns the current row, not the department's last row, because the default frame ends at the current row. Fix it with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or use FIRST_VALUE with the opposite ORDER BY.
SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
  FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER w AS lowest_paid,
  LAST_VALUE(name)  OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS highest_paid
FROM employee
WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL AND salary IS NOT NULL
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary);   -- named window: MySQL 8, PostgreSQL

Practical uses

  • Deduplicate (keep the latest reading per IoT sensor):
    DELETE FROM sensor_reading WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM (SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY sensor_id, reading_ts ORDER BY id DESC) rn
                  FROM sensor_reading) x WHERE rn > 1);
  • Latest status per incident: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY incident_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1.
  • Gap detection (sensor went silent): reading_ts - LAG(reading_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY sensor_id ORDER BY reading_ts) > INTERVAL '5' MINUTE.
  • Top N per group, month-over-month change, percent of total: amount * 100.0 / SUM(amount) OVER ().

Likely follow-ups:

  • Window function vs GROUP BY? GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group. A window function keeps all rows and adds the aggregate alongside each one.
  • Can you filter on a window result in WHERE? No, because windows are evaluated after WHERE. Use a subquery or CTE (or QUALIFY where supported).
  • Performance? Each distinct PARTITION BY/ORDER BY combination needs a sort. An index matching (partition cols, order cols) can avoid it, and you should reuse the same window (a named WINDOW) where possible.
  • Which versions support them? MySQL 8.0+, PostgreSQL 8.4+, SQL Server 2005+ (frames since 2012), and Oracle 8i+.
E5 ACID properties Co. 2
  • Atomicity: either the whole transaction happens or none of it does. On failure it rolls back (@Transactional rolls back on a RuntimeException).
  • Consistency: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another. Constraints, FKs and triggers still hold afterwards.
  • Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted work. The isolation levels are READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE. They prevent dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantom reads respectively.
  • Durability: once a transaction commits, it survives a crash. This is done with write-ahead/redo logs.

Example: a money transfer debits one account and credits another, and both must succeed together.

Scenario: transfer ₹500 from account A (balance 1000) to account B (balance 200).

CREATE TABLE account (id INT PRIMARY KEY, holder VARCHAR(50),
                      balance DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0));

START TRANSACTION;                                   -- BEGIN in PostgreSQL / SQL Server
UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;   -- A
UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;   -- B
INSERT INTO transactions(sender_id, receiver_id, amount) VALUES (1, 2, 500);
COMMIT;                                              -- or ROLLBACK on any error
Property Meaning In the transfer
Atomicity All statements succeed, or none take effect If the credit to B fails (for example the server crashes after the debit), the debit from A is rolled back. Money is never lost halfway. Implemented with the undo log / rollback segments.
Consistency A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, and all constraints hold CHECK (balance >= 0), foreign keys and the business rule "total money A+B stays 1200" hold before and after. If A had only 300, the CHECK fails and the transaction rolls back.
Isolation Concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate state (to a degree set by the isolation level) Another transaction reading A and B mid-transfer never sees A=500 and B=200 (₹500 "missing"). Implemented with locks and/or MVCC.
Durability Once committed, the change survives crashes After COMMIT returns, A=500 and B=700 survive a power failure. Implemented with the write-ahead / redo log flushed to disk.

In Spring Boot:

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class TransferService {
    private final AccountRepository accounts;

    @Transactional(isolation = Isolation.READ_COMMITTED, rollbackFor = Exception.class)
    public void transfer(Long fromId, Long toId, BigDecimal amount) {
        // Lock rows in a consistent order (lower id first) to avoid deadlocks
        Account from = accounts.findByIdForUpdate(fromId);   // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
        Account to   = accounts.findByIdForUpdate(toId);
        if (from.getBalance().compareTo(amount) < 0) {
            throw new InsufficientFundsException(fromId);    // RuntimeException, so the transaction rolls back
        }
        from.debit(amount);
        to.credit(amount);
        // JPA dirty checking flushes both UPDATEs at commit, atomically
    }
}

public interface AccountRepository extends JpaRepository<Account, Long> {
    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @Query("select a from Account a where a.id = :id")
    Account findByIdForUpdate(@Param("id") Long id);
}

Gotchas worth mentioning: by default Spring rolls back only on unchecked exceptions (use rollbackFor). @Transactional also does nothing on self-invocation (a call from inside the same class bypasses the proxy) or on private methods.

Read anomalies

Anomaly What happens Bank example
Dirty read T2 reads data T1 has written but not committed T1 debits A to 500 and has not committed. T2 reads 500 and approves a loan. T1 rolls back, so T2 acted on a value that never existed.
Non-repeatable read T1 reads the same row twice and gets different values, because T2 updated and committed in between A statement job reads A=1000, a transfer commits, and the job re-reads A=500 within the same transaction.
Phantom read T1 runs the same range query twice and gets different rows, because T2 inserted or deleted matching rows SELECT COUNT(*) FROM transactions WHERE amount > 1000 returns 2, then T2 inserts a new large transfer, and it returns 3.
Lost update (bonus) Two transactions read, modify and write the same row; one overwrites the other Two deposits each read 1000, add 100 and write 1100. The result should be 1200. Prevent it with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, an atomic SET balance = balance + x, or optimistic @Version.

Isolation levels (SQL standard)

Level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom
READ UNCOMMITTED Possible Possible Possible
READ COMMITTED Prevented Possible Possible
REPEATABLE READ Prevented Prevented Possible in the standard; mostly prevented in InnoDB and PostgreSQL
SERIALIZABLE Prevented Prevented Prevented

Database defaults and implementation notes

Database Default Notes
MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ MVCC snapshot reads plus next-key/gap locks for locking reads, which prevents most phantoms
PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED Its REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation (no phantoms). SERIALIZABLE is SSI and can abort transactions with serialization failures, so retry them. READ UNCOMMITTED behaves like READ COMMITTED.
SQL Server READ COMMITTED (lock-based) READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT switches it to MVCC. There is also a SNAPSHOT level.
Oracle READ COMMITTED Supports only READ COMMITTED, SERIALIZABLE and READ ONLY

Higher isolation means fewer anomalies but more locking or aborts, so less concurrency. Most applications stay at READ COMMITTED and protect critical rows with explicit locking (FOR UPDATE) or optimistic locking (@Version):

@Entity
public class Account {
    @Id Long id;
    BigDecimal balance;
    @Version Long version;   // UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND version=?  → OptimisticLockException on a conflict
}

Likely follow-ups:

  • Optimistic vs pessimistic locking? Optimistic uses a version column, detects conflicts at write time and retries; it suits low contention. Pessimistic uses SELECT FOR UPDATE and blocks other writers; it suits high-contention money movement.
  • How do you keep ACID across microservices? You can't with a single database transaction. Use the Saga pattern (choreography or orchestration with compensating actions), the transactional outbox, and idempotent consumers. Avoid 2PC/XA in microservices.
  • What does propagation = REQUIRES_NEW do? It suspends the current transaction and starts an independent one, for example for an audit log that must be saved even if the outer transaction rolls back.
  • How do deadlocks happen, and how do you avoid them? Two transactions lock rows in opposite order. Lock in a consistent order, keep transactions short, and retry on deadlock errors.
E6 Stored procedures: what, why, "hierarchy" Hexaware

What: a precompiled, named block of SQL plus procedural logic, stored in the database. It accepts IN/OUT/INOUT parameters and is invoked with CALL or EXEC. Why: it saves network round-trips because the logic runs next to the data, gives a reusable and centrally owned piece of business logic, offers security (grant EXECUTE without granting table access), and benefits from a cached execution plan. Downsides: it is harder to version, test and port, and logic gets split between the app and the DB.

Hierarchy / how the DB objects relate:

  • Nested procedures: a procedure can CALL other procedures. For example, process_order calls validate_stock, then create_invoice, then log_audit. Nesting depth is limited (SQL Server allows 32). Transaction handling, i.e. who commits, should normally sit in the outermost procedure.
  • Functions: return a single value or a table and can be used inside SELECT/WHERE. They generally cannot perform DML or commit. Procedures can call functions. A function cannot call a procedure that modifies data.
  • Triggers: run automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. They can call procedures.
  • Views: saved SELECTs (a virtual table). Procedures and functions can query them.
-- MySQL
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE raise_dept_salary(IN p_dept INT, IN p_pct DECIMAL(5,2))
BEGIN
  UPDATE employee SET salary = salary * (1 + p_pct/100) WHERE dept_id = p_dept;
  CALL log_audit('RAISE', p_dept);      -- nested call
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL raise_dept_salary(10, 5);

From Spring you can call it with @Procedure (Spring Data JPA), SimpleJdbcCall, or entityManager.createStoredProcedureQuery(...).

What

A stored procedure is a named, precompiled block of SQL and procedural logic (variables, IF, loops, cursors, error handlers) stored in the database and executed with CALL (MySQL/PostgreSQL) or EXEC (SQL Server). It can take IN, OUT and INOUT parameters, run DML and DDL, manage transactions, and return result sets.

Why use them

  • Fewer network round-trips: one call runs many statements, which helps with bulk or batch operations such as nightly aggregation of IoT readings.
  • Logic close to the data, which suits heavy set-based processing.
  • Security: grant EXECUTE on the procedure without granting table access.
  • Reuse by several applications or report tools.
  • Plan caching (in SQL Server and Oracle especially).

Hierarchy and comparison of database objects

Object Returns Usable in SELECT? DML allowed? Transaction control Invoked by
View Virtual table (a stored query) Yes, like a table Simple views are updatable No Querying it
Function (UDF) A single value (scalar) or a table (table-valued) Yes (SELECT fn(x)) Generally no side effects (MySQL allows some; SQL Server forbids them) No Expressions
Stored procedure 0..n result sets and OUT params No Yes Yes (COMMIT/ROLLBACK inside, in most databases) CALL/EXEC from an app or another procedure
Trigger Nothing No Yes Runs inside the triggering transaction Automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (BEFORE/AFTER, row or statement level)
Package (Oracle) Container n/a n/a n/a Groups related procedures and functions with shared state

Nesting (the "hierarchy" in practice):

  • A procedure can call other procedures and functions. MySQL allows recursive calls only if max_sp_recursion_depth > 0; SQL Server limits nesting to 32 levels (@@NESTLEVEL).
  • A function can call other functions, but generally cannot call a procedure that modifies data (rules vary by database).
  • A trigger can call procedures or functions and can fire other triggers (cascading triggers). This is a common source of hidden behaviour and debugging pain.
  • A view can use functions.

MySQL example: fund transfer with IN/OUT parameters and error handling

DELIMITER $$

CREATE PROCEDURE transfer_funds(
    IN  p_from    INT,
    IN  p_to      INT,
    IN  p_amount  DECIMAL(12,2),
    OUT p_status  VARCHAR(30),
    OUT p_new_bal DECIMAL(12,2)
)
BEGIN
    DECLARE v_balance DECIMAL(12,2);

    -- Any SQL error: roll back and report it
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION
    BEGIN
        ROLLBACK;
        SET p_status = 'ERROR';
    END;

    START TRANSACTION;

    SELECT balance INTO v_balance FROM account WHERE id = p_from FOR UPDATE;

    IF v_balance IS NULL THEN
        SET p_status = 'ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND';
        ROLLBACK;
    ELSEIF v_balance < p_amount THEN
        SET p_status = 'INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS';
        ROLLBACK;
    ELSE
        UPDATE account SET balance = balance - p_amount WHERE id = p_from;
        UPDATE account SET balance = balance + p_amount WHERE id = p_to;
        INSERT INTO transactions(sender_id, receiver_id, amount) VALUES (p_from, p_to, p_amount);
        COMMIT;
        SET p_status  = 'SUCCESS';
        SET p_new_bal = v_balance - p_amount;
    END IF;
END$$

DELIMITER ;

-- Call it
CALL transfer_funds(1, 2, 500, @status, @bal);
SELECT @status, @bal;

DELIMITER is a MySQL client command. It changes the statement terminator so the ; characters inside the body do not end the CREATE statement.

A function and a trigger, for comparison:

DELIMITER $$
CREATE FUNCTION total_received(p_user INT) RETURNS DECIMAL(12,2)
DETERMINISTIC READS SQL DATA
BEGIN
  RETURN (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) FROM transactions WHERE receiver_id = p_user);
END$$

CREATE TRIGGER trg_audit_salary
AFTER UPDATE ON employee FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF NOT (OLD.salary <=> NEW.salary) THEN       -- <=> is MySQL's NULL-safe equality
    INSERT INTO salary_audit(emp_id, old_salary, new_salary, changed_at)
    VALUES (OLD.id, OLD.salary, NEW.salary, NOW());
  END IF;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

SELECT id, first_name, total_received(id) FROM users;   -- a function works inside SELECT

Equivalent syntax in other dialects (briefly): PostgreSQL uses CREATE PROCEDURE ... LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ ... $$ (procedures since v11; earlier versions had functions only) and CALL. SQL Server uses CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.transfer_funds @from INT, @status VARCHAR(30) OUTPUT AS BEGIN ... END and EXEC. Oracle uses CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE ... (p_from IN NUMBER, p_status OUT VARCHAR2) IS BEGIN ... END;.

Calling from Spring

Option 1: Spring Data JPA @Procedure

@Entity
@NamedStoredProcedureQuery(
    name = "Account.transferFunds",
    procedureName = "transfer_funds",
    parameters = {
        @StoredProcedureParameter(mode = ParameterMode.IN,  name = "p_from",    type = Integer.class),
        @StoredProcedureParameter(mode = ParameterMode.IN,  name = "p_to",      type = Integer.class),
        @StoredProcedureParameter(mode = ParameterMode.IN,  name = "p_amount",  type = BigDecimal.class),
        @StoredProcedureParameter(mode = ParameterMode.OUT, name = "p_status",  type = String.class),
        @StoredProcedureParameter(mode = ParameterMode.OUT, name = "p_new_bal", type = BigDecimal.class)
    })
public class Account { /* ... */ }

public interface AccountRepository extends JpaRepository<Account, Long> {

    // Multiple OUT params are returned as Map<String, Object>
    @Procedure(name = "Account.transferFunds")
    Map<String, Object> transferFunds(@Param("p_from") Integer from,
                                      @Param("p_to") Integer to,
                                      @Param("p_amount") BigDecimal amount);

    // Simple procedure with a single OUT param, without a named query
    @Procedure(procedureName = "count_active_sensors")
    Integer countActiveSensors(Integer zoneId);
}

Option 2: SimpleJdbcCall (JDBC, no entity needed, flexible)

@Repository
public class TransferDao {
    private final SimpleJdbcCall transferCall;

    public TransferDao(DataSource ds) {
        this.transferCall = new SimpleJdbcCall(ds).withProcedureName("transfer_funds");
        // Metadata lookup discovers the params. Or declare them explicitly:
        // .withoutProcedureColumnMetaDataAccess().declareParameters(new SqlParameter("p_from", Types.INTEGER), ...)
    }

    public TransferResult transfer(int from, int to, BigDecimal amount) {
        Map<String, Object> out = transferCall.execute(new MapSqlParameterSource()
                .addValue("p_from", from)
                .addValue("p_to", to)
                .addValue("p_amount", amount));
        return new TransferResult((String) out.get("p_status"), (BigDecimal) out.get("p_new_bal"));
    }
}

For functions use new SimpleJdbcCall(ds).withFunctionName("total_received").executeFunction(BigDecimal.class, params). Other options are EntityManager.createStoredProcedureQuery(...) and plain JdbcTemplate.call(...).

Pros and cons

Pros Cons
Fewer round-trips, so faster bulk operations Business logic split between Java and the database is harder to find, review and debug
Fine-grained security (EXECUTE only) Vendor lock-in: PL/SQL, T-SQL and MySQL procedural SQL are not portable
Reuse across applications and BI tools Harder to unit test, version (needs Flyway/Liquibase) and run in CI
Plan caching Scales with the database, which is usually the hardest tier to scale out
Good for heavy set-based ETL and reporting Hidden side effects (especially triggers), and weak IDE/refactoring support

Typical stance in a Spring Boot microservice: keep business logic in the service layer, and use procedures selectively for heavy batch/report jobs or legacy integration. Keep them in version control and deploy them with Flyway or Liquibase migrations.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Procedure vs function in one line? A function returns a value and can be used in SQL expressions. A procedure is CALLed, can have several OUT params or result sets, and can control transactions.
  • Can a procedure return a result set? Yes. A plain SELECT inside a MySQL procedure returns one; in Spring, read it with SimpleJdbcCall.returningResultSet(...).
  • How do you prevent SQL injection in a procedure? Use parameters. Avoid dynamic SQL built by string concatenation; if dynamic SQL is unavoidable, use PREPARE ... USING or sp_executesql with parameters.
  • Why are triggers risky? They are invisible to application developers, cascade, slow down writes and complicate bulk loads. Use them sparingly, for example for auditing.
E7 Table A and Table B hold the same records: what does INNER JOIN return? Hexaware

If the join column is unique in both tables, you get every row once, i.e. as many rows as the table has. Duplicates multiply and NULLs never match (NULL = NULL evaluates to unknown).

A.val: 1, 1, 2, NULL        B.val: 1, 1, 2, NULL
SELECT * FROM A JOIN B ON A.val = B.val;
-> val 1: 2 x 2 = 4 rows
-> val 2: 1 x 1 = 1 row
-> NULL : 0 rows
Total = 5 rows (not 4)

For a value that appears m times in A and n times in B, the join produces m x n rows.

Short answer: an INNER JOIN returns every pair of rows (a from A, b from B) for which the join condition is TRUE. If both tables have the same unique values, you get one row per value, the same number of rows as each table. Duplicates multiply, and NULLs never match.

Case 1: same records, unique values

A.id: 1, 2, 3          B.id: 1, 2, 3
SELECT A.id AS a_id, B.id AS b_id FROM A INNER JOIN B ON A.id = B.id;
a_id b_id
1 1
2 2
3 3

That is 3 rows. LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins would also return exactly 3 rows here, because every row has a match.

Case 2: same records, with duplicates (the interview trick)

A.id: 1, 1, 2          B.id: 1, 1, 2
value count in A count in B rows produced
1 2 2 2 × 2 = 4
2 1 1 1 × 1 = 1

Total: 5 rows, not 3. Each A row with value 1 matches both B rows with value 1.

a_id b_id
1 1
1 1
1 1
1 1
2 2

Rule: for each join key, output rows = (count in A) × (count in B).

Case 3: NULLs in both tables

A.id: 1, 2, NULL       B.id: 1, 2, NULL

INNER JOIN returns 2 rows (1 and 2). NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so the NULL rows never pair.

  • To match NULLs on purpose: ON A.id = B.id OR (A.id IS NULL AND B.id IS NULL), MySQL's ON A.id <=> B.id, or the standard IS NOT DISTINCT FROM (PostgreSQL, SQL Server 2022+).
  • LEFT JOIN would return 3 rows, with NULL | NULL for A's NULL row (unmatched, so B's columns are NULL-padded). FULL JOIN would return 4 rows: the two matches, plus A's NULL and B's NULL as separate unmatched rows.

Mixed worked example

A.id: 1, 2, 2, 3, NULL       B.id: 2, 2, 3, 4, NULL
key A count B count INNER rows
1 1 0 0
2 2 2 4
3 1 1 1
4 0 1 0
NULL 1 1 0

INNER = 5. LEFT = 5 + 2 unmatched A rows (1 and NULL) = 7. RIGHT = 5 + 2 unmatched B rows (4 and NULL) = 7. FULL = 5 + 2 + 2 = 9.

Same records, but no join condition (or ON 1=1)

That is a CROSS JOIN (Cartesian product): 3 × 3 = 9 rows for Case 1.

Related set operations interviewers sometimes want instead

  • SELECT * FROM A INTERSECT SELECT * FROM B returns the common rows with duplicates removed (Case 2 gives {1, 2}). In set operations, NULLs are treated as equal.
  • A EXCEPT B (MINUS in Oracle) returns rows in A but not in B. For tables with identical records it returns nothing.
  • UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you avoid row multiplication? Join on a unique key, deduplicate first (SELECT DISTINCT or ROW_NUMBER in a CTE), or use EXISTS when you only need to filter.
  • How do you check that two tables are identical? Run (A EXCEPT B) UNION ALL (B EXCEPT A) and confirm it is empty, and also compare COUNT(*) (and per-key counts) to catch differences in duplicates.
  • Is there any difference between JOIN and INNER JOIN? No. INNER is optional.
E8 20 records starting from the 5th row (first and last name) Co. 2 
-- MySQL / PostgreSQL
SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 4;          -- MySQL also accepts: LIMIT 4, 20

-- Oracle 12c+ / SQL Server 2012+
SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users
ORDER BY id
OFFSET 4 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;

OFFSET 4 skips rows 1–4, so the result begins at row 5. Always include ORDER BY, because without it the row order is not deterministic. For pagination the general formula is OFFSET (page-1)*size. Spring Data's Pageable produces this SQL for you.

"Starting from the 5th row" means skip 4 rows and take 20, which gives rows 5–24 in the chosen order (ids 5–24 if ordered by id).

Why ORDER BY is mandatory

Tables are unordered sets. Without ORDER BY, the database may return rows in any order (insertion order, index order, or whatever a parallel scan produces), and the "5th row" can change between executions. That causes duplicated or skipped rows across pages. Always order by a unique column, or add a unique tie-breaker such as ORDER BY last_name, id.

MySQL

SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM users
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 4;

-- equivalent shorthand: LIMIT offset, count
SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users ORDER BY id LIMIT 4, 20;

PostgreSQL

SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 4;
-- the SQL-standard form also works
SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users ORDER BY id OFFSET 4 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;

SQL Server 2012+

SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM users
ORDER BY id                         -- ORDER BY is REQUIRED for OFFSET/FETCH
OFFSET 4 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;

SQL Server 2008 and older (no OFFSET) use ROW_NUMBER:

SELECT first_name, last_name FROM (
  SELECT first_name, last_name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM users
) t
WHERE rn BETWEEN 5 AND 24;

Or TOP with NOT IN (works, but clumsy):

SELECT TOP 20 first_name, last_name FROM users
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT TOP 4 id FROM users ORDER BY id)
ORDER BY id;

Oracle 12c+

SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users
ORDER BY id
OFFSET 4 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;

Oracle 11g and older use ROWNUM. ROWNUM is assigned before ORDER BY, so you need nested queries:

SELECT first_name, last_name FROM (
  SELECT a.*, ROWNUM rn FROM (
    SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users ORDER BY id
  ) a
  WHERE ROWNUM <= 24          -- upper bound in the middle layer (stops early)
)
WHERE rn >= 5;                -- lower bound outside

WHERE ROWNUM >= 5 on its own returns nothing. The first candidate row gets ROWNUM 1, fails the test and is discarded, so the next candidate also gets ROWNUM 1, and so on.

Dialect summary

Database Syntax
MySQL LIMIT 20 OFFSET 4 or LIMIT 4, 20
PostgreSQL LIMIT 20 OFFSET 4 or OFFSET 4 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY
SQL Server 2012+ ORDER BY … OFFSET 4 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY
SQL Server (old) TOP / ROW_NUMBER() BETWEEN 5 AND 24
Oracle 12c+ OFFSET 4 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY
Oracle (old) Nested ROWNUM

General formula: page p (1-based) of size s uses OFFSET (p−1)·s. "From row r" uses OFFSET r−1.

Performance: why OFFSET gets slow, and keyset (seek) pagination

OFFSET 1000000 still makes the database read and discard a million rows, so cost grows with page depth. Rows inserted or deleted between page loads also cause duplicates or skips.

Keyset pagination remembers the last key seen and seeks to it through the index:

-- first page
SELECT id, first_name, last_name FROM users ORDER BY id LIMIT 20;

-- next page: the client sends the last id it received (say 24)
SELECT id, first_name, last_name FROM users
WHERE id > 24
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 20;

-- multi-column sort (last_name, id): row-value comparison (MySQL, PostgreSQL)
SELECT id, first_name, last_name FROM users
WHERE (last_name, id) > (:lastName, :lastId)
ORDER BY last_name, id
LIMIT 20;
-- SQL Server / Oracle: WHERE last_name > :ln OR (last_name = :ln AND id > :lastId)
OFFSET Keyset
Deep page cost O(offset + n) O(log N + n) with an index
Jump to page 57 Easy Not directly (next/previous only)
Stable under inserts No Yes
Typical use Admin tables with page numbers Infinite scroll, live alert feeds, APIs, exports

In Spring Data:

// Offset-based: page 0 = rows 1–20
Page<User> page = userRepo.findAll(PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("id")));

// "Start at row 5" is not page-aligned, so use a native query with LIMIT/OFFSET or OffsetScrollPosition

// Keyset: simple derived query
List<User> findTop20ByIdGreaterThanOrderByIdAsc(Long lastId);

// Keyset: Spring Data 3.1+ scrolling API
Window<User> findFirst20ByOrderByIdAsc(ScrollPosition position);   // call with ScrollPosition.keyset()

Page triggers an extra COUNT(*) query. Use Slice when you do not need the total.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not use SELECT *? It fetches unneeded columns, defeats covering indexes, and breaks when the schema changes. Select only first_name and last_name.
  • How does Angular's paginator map to this? It sends page and size to Spring's Pageable, and the response contains content and totalElements.
  • Is ORDER BY by itself enough? Only if the ordering is unique. Otherwise add a unique tie-breaker such as id.
E9 INNER JOIN between two tables Co. 2 
SELECT e.id, e.name, e.salary, d.name AS department
FROM employee e
INNER JOIN department d ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE e.salary > 50000;

Only rows that match in both tables are returned. Employees with no department, or a NULL dept_id, are excluded. If you need them, use LEFT JOIN.

Using employee and department from the sample data:

SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept
FROM employee e
INNER JOIN department d ON e.dept_id = d.id;

This returns 8 rows: every employee whose dept_id matches a department. Arjun (NULL dept_id) and Finance (no employees) are excluded.

Older comma syntax (works, but avoid it, because forgetting the WHERE clause produces a Cartesian product):

SELECT e.name, d.name FROM employee e, department d WHERE e.dept_id = d.id;
