USING / NATURAL: JOIN ... USING (col) needs the same column name in both tables. NATURAL JOIN joins on all same-named columns, which is dangerous here because both tables have id and name.

Join types compared (small example)

L (employee subset)          R (department subset)
id name  dept_id             id name
1  Asha  1                   1  Engineering
7  Neha  3                   2  Operations
8  Arjun NULL                3  Analytics
Join Rule Result (L.name / R.name) Rows
INNER Matches only Asha/Engineering, Neha/Analytics 2
LEFT All of L, plus matches or NULL Asha/Engineering, Neha/Analytics, Arjun/NULL 3
RIGHT All of R, plus matches or NULL Asha/Engineering, NULL/Operations, Neha/Analytics 3
FULL OUTER All of both Asha/Engineering, Neha/Analytics, Arjun/NULL, NULL/Operations 4
CROSS Every combination 3 × 3 9
SELF A table joined to itself see below — 
-- LEFT anti-join: employees without a department
SELECT e.name FROM employee e LEFT JOIN department d ON d.id = e.dept_id WHERE d.id IS NULL;   -- Arjun

-- Departments without employees (often better written as NOT EXISTS)
SELECT d.name FROM department d
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employee e WHERE e.dept_id = d.id);                           -- Finance

-- CROSS JOIN: e.g. every sensor × every hour slot for a report grid
SELECT s.sensor_id, h.slot FROM sensor s CROSS JOIN hour_slot h;

-- SELF JOIN: needs a manager_id column, e.g. employee(id, name, manager_id)
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employee e LEFT JOIN employee m ON m.id = e.manager_id;

-- SELF JOIN: pairs in the same department (e1.id < e2.id avoids mirror duplicates and self-pairs)
SELECT e1.name, e2.name, e1.dept_id
FROM employee e1 JOIN employee e2 ON e1.dept_id = e2.dept_id AND e1.id < e2.id;
  • RIGHT JOIN is just LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped. Most teams standardise on LEFT for readability.
  • MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN. Emulate it with LEFT JOIN … UNION … RIGHT JOIN (see E3).

How databases execute joins (bonus depth)

Algorithm Best when
Nested loop (with index lookup) Small outer input, indexed inner join column
Hash join Large unsorted inputs with equality conditions (PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle; MySQL 8.0.18+)
Merge join Both inputs already sorted on the join key

Index the foreign-key column (employee.dept_id). MySQL InnoDB creates that index automatically for FK constraints; PostgreSQL does not.

Likely follow-ups:

  • ON vs WHERE in a LEFT JOIN? A condition in ON filters the right table before matching, so unmatched left rows are kept. A condition in WHERE filters after the join and can drop the NULL-padded rows.
  • Join vs subquery: which is faster? Modern optimizers often produce the same plan. Use EXISTS for semi-joins and JOIN when you need columns from both tables, and check with EXPLAIN.
  • What is the JPA N+1 problem? A lazy association is loaded once per row. Fix it with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or batch fetching.
E10 Highest receiver amount Hexaware 
-- (a) Receiver who received the highest TOTAL amount
SELECT receiver_id, SUM(amount) AS total_received
FROM transactions
GROUP BY receiver_id
ORDER BY total_received DESC
LIMIT 1;                                  -- Oracle/SQL Server: FETCH FIRST 1 ROWS ONLY / TOP 1

-- with the receiver's name, and ties kept
SELECT u.first_name, u.last_name, t.total_received FROM (
  SELECT receiver_id, SUM(amount) AS total_received,
         RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM transactions GROUP BY receiver_id
) t JOIN users u ON u.id = t.receiver_id
WHERE t.rnk = 1;

-- (b) The single largest transaction and who received it
SELECT receiver_id, amount FROM transactions
WHERE amount = (SELECT MAX(amount) FROM transactions);

Ask the interviewer which meaning they intend: the highest total, or the single biggest transaction.

The question is ambiguous, so clarify it first: "Do you mean the user who received the highest total, or the single largest transaction?" Interviewers like to see that. Both answers are below.

Interpretation A: the receiver with the highest total received

Totals: user 2 = 1200, user 3 = 1700, user 4 = 1700. There is a tie.

Naive LIMIT 1 (misses ties):

SELECT receiver_id, SUM(amount) AS total_received
FROM transactions
GROUP BY receiver_id
ORDER BY total_received DESC
LIMIT 1;                         -- returns only 3 OR 4, chosen arbitrarily

SQL Server handles ties with SELECT TOP 1 WITH TIES receiver_id, SUM(amount) ... ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC. Oracle 12c+ and PostgreSQL 13+ use FETCH FIRST 1 ROWS WITH TIES.

Tie-safe with RANK, including the name:

WITH totals AS (
  SELECT receiver_id, SUM(amount) AS total_received
  FROM transactions
  GROUP BY receiver_id
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT t.*, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_received DESC) AS rnk
  FROM totals t
)
SELECT u.id, u.first_name, u.last_name, r.total_received
FROM ranked r
JOIN users u ON u.id = r.receiver_id
WHERE r.rnk = 1;
id first_name last_name total_received
3 Meena Iyer 1700
4 John Dsouza 1700

Tie-safe without window functions (HAVING = MAX of the sums):

SELECT u.first_name, u.last_name, SUM(t.amount) AS total_received
FROM transactions t
JOIN users u ON u.id = t.receiver_id
GROUP BY u.id, u.first_name, u.last_name
HAVING SUM(t.amount) = (
  SELECT MAX(s) FROM (SELECT SUM(amount) AS s FROM transactions GROUP BY receiver_id) x
);

The derived table must have an alias (x) in MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server.

Interpretation B: the single highest transaction and its receiver

SELECT t.id, u.first_name, u.last_name, t.amount
FROM transactions t
JOIN users u ON u.id = t.receiver_id
WHERE t.amount = (SELECT MAX(amount) FROM transactions);
id first_name last_name amount
3 John Dsouza 1500

WHERE amount = (SELECT MAX…) is automatically tie-safe.

Variations interviewers chain on

-- Net balance per user (received − sent), including users with no transactions
SELECT u.id, u.first_name,
       COALESCE(r.recv, 0) - COALESCE(s.sent, 0) AS net
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN (SELECT receiver_id, SUM(amount) recv FROM transactions GROUP BY receiver_id) r ON r.receiver_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT sender_id,   SUM(amount) sent FROM transactions GROUP BY sender_id)   s ON s.sender_id   = u.id;
-- Aggregate in subqueries BEFORE joining. Joining transactions twice and then summing multiplies rows (see E7).

-- Highest single amount received per receiver
SELECT receiver_id, MAX(amount) FROM transactions GROUP BY receiver_id;

-- Show sender and receiver names: join users twice with different aliases
SELECT t.id, s.first_name AS sender, r.first_name AS receiver, t.amount
FROM transactions t
JOIN users s ON s.id = t.sender_id
JOIN users r ON r.id = t.receiver_id;

Net result for the first five users: Asha −700, Ravi −300, Meena +1000, John +500, Priya −500. (Check: 0−700, 1200−1500, 1700−700, 1700−1200, 0−500. The values sum to 0, as they should.)

Edge cases:

  • Users who received nothing do not appear in a GROUP BY on transactions. Start from users LEFT JOIN ... if they must appear with 0.
  • A receiver_id that is NULL, or that has no matching user (orphan data), is dropped by the INNER JOIN.
  • Use DECIMAL, not FLOAT, for money.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Top 3 receivers? Use DENSE_RANK() <= 3 on the totals, or LIMIT 3 if ties don't matter.
  • Highest receiver per month? Partition the RANK by month: DATE_FORMAT(created_at,'%Y-%m') in MySQL, date_trunc('month', created_at) in PostgreSQL.
  • Which index helps? (receiver_id, amount), which is a covering index for the GROUP BY plus SUM.
E11 Explain Angular

Angular is Google's component-based, TypeScript framework for building SPAs. Its main pieces:

  • Components (template + class + styles) and standalone components, which are the default since v17 and don't need an NgModule. Older apps use NgModules.
  • Data binding: interpolation {{ }}, property binding [prop], event binding (event), and two-way binding [(ngModel)].
  • Dependency injection: services declared with @Injectable({providedIn:'root'}) hold shared logic and API calls.
  • RxJS Observables for async work, e.g. HttpClient, async pipe, switchMap, debounceTime.
  • Router: lazy-loaded routes, guards (canActivate), resolvers.
  • Forms: template-driven and reactive (FormGroup, validators).
  • Signals (v16+): signal(), computed(), effect() give fine-grained reactivity. Together with zoneless change detection they are the newer alternative to Zone.js.
  • Also: directives, pipes, HTTP interceptors (attach JWTs, handle errors), lifecycle hooks (ngOnInit, ngOnDestroy), and the CLI for scaffolding and builds.

One-liner: Angular is Google's TypeScript-based, component-driven framework for building single-page applications. It ships "batteries included": a router, HttpClient, forms, dependency injection, testing tools and the CLI, all in one opinionated, consistent structure. That is why it is popular for large enterprise dashboards.

Big picture

            ┌──────────────── Angular App ────────────────┐
 Browser ── │ Router → Components (Template + Class + CSS) │
            │            │  data binding / signals         │
            │            ▼                                 │
            │  Directives, Pipes      Services (DI)  ──────┼──► HttpClient → Interceptors → Spring Boot REST
            │                          RxJS / Signals      │    WebSocket/STOMP → live alerts
            └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

1. Components and templates

A component is a TypeScript class, a template (HTML) and styles. Modern Angular (v14+, and the default since v17) uses standalone components, which declare their own imports with no NgModule needed.

import { Component, ChangeDetectionStrategy, input, output, signal, computed } from '@angular/core';
import { DatePipe } from '@angular/common';

export interface Incident { id: number; title: string; severity: 'LOW'|'MEDIUM'|'HIGH'; reportedAt: string; }

@Component({
  selector: 'app-incident-list',
  standalone: true,                       // default (and can be omitted) from Angular v19
  imports: [DatePipe],
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
  template: `
    <input placeholder="Filter" (input)="filter.set($any($event.target).value)" />

    @if (filtered().length) {
      <ul>
        @for (inc of filtered(); track inc.id) {
          <li [class.high]="inc.severity === 'HIGH'" (click)="selected.emit(inc)">
            {{ inc.title }}: {{ inc.reportedAt | date:'short' }}
          </li>
        } @empty {
          <li>No incidents</li>
        }
      </ul>
    } @else {
      <p>No incidents match "{{ filter() }}"</p>
    }
  `,
  styles: [`.high { color: crimson; font-weight: 600; }`]
})
export class IncidentListComponent {
  incidents = input.required<Incident[]>();      // signal input (v17.1+)
  selected  = output<Incident>();                // output function (v17.3+)
  filter    = signal('');
  filtered  = computed(() =>
    this.incidents().filter(i => i.title.toLowerCase().includes(this.filter().toLowerCase())));
}

Classic (NgModule) equivalent, still common in existing codebases:

@Component({ selector: 'app-incident-list', templateUrl: './incident-list.component.html' })
export class IncidentListComponent {
  @Input() incidents: Incident[] = [];
  @Output() selected = new EventEmitter<Incident>();
}

@NgModule({
  declarations: [IncidentListComponent],        // components/directives/pipes owned by this module
  imports: [CommonModule, FormsModule],         // other modules needed by those templates
  exports: [IncidentListComponent],             // what other modules may use
  providers: [IncidentService]                  // module-level DI (prefer providedIn: 'root')
})
export class IncidentModule {}

Classic template syntax: <li *ngFor="let i of incidents; trackBy: trackById">, <p *ngIf="loading; else done">, [ngSwitch]. The new control flow (@if, @for, @switch, @defer) is built in, needs no import, makes track mandatory, and is faster. Run ng generate @angular/core:control-flow to migrate.

2. Data binding (four types)

Type Syntax Direction Example
Interpolation {{ expr }} Component → view {{ sensor.name }}
Property binding [prop]="expr" Component → view [disabled]="!form.valid", [class.active], [style.width.px]
Event binding (event)="handler()" View → component (click)="ack(alert)"
Two-way [(ngModel)]="x" or [(value)] Both Banana-in-a-box. With signals, use model() inputs (v17.2+)

Also: attribute binding [attr.aria-label] and template reference variables #searchBox.

3. Directives

  • Component: a directive with a template.
  • Structural: changes the DOM layout. Classic *ngIf, *ngFor, *ngSwitch; now mostly replaced by @if and @for.
  • Attribute: changes the appearance or behaviour of an element. Built-ins are ngClass and ngStyle; you can write your own:
@Directive({ selector: '[appSeverity]', standalone: true })
export class SeverityDirective {
  appSeverity = input<'LOW'|'MEDIUM'|'HIGH'>();
  private el = inject(ElementRef);
  constructor() {
    effect(() => {
      const colors = { LOW: '#2e7d32', MEDIUM: '#f9a825', HIGH: '#c62828' };
      this.el.nativeElement.style.borderLeft = `4px solid ${colors[this.appSeverity() ?? 'LOW']}`;
    });
  }
}
// <div [appSeverity]="alert.severity">...</div>

Host directives (hostDirectives) let you compose behaviours onto a component.

4. Pipes

Pipes transform values in templates. Built-in pipes: date, currency, decimal, percent, uppercase, json, async, keyvalue, slice.

@Pipe({ name: 'timeAgo', standalone: true })      // pure by default: re-runs only when the input reference changes
export class TimeAgoPipe implements PipeTransform {
  transform(iso: string): string {
    const mins = Math.floor((Date.now() - new Date(iso).getTime()) / 60000);
    return mins < 1 ? 'just now' : mins < 60 ? `${mins} min ago` : `${Math.floor(mins / 60)} h ago`;
  }
}

The async pipe subscribes to an Observable or Promise, unsubscribes automatically on destroy, and marks the component for check under OnPush.

5. Services and dependency injection

A service is a class holding reusable logic or state (API calls, caching, WebSocket connections). Angular's hierarchical injector creates instances and passes them in.

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })              // app-wide singleton, tree-shakable
export class IncidentService {
  private http = inject(HttpClient);             // inject() function (v14+); constructor injection also works
  private base = '/api/incidents';

  list(params: { page: number; size: number }) {
    return this.http.get<Page<Incident>>(this.base, { params: { ...params } });
  }
  acknowledge(id: number) {
    return this.http.patch<void>(`${this.base}/${id}/ack`, {});
  }
}
  • Injector hierarchy: environment/root injector, then route-level providers, then the element injector (component providers: [...] gives each component instance its own copy).
  • Tokens: InjectionToken<AppConfig>('APP_CONFIG') with { provide: APP_CONFIG, useValue: {...} }. Other provider types are useClass, useFactory and useExisting.
  • Resolution modifiers: inject(X, { optional: true, self: true, skipSelf: true, host: true }).

6. Routing and guards

// app.routes.ts
export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: 'login', loadComponent: () => import('./auth/login.component').then(m => m.LoginComponent) },
  {
    path: '',
    canActivate: [authGuard],
    children: [
      { path: 'dashboard', loadComponent: () => import('./dashboard/dashboard.component').then(m => m.DashboardComponent) },
      { path: 'incidents', loadChildren: () => import('./incidents/incident.routes').then(m => m.INCIDENT_ROUTES) },
      { path: 'admin', canMatch: [roleGuard('ADMIN')], loadComponent: () => import('./admin/admin.component').then(m => m.AdminComponent) },
      { path: 'incidents/:id', loadComponent: () => import('./incidents/detail.component').then(m => m.DetailComponent),
        resolve: { incident: incidentResolver } },
    ]
  },
  { path: '**', redirectTo: 'dashboard' }
];

// Functional guards (v15+; class-based guards are deprecated)
export const authGuard: CanActivateFn = () => {
  const auth = inject(AuthService);
  return auth.isLoggedIn() ? true : inject(Router).createUrlTree(['/login']);
};

export const roleGuard = (role: string): CanMatchFn => () => inject(AuthService).hasRole(role);
Guard Purpose
canActivate / canActivateChild Can the user enter this route or its children?
canMatch Should this route definition match at all? (Also prevents lazy-loading the chunk for unauthorised users.)
canDeactivate Can the user leave? (For example, unsaved form changes.)
resolve Prefetch data before activation

Read route parameters with inject(ActivatedRoute).paramMap, or bind them directly to inputs using withComponentInputBinding().

Security note: guards are a UX feature. The real authorisation is enforced on the Spring Boot side (Spring Security, @PreAuthorize).

7. HttpClient and interceptors

// Functional interceptor (v15+)
export const jwtInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => {
  const router = inject(Router);                 // call inject() synchronously, not inside the async callback
  const token = inject(AuthService).token();
  const authReq = token ? req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } }) : req;
  return next(authReq).pipe(
    catchError((err: HttpErrorResponse) => {
      if (err.status === 401) router.navigate(['/login']);   // or try a refresh-token flow
      return throwError(() => err);
    })
  );
};

// main.ts, standalone bootstrap
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, {
  providers: [
    provideRouter(routes, withComponentInputBinding()),
    provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([jwtInterceptor, loadingInterceptor, errorInterceptor])),
    provideAnimationsAsync(),
  ]
});

Classic version: a class implementing HttpInterceptor, registered with { provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS, useClass: JwtInterceptor, multi: true } in AppModule. Interceptors run in the order they are provided for requests, and in reverse order for responses.

Typical interceptors: JWT/auth header, global error toast, loading spinner, retry with backoff, caching, correlation-ID header (X-Correlation-Id) for tracing across microservices.

8. RxJS

Angular's HttpClient, Router events and forms valueChanges all expose Observables.

Operator Use
map, filter, tap Transform, filter, side effects
switchMap Cancel the previous inner request (search-as-you-type, route parameter changes)
mergeMap Run inner requests in parallel
concatMap Run inner requests in order, queued (ordered saves)
exhaustMap Ignore new triggers while one is running (prevents double-submitting login)
debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged Throttle user input
combineLatest, forkJoin, withLatestFrom Combine streams (forkJoin is like Promise.all)
catchError, retry({count, delay}) Error handling
takeUntilDestroyed() Auto-unsubscribe (v16+)
shareReplay(1) Cache and multicast 
search = new FormControl('', { nonNullable: true });
results$ = this.search.valueChanges.pipe(
  debounceTime(300),
  distinctUntilChanged(),
  filter(q => q.length >= 2),
  switchMap(q => this.api.searchSensors(q).pipe(catchError(() => of([]))))
);

Subjects: Subject (no initial value), BehaviorSubject (holds the current value; classic service state), ReplaySubject(n). Hot vs cold: HTTP Observables are cold, and each subscribe triggers a new request.

9. Signals (Angular 16+, the modern reactivity primitive)

count    = signal(0);                         // writable
double   = computed(() => this.count() * 2);  // derived, memoized, lazy
constructor() {
  effect(() => console.log('count changed', this.count()));  // side effects (logging, localStorage, manual DOM)
}
inc() { this.count.update(c => c + 1); }      // or .set(5)
  • Interop with RxJS: toSignal(obs$, { initialValue: [] }) and toObservable(sig) from @angular/core/rxjs-interop.
  • Newer APIs: input(), output(), model(), viewChild(), linkedSignal(), and resource()/httpResource() for async data. Check which are stable in your Angular version.
  • Why signals: fine-grained change tracking (Angular knows exactly which views depend on which signal), no manual subscriptions in templates, and they enable zoneless change detection.

10. Change detection

  • Default: Zone.js patches async APIs (events, timers, XHR). After any of them, Angular checks the whole component tree from top to bottom.
  • OnPush: a component is checked only when (a) an @Input reference changes, (b) an event fires inside it, (c) the async pipe emits or a signal it reads changes, or (d) markForCheck() is called. You must use immutable updates: this.items = [...this.items, x], not push.
  • Zoneless: provideZonelessChangeDetection() drops Zone.js and relies on signals, the async pipe and events. It became stable in v20 and is the default for new projects in recent versions.
  • Tools: ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck() / detectChanges(), plus track in @for to avoid re-rendering whole lists.
  • A real-time dashboard receiving many WebSocket messages per second must use OnPush or signals, and often buffers or throttles updates (bufferTime(500)).

11. Lifecycle hooks (in order)

Hook When / use
constructor DI only; keep it light
ngOnChanges(changes) Before ngOnInit and whenever an @Input reference changes
ngOnInit Once, after the first inputs are set. Load data and set up subscriptions.
ngDoCheck Every change-detection run (custom change detection; use rarely)
ngAfterContentInit / ngAfterContentChecked Projected <ng-content> is ready or checked
ngAfterViewInit / ngAfterViewChecked The component's view and children are ready. Access @ViewChild (for example, initialise a Leaflet map or chart here).
ngOnDestroy Clean up: unsubscribe, close the WebSocket, clear intervals. DestroyRef.onDestroy() and takeUntilDestroyed() are the modern helpers.

Newer: afterNextRender() and afterRender()/afterEveryRender() are browser-only DOM hooks, which matter for SSR-safe third-party libraries.

12. Forms: reactive vs template-driven

Template-driven Reactive
Module/imports FormsModule ReactiveFormsModule
Model defined in The template (ngModel) The component class (FormGroup/FormControl)
Data flow Asynchronous, mutable Synchronous, explicit, immutable-friendly
Validation Directives (required, minlength) Functions (Validators.required, custom/async validators)
Dynamic fields Awkward FormArray makes it easy
Testing Harder (needs the DOM) Easy (pure class)
Best for Simple forms (login, search) Complex forms (incident creation with dynamic checklists) 
// Reactive form with typed forms (v14+)
private fb = inject(NonNullableFormBuilder);
form = this.fb.group({
  title:    ['', [Validators.required, Validators.maxLength(120)]],
  severity: ['MEDIUM' as 'LOW'|'MEDIUM'|'HIGH', Validators.required],
  location: this.fb.group({ lat: [0, Validators.required], lng: [0, Validators.required] }),
  tags:     this.fb.array<string>([])
});
submit() {
  if (this.form.invalid) { this.form.markAllAsTouched(); return; }
  this.incidentService.create(this.form.getRawValue()).subscribe();
}
<form [formGroup]="form" (ngSubmit)="submit()">
  <input formControlName="title" />
  @if (form.controls.title.touched && form.controls.title.hasError('required')) {
    <small class="error">Title is required</small>
  }
  <button [disabled]="form.invalid">Save</button>
</form>
<!-- Template-driven -->
<form #f="ngForm" (ngSubmit)="login(f.value)">
  <input name="username" ngModel required />
  <input name="password" type="password" ngModel required minlength="8" />
  <button [disabled]="f.invalid">Login</button>
</form>

(Signal-based forms are arriving in newer versions as an experimental API. Mention that only if asked.)

Other features worth mentioning

  • @defer: lazy-load part of a template (@defer (on viewport) { <heavy-chart/> } @placeholder { ... }).
  • SSR and hydration (@angular/ssr).
  • The CLI: ng new, ng g c, ng build (esbuild/Vite since v17), ng test, ng update.
  • Environments and file replacement.
  • Content projection with <ng-content select="...">.
  • ViewEncapsulation (Emulated, None or ShadowDom).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Angular vs AngularJS? AngularJS (1.x) is JavaScript with MVC, $scope and digest cycles, and is end-of-life. Angular (2+) is TypeScript, components, RxJS and AOT compilation, and a complete rewrite.
  • What is AOT? Ahead-of-time compilation turns templates into JavaScript at build time, which gives faster startup, earlier template error detection, and smaller bundles. It is the default.
  • Observable vs Promise? An Observable is lazy, can emit many values, can be cancelled (unsubscribed), and has operators. A Promise is eager, resolves once, and cannot be cancelled.
  • How do you share data between components? Parent to child with input()/@Input, child to parent with output()/@Output, and between unrelated components with a shared service holding a signal or BehaviorSubject (or NgRx/SignalStore for large apps).

Example components a Smart City dashboard would have (talking points with code)

These are illustrations of typical components. Describe only the ones you actually built, in your own project's terms.

1. Map view (incidents and sensors on a map)

@Component({
  selector: 'app-city-map',
  standalone: true,
  template: `<div #mapEl class="map"></div>`,
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
})
export class CityMapComponent {
  incidents = input<Incident[]>([]);
  private mapEl = viewChild.required<ElementRef<HTMLDivElement>>('mapEl');
  private map?: L.Map;
  private layer = L.layerGroup();

  constructor() {
    afterNextRender(() => {                       // DOM is ready (SSR-safe)
      this.map = L.map(this.mapEl().nativeElement).setView([12.97, 77.59], 12);
      L.tileLayer('https://{s}.tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png').addTo(this.map);
      this.layer.addTo(this.map);
    });
    effect(() => {                                // re-draw markers when the input signal changes
      const list = this.incidents();
      this.layer.clearLayers();
      list.forEach(i => L.marker([i.lat, i.lng]).bindPopup(i.title).addTo(this.layer));
    });
    inject(DestroyRef).onDestroy(() => this.map?.remove());
  }
}

Talking points: marker clustering for thousands of devices, GeoJSON layers for zones/wards, a bounding-box query to fetch only the visible area, and running the map outside Angular's zone (NgZone.runOutsideAngular) to avoid excessive change detection.

2. Live alert feed over WebSocket (STOMP with Spring)

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class AlertStreamService {
  private auth = inject(AuthService);                    // inject() must run in an injection context (field initialiser)
  private client = new Client({                          // @stomp/stompjs
    brokerURL: 'wss://[host]/ws',
    reconnectDelay: 5000,
    beforeConnect: () => { this.client.connectHeaders = { Authorization: `Bearer ${this.auth.token()}` }; }
  });
  private _alerts = signal<Alert[]>([]);
  readonly alerts = this._alerts.asReadonly();
  readonly highCount = computed(() => this._alerts().filter(a => a.severity === 'HIGH').length);

  connect() {
    this.client.onConnect = () =>
      this.client.subscribe('/topic/alerts', msg => {
        const alert: Alert = JSON.parse(msg.body);
        this._alerts.update(list => [alert, ...list].slice(0, 200));   // cap the list size
      });
    this.client.activate();
  }
  disconnect() { this.client.deactivate(); }
}

Back-end side: Spring @EnableWebSocketMessageBroker, with SimpMessagingTemplate.convertAndSend("/topic/alerts", alert) fed by a Kafka consumer. Talking points: reconnect and backoff, deduplication by alert ID, throttling UI updates, audible or visual escalation for HIGH severity, and acknowledging alerts through REST.

3. Charts (KPI widgets)

These show incidents per hour, average response time, and sensor values over time, built with [ngx-charts / Chart.js via ng2-charts / ECharts / Highcharts]. Talking points: time-window selectors, server-side aggregation (do not send raw readings to the browser), and @defer (on viewport) for heavy charts.

4. Role-based menus

export const MENU: MenuItem[] = [
  { label: 'Dashboard', route: '/dashboard', roles: ['OPERATOR', 'SUPERVISOR', 'ADMIN'] },
  { label: 'Incidents', route: '/incidents', roles: ['OPERATOR', 'SUPERVISOR'] },
  { label: 'Reports',   route: '/reports',   roles: ['SUPERVISOR', 'ADMIN'] },
  { label: 'User Admin', route: '/admin',    roles: ['ADMIN'] },
];

@Component({
  selector: 'app-side-nav', standalone: true, imports: [RouterLink, RouterLinkActive],
  template: `
    @for (item of visibleMenu(); track item.route) {
      <a [routerLink]="item.route" routerLinkActive="active">{{ item.label }}</a>
    }`
})
export class SideNavComponent {
  private auth = inject(AuthService);
  visibleMenu = computed(() => MENU.filter(m => m.roles.some(r => this.auth.roles().includes(r))));
}

Roles come from JWT claims. The same roles protect routes (canMatch) and, most importantly, the APIs (Spring Security).

5. JWT interceptor: see E11 §7. Mention attaching the token, handling 401 with a refresh token (queueing concurrent requests during the refresh), and logging out on refresh failure.

Other typical components: a paginated and filterable incident grid (server-side paging, see E8), an incident detail and workflow timeline, SOP checklists, a CCTV camera tile grid, a device health/status board, a notifications bell, and dark/light themes for control-room screens.

Delivery tips

  • Lead with business context, then the components, then one hard problem you solved.
  • Quantify: "[N] screens", "[N] reusable components", "load time from [X]s to [Y]s", "[N] alerts per minute rendered smoothly".
  • Expect deep-dive follow-ups on anything you mention: OnPush, the interceptor order, how you unsubscribe, how token refresh works.

What interviewers look for: real ownership (not "we did"), understanding of why a choice was made, awareness of performance and security, and the ability to connect the UI to back-end APIs end to end.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you avoid memory leaks? Use the async pipe or signals, takeUntilDestroyed(), close WebSockets and clear intervals in ngOnDestroy/DestroyRef.
  • How do you handle thousands of map markers? Clustering, viewport-based fetching, canvas renderers, and updating outside the zone.
  • Where do you keep the JWT? In memory or a short-lived store, with a refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie if the backend supports it. Avoid localStorage for long-lived tokens because of XSS risk.
  • How do you test a component? TestBed with provideHttpClientTesting()/HttpTestingController, plus mocked services and harnesses for Material components.
E13 Basic JavaScript concepts
  • Types: the primitives are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol. Everything else is an object, including arrays and functions. typeof null === 'object' is a historical quirk.
  • Closures: a function remembers the variables of the scope where it was defined, even after that scope has returned. Closures are used for private state, factories and memoisation.
  • this: set by how a function is called. As an object method it is the object. In a plain call it is undefined in strict mode, or window otherwise. call/apply/bind set it explicitly. Arrow functions don't have their own this and inherit it lexically.
  • Promises / async-await: a Promise is a future value that is pending, fulfilled or rejected. async/await is syntactic sugar over promises; use try/catch for errors and Promise.all to run work in parallel.
  • Event loop: JS runs on a single thread with a call stack. When the stack is empty, all microtasks run first (promise callbacks), then the next macrotask (setTimeout, I/O). So setTimeout(fn,0) runs after Promise.resolve().then(fn).
  • == vs ===: == coerces types ('5' == 5 is true, null == undefined is true). === compares value and type with no coercion. Default to ===.

1. Data types

  • Primitives (7): string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, null. They are immutable and copied by value.
  • Object (reference) types: objects, arrays, functions, Date, Map, Set and so on. They are copied by reference.
typeof 42          // "number"
typeof 10n         // "bigint"
typeof 'hi'        // "string"
typeof undefined   // "undefined"
typeof null        // "object"   ← a historical bug
typeof []          // "object"   → use Array.isArray([]) === true
typeof function(){}// "function"
typeof Symbol()    // "symbol"

let a = { x: 1 }; let b = a; b.x = 2;
console.log(a.x);  // 2 (same reference)
let c = structuredClone(a);   // deep copy; { ...a } is only a shallow copy

Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including [], {} and '0'.

2. Scope

  • Global, function and block scope. let and const are block-scoped; var is function-scoped (see E14).
  • Lexical scope: a function sees variables where it is defined, not where it is called.
const city = 'Bengaluru';
function outer() {
  const zone = 'North';
  function inner() { return `${city}-${zone}`; }   // looks up the scope chain
  return inner();
}
outer(); // "Bengaluru-North"

3. Closures

A closure is a function bundled with references to its outer variables, which stay alive after the outer function returns.

function createCounter() {
  let count = 0;                       // private state
  return {
    inc: () => ++count,
    get: () => count
  };
}
const c1 = createCounter();
c1.inc(); c1.inc();
console.log(c1.get());   // 2
console.log(c1.count);   // undefined (truly private)

Uses: data privacy and the module pattern, function factories, memoization, debounce, event handlers, and RxJS operators.

function debounce(fn, ms) {
  let t;
  return (...args) => { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms); };
}

4. this binding (determined by how a function is called)

Call style this is
obj.method() obj (implicit binding)
fn() plain call undefined in strict mode or modules; globalThis in sloppy mode
fn.call(o, a) / fn.apply(o, [a]) / fn.bind(o) o (explicit binding)
new Fn() The newly created object
Arrow function Lexical: inherited from the enclosing scope; cannot be rebound 
const sensor = {
  name: 'AQI-01',
  regular() { return this.name; },
  arrow: () => this?.name,                        // `this` comes from module scope, so undefined
  delayed() { setTimeout(() => console.log(this.name), 0); }   // the arrow keeps the outer `this`
};
sensor.regular();          // "AQI-01"
sensor.arrow();            // undefined
const f = sensor.regular;
f();                       // TypeError in strict mode (this is undefined); undefined in sloppy mode
f.call({ name: 'X' });     // "X"
sensor.delayed();          // "AQI-01"

This is why Angular templates and RxJS callbacks commonly use arrow functions: they keep the component's this.

5. Prototypes and inheritance

Every object has an internal [[Prototype]] link. Property lookup walks the prototype chain. class is syntactic sugar over prototypes.

function Device(id) { this.id = id; }
Device.prototype.describe = function () { return `Device ${this.id}`; };

const d = new Device(7);
d.describe();                                     // "Device 7" (found on Device.prototype)
Object.getPrototypeOf(d) === Device.prototype;    // true
d.hasOwnProperty('describe');                     // false

class Camera extends Device {
  constructor(id, url) { super(id); this.url = url; }
  describe() { return `${super.describe()} (camera)`; }
}
new Camera(9, 'rtsp://...').describe();           // "Device 9 (camera)"

6. Promises and async/await

function fetchSensor(id) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => (id > 0 ? resolve({ id, value: 42 }) : reject(new Error('bad id'))), 100));
}

fetchSensor(1)
  .then(s => s.value)
  .then(v => console.log(v))       // 42
  .catch(e => console.error(e))
  .finally(() => console.log('done'));

async function load() {
  try {
    const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetchSensor(1), fetchSensor(2)]);   // parallel
    return a.value + b.value;
  } catch (e) {
    console.error(e.message);
  }
}
Combinator Resolves when Rejects when
Promise.all All fulfil Any rejects (fails fast)
Promise.allSettled All settle Never; returns {status, value/reason} for each
Promise.race The first one settles The first one settles with a rejection
Promise.any The first one fulfils All reject (AggregateError)

Pitfall: await inside a for loop runs requests sequentially. Use Promise.all(items.map(fetch)) for parallel calls.

7. The event loop: microtasks vs macrotasks

JavaScript runs on a single thread. The event loop works like this:

  1. Run the current synchronous code (the call stack).
  2. Drain all microtasks: Promise .then/catch/finally, await continuations, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver.
  3. Render (in browsers), if needed.
  4. Take one macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events, MessageChannel), then go back to step 2.
console.log('1: sync');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2: timeout (macrotask)'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3: promise (microtask)'));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('4: queueMicrotask'));
(async () => {
  console.log('5: async fn body runs sync');
  await null;
  console.log('6: after await (microtask)');
})();
console.log('7: sync');

Output:

1: sync
5: async fn body runs sync
7: sync
3: promise (microtask)
4: queueMicrotask
6: after await (microtask)
2: timeout (macrotask)

Why: the synchronous lines run first (1, 5, 7). Then all microtasks run in the order they were queued (3, 4, 6). Then the macrotask runs (2). An endless stream of microtasks can starve rendering and timers. Node.js also has process.nextTick, which runs before promise microtasks.

8. == vs ===

  • === is strict equality: no type coercion. Use it by default.
  • == is loose equality: it coerces types first.
0 == ''            // true   ('' → 0)
0 === ''           // false
'5' == 5           // true
null == undefined  // true   (the one useful case: x == null checks both)
null === undefined // false
null == 0          // false
[] == false        // true   ([] → '' → 0, false → 0)
NaN == NaN         // false  → use Number.isNaN(x)
Object.is(NaN, NaN)// true;  Object.is(0, -0) → false
{} === {}          // false  (different references)

9. Spread, rest and destructuring

// Spread: expand
const base = { severity: 'LOW', status: 'OPEN' };
const incident = { ...base, id: 1, severity: 'HIGH' };   // later keys win → severity 'HIGH'
const all = [...[1, 2], ...[3, 4]];                      // [1,2,3,4]
Math.max(...[3, 9, 2]);                                   // 9

// Rest: collect
function log(level, ...msgs) { console.log(level, msgs); }
log('INFO', 'a', 'b');                                    // INFO ['a','b']
const { id, ...rest } = incident;                         // rest = {severity:'HIGH', status:'OPEN'}

// Destructuring with defaults and renaming
const { status: st = 'NEW', location: { lat = 0 } = {} } = incident;   // st='OPEN', lat=0
const [first, , third = 'x'] = ['a', 'b'];                // first='a', third='x'
[a1, b1] = [b1, a1];                                      // swap

// Optional chaining and nullish coalescing
const zone = incident.location?.zone ?? 'Unknown';        // ?? replaces only null/undefined, not 0 or ''

Other quick ones: map/filter/reduce; template literals; modules (import/export); Map/Set; immutability with Object.freeze (shallow); JSON.parse/JSON.stringify.

Likely follow-ups:

  • What does [1,2,3].map(parseInt) return? [1, NaN, NaN], because map passes (value, index) and parseInt treats the index as the radix.
  • Shallow vs deep copy? Spread and Object.assign copy only the top level. structuredClone copies deeply (but not functions).
  • Arrow vs regular function? An arrow has no own this, arguments or prototype, and cannot be used with new.
  • What is event delegation? One listener on a parent handles events from its children via bubbling and event.target.
E14 var, let, const and hoisting (TDZ)
Scope Re-declare Re-assign Hoisted
var function yes yes yes, initialised to undefined
let block no yes yes, but stays in the TDZ until its declaration line
const block no no (object contents can still change) yes, but stays in the TDZ 
console.log(a);   // undefined   (var is hoisted and initialised)
var a = 1;

console.log(b);   // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization (TDZ)
let b = 2;

const c = { x: 1 };
c.x = 2;          // OK: the object itself is mutable
// c = {};        // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));  // 3 3 3
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j));  // 0 1 2 (new binding per iteration)

sayHi();          // "hi": function declarations are fully hoisted
function sayHi() { console.log('hi'); }

Comparison

var let const
Scope Function (or global) Block {} Block
Hoisted? Yes, initialised to undefined Yes, but uninitialised (TDZ) Yes, uninitialised (TDZ)
Access before declaration undefined ReferenceError ReferenceError
Redeclare in the same scope Allowed SyntaxError SyntaxError
Reassign Yes Yes No (TypeError)
Must initialise at declaration No No Yes
Creates a property on window (global scope) Yes No No

Hoisting

During the creation phase of each scope, JavaScript registers declarations before running code. The code is not physically moved.

console.log(a);   // undefined   (var is hoisted and initialised to undefined)
var a = 10;
console.log(a);   // 10

console.log(b);   // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
let b = 20;

console.log(c);   // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'c' before initialization
const c = 30;

console.log(d);   // ReferenceError: d is not defined   (never declared, a different message)

Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)

The TDZ is the period from the start of the block until the let/const declaration line runs.

let x = 'outer';
{
  // TDZ for the inner x starts here. It shadows the outer x even before its declaration.
  console.log(x);    // ReferenceError (not 'outer'!)
  let x = 'inner';
}

typeof undeclaredVar;   // "undefined" (safe)
typeof y;               // ReferenceError: y is in its TDZ
let y = 1;

function f(p = q, q = 1) {}   // f() → ReferenceError: q is accessed in its TDZ (default params are evaluated left to right)

Function scope vs block scope

function test() {
  if (true) {
    var v = 'var';
    let l = 'let';
    const k = 'const';
  }
  console.log(v);   // "var"  (var ignores the block)
  console.log(l);   // ReferenceError: l is not defined
}

Redeclaration

var n = 1;
var n = 2;        // fine, silently overwrites (a source of bugs)

let m = 1;
let m = 2;        // SyntaxError: Identifier 'm' has already been declared

let s = 1;
{ let s = 2; }    // fine: a different block, so this is shadowing, not redeclaration

const with objects and arrays

const makes the binding immutable, not the value.

const cfg = { refreshMs: 5000 };
cfg.refreshMs = 1000;      // allowed (mutating the object)
cfg = {};                  // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

const ids = [1, 2];
ids.push(3);               // allowed → [1,2,3]

const frozen = Object.freeze({ a: 1, nested: { b: 2 } });
frozen.a = 99;             // ignored (TypeError in strict mode)
frozen.nested.b = 99;      // allowed: freeze is SHALLOW

The classic loop closure question

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log('var:', i), 0);
}
// var: 3
// var: 3
// var: 3

for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log('let:', j), 0);
}
// let: 0
// let: 1
// let: 2

Why: var i is one function-scoped variable shared by all callbacks. By the time the timeouts run (macrotasks, after the loop finishes), i is 3. let j creates a new binding for each iteration, so each closure captures its own value.

Pre-ES6 fixes, which interviewers sometimes ask for:

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  (function (k) { setTimeout(() => console.log(k), 0); })(i);   // IIFE captures a copy
}
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(console.log, 0, i);                                 // pass it as a setTimeout argument
}

Function declarations vs function expressions

greet();                         // "hello": declarations are fully hoisted (name AND body)
function greet() { console.log('hello'); }

sayHi();                         // TypeError: sayHi is not a function (var hoisted as undefined)
var sayHi = function () { console.log('hi'); };

sayBye();                        // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'sayBye' before initialization (TDZ)
const sayBye = () => console.log('bye');

// Classes are hoisted like let (TDZ)
new Foo();                       // ReferenceError
class Foo {}

Precedence quiz:

console.log(typeof foo);   // "function"
var foo = 1;
function foo() {}
console.log(typeof foo);   // "number"

Why: during creation, the function declaration initialises foo, and the var foo declaration is ignored because the name already exists. At runtime, foo = 1 reassigns it.

Best practice

Use const by default, let when you must reassign, and never var in modern code. ESLint has the no-var and prefer-const rules for this, and they are commonly enabled in Angular projects.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Are let and const hoisted? Yes, they are hoisted but not initialised. That is exactly what the TDZ is.
  • What does this print: let a = 1; { console.log(a); let a = 2; }? A ReferenceError, because the inner a is in its TDZ and shadows the outer one.
  • Why does global var matter? var x at the top level becomes window.x and can clash with other scripts. let and const live in a separate declarative scope.

It is not a statement of what you did. Keep only what is true for you, and use numbers you can defend. Interviewers routinely ask "how exactly?" about any claim.

Tips

  • Don't recite your résumé or your personal history (hometown, hobbies) unless asked. Keep it professional.
  • End with a hook. Your last sentence should invite the interviewer to ask about your strongest project.
  • Tailor the proof points to the job description. If they stress microservices, lead with that achievement.
  • Practise out loud with a timer. Aim for about 90 seconds and avoid filler words.
  • Say "I" for your own contributions and "we" for team outcomes. Be honest about which is which.
  • Do not disclose confidential client names, city contracts or internal metrics if your NDA forbids it. Say "a large Indian city deployment" instead.

What interviewers look for: clarity, relevance to the role, evidence of ownership and growth, communication skill, and whether your story matches your résumé.

Describe what your project actually does. The flow below is a typical shape to adapt.

"Our system is [microservices / modular monolith]. The Angular SPA calls an API Gateway ([Spring Cloud Gateway / NGINX]). Typical Spring Boot service layout

incident-service/
 └─ src/main/java/com/trinity/incident/
     ├─ controller/     REST endpoints (@RestController)
     ├─ service/        business logic (interfaces + impl)
     ├─ repository/     Spring Data JPA repositories
     ├─ entity/         JPA entities
     ├─ dto/            request/response DTOs, mapper/ (MapStruct)
     ├─ config/         security, Kafka, Swagger, CORS config
     ├─ client/         Feign/WebClient clients to other services
     ├─ messaging/      Kafka producers/consumers
     ├─ exception/      custom exceptions + @RestControllerAdvice
     └─ util/
 └─ src/main/resources/ application.yml, db/migration (Flyway)
 └─ src/test/java/       unit + integration tests

Typical Angular layout

src/app/
 ├─ core/        singleton services, interceptors, guards, auth
 ├─ shared/      reusable components, pipes, directives, models
 ├─ features/    incident/, devices/, dashboard/, reports/ (lazy-loaded)
 ├─ layout/      header, sidebar, shell
 └─ app.routes.ts / app.config.ts
src/environments/  environment.ts, environment.prod.ts

Template answer

"At a high level we follow [microservices / a modular monolith moving to microservices]. The Angular SPA talks to an API gateway ([Spring Cloud Gateway / Nginx / Kong]), which routes to the Spring Boot services. Services register in [Eureka / Kubernetes service discovery] and pull configuration from [Spring Cloud Config / ConfigMaps]. Synchronous calls use [REST with OpenFeign/WebClient]. Asynchronous flows use [Kafka]. Each service owns its database/schema. Cross-cutting pieces include [Keycloak/auth-service] for auth, [ELK/EFK] for logs, [Prometheus + Grafana] for metrics, and [Zipkin/Jaeger/OpenTelemetry] for tracing. Inside each service we use a layered architecture: controller → service → repository, with DTOs and mappers at the boundaries."

 [Angular SPA] ──HTTPS/WSS──► [API Gateway] ──► [auth-service]
                                   │
               ┌───────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
               ▼                   ▼                     ▼
       [incident-service]  [device-service]     [notification-service]
               │   ▲               │                     ▲
               ▼   │               ▼                     │
             [DB]  └──────── [Kafka topics] ─────────────┘
                                   ▲
                       [integration/adapters] ◄── IoT gateways / vendor APIs

Typical Spring Boot service layout (layered, package-by-layer within a feature)

incident-service/
├── pom.xml (or build.gradle)
├── Dockerfile
├── src/main/java/com/[company]/[product]/incident/
│   ├── IncidentServiceApplication.java
│   ├── config/                 # SecurityConfig, KafkaConfig, OpenApiConfig, WebSocketConfig, CorsConfig
│   ├── controller/             # @RestController: IncidentController (thin; validation + mapping only)
│   ├── dto/                    # request/response records: CreateIncidentRequest, IncidentResponse
│   ├── mapper/                 # MapStruct mappers: IncidentMapper
│   ├── service/                # interfaces + impl: IncidentService, IncidentServiceImpl (business logic, @Transactional)
│   ├── repository/             # Spring Data JPA: IncidentRepository, specifications/custom queries
│   ├── entity/  (or domain/)   # @Entity classes: Incident, IncidentStatus (enum), AuditableEntity (base)
│   ├── messaging/              # Kafka producers/consumers: IncidentEventPublisher, SensorAlertListener
│   ├── client/                 # Feign/WebClient clients to other services or third parties
│   ├── exception/              # custom exceptions + GlobalExceptionHandler (@RestControllerAdvice)
│   ├── security/               # JWT filter, permission evaluators
│   ├── scheduler/              # @Scheduled jobs (SLA breach checks, data pulls)
│   └── util/                   # small helpers/constants (keep minimal)
├── src/main/resources/
│   ├── application.yml         # + application-dev.yml / -qa.yml / -prod.yml (profiles)
│   ├── db/migration/           # Flyway: V1__init.sql, V2__add_incident_priority.sql
│   └── logback-spring.xml
└── src/test/java/...           # unit tests (Mockito), slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest), Testcontainers ITs

Alternatives to mention: package-by-feature (incident/, assignment/, sop/, each with its own controller, service and repository), or hexagonal / ports & adapters (domain/, application/, adapters/in/web, adapters/out/persistence). Say which one your project uses and why. Shared code (common DTOs, exception model, security utilities) usually lives in a common library JAR, which should be kept small to avoid coupling.

Typical Angular layout (feature-folder, standalone)

src/
├── main.ts                      # bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig)
├── app/
│   ├── app.config.ts            # provideRouter, provideHttpClient(withInterceptors(...))
│   ├── app.routes.ts            # top-level lazy routes
│   ├── core/                    # singletons, loaded once
│   │   ├── auth/                # auth.service.ts, auth.guard.ts, role.guard.ts
│   │   ├── interceptors/        # jwt.interceptor.ts, error.interceptor.ts, loading.interceptor.ts
│   │   ├── services/            # websocket.service.ts, notification.service.ts
│   │   └── layout/              # shell, header, side-nav (role-based menu)
│   ├── shared/                  # reusable, stateless building blocks
│   │   ├── components/          # data-table, confirm-dialog, map-widget, kpi-card
│   │   ├── directives/          # has-role.directive.ts, severity.directive.ts
│   │   ├── pipes/               # time-ago.pipe.ts
│   │   └── models/              # shared interfaces / enums
│   └── features/                # one folder per business feature, lazy loaded
│       ├── dashboard/
│       ├── incidents/
│       │   ├── incident.routes.ts
│       │   ├── incident-list/   # .ts / .html / .scss / .spec.ts
│       │   ├── incident-detail/
│       │   ├── incident-form/
│       │   └── data-access/     # incident.service.ts, incident.store.ts (signals/NgRx)
│       ├── devices/
│       ├── reports/
│       └── admin/
├── environments/                # environment.ts, environment.prod.ts (API base URLs; no secrets!)
└── assets/                      # icons, map styles, i18n json

Classic NgModule apps follow the same idea with CoreModule (imported once), SharedModule, and lazy-loaded FeatureModules using loadChildren.

Delivery tips

  • Explain why: "Each service owns its data so teams can deploy independently", "Kafka decouples the device ingestion rate from processing", "a thin controller keeps business logic testable".
  • Mention conventions: DTOs never expose entities, a global exception handler, consistent API error format, and versioned APIs (/api/v1).
  • Be ready to discuss trade-offs and pain points: distributed transactions, shared libraries, and the cost of local development with many services.

What interviewers look for: whether you know the structure beyond your own folder, separation of concerns, the reasoning behind decisions, and familiarity with cross-cutting concerns (security, configuration, observability).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why use DTOs instead of returning entities? To decouple the API contract from the schema, avoid lazy-loading and serialisation issues, prevent over-posting, and allow API versioning.
  • Package-by-layer vs package-by-feature? By-layer is simple for small services. By-feature scales better, keeps related code together, and allows package-private encapsulation.
  • Where does validation happen? Format and required checks use Bean Validation on DTOs at the controller. Business rules belong in the service layer. Integrity is enforced by DB constraints.
  • How do the services share code? Through a small versioned common library for DTOs and errors. Avoid sharing domain entities between services.
